mem.t: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”

sat.t: Family Day: The Little Things Celebration Party
sat.d: Together find the “little things” worth celebrating this week: learning to tie shoelaces, bravely visiting the dentist, Mom finally getting to bed early one night, Grandpa's flowers blooming. Write each one on a slip of paper and stick it on the wall as a “celebration wall.” Prepare simple snacks or homemade drinks. As each slip is read out, everyone claps and cheers, and the person being celebrated can wear a paper crown. At the end read Psalm 118:24 together and thank God for every little thing this week.

sun: Whose mood has been affecting the “temperature” of your home most lately? Are you the thermometer or the thermostat?
Was there a moment this week when things were not going well, yet you experienced “rejoicing in the Lord”?
How can you bring the celebration and thankfulness of your home to a family in your group who has had a very hard time lately? Which small habit of joy do you want to keep up next week?

lessons.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
lessons.theme: The source of joy is the Lord, not whether my children obey

v: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Be still. You don't have to force a smile. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you know how I feel today. I won't depend on my circumstances; I come to depend on you.” Let his presence slowly shine into your heart like the morning light.
teach: When Paul wrote Philippians he was in prison, his future uncertain, and some were even taking the chance to attack him. Yet this book is called the “letter of joy.” He says, “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’” He says it twice, as if he knew the readers would answer, “Paul, you don't understand my situation.” He did understand, because he wrote from the worst of situations. This joy is not a greenhouse flower; it grows out of cracks in the rock.

For many parents, joy has a conditional switch. When the children behave, there is sunshine in the home; when they fuss, do badly at school or drag their feet over homework, the whole house fills with dark clouds. So children learn one thing: Mom and Dad's mood depends on me to keep it up. That is far too heavy a burden for a child. Paul's key words are “in the Lord.” The plug for joy is not plugged into our children but into the Lord. When the plug is in the right place, even if the child acts up today, the light will not go out.

This does not mean parents should pretend to be happy. Scripture also speaks of “a time to weep, and a time to laugh,” and sadness and weariness can be brought to God. Joy is not the absence of tears; it is a deeper foundation beneath the tears: the Lord is at hand, and he reigns. Paul goes on to say that in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, we make our requests known to God, and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard our hearts. If you have been low for a long time, can't get out of bed, or have lost hope, please find a doctor, a counselor and a pastor to walk with you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, not on others, and not on circumstances. When parents build their joy on their children's performance, they let the children rule the home; when parents rejoice in the Lord, they let Jesus reign. Living from the heart by the Spirit brings joy; living from the head by yourself brings worry.
q: Who is God? — God is the Lord who is near, who reigns over everything, and who gives peace beyond understanding.
Who am I? — Whose hand is my joy switch most often in: my child's, my spouse's, my work's, or the Lord's?
How should I respond? — When something upsets me today, how will I turn it into prayer and thanksgiving?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, on the very night he was betrayed, Jesus said to his disciples, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” The cross was right before him, yet he spoke of joy, because his joy was rooted in his relationship with the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that my joy is often led around by my children's performance: if they behave I am glad, and if they fuss I am gloomy all day. Please plug my joy back into you. When I am troubled, remind me to tell you everything with prayer and thanksgiving. Let my children see on my face the joy that comes from the Lord. Amen.
acts: Whenever you feel irritable today, stop and say a word of thanks before you deal with the matter.
Write Philippians 4:4 on a sticky note and put it in the kitchen or by the front door.
When your child comes home, greet them first with a smile and the words, “It's so good to see you.”
lessons.noon: “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’” — Lord, right now I don't depend on my circumstances; I rejoice in you.

fam.key: We rejoice in Jesus always.

lamb.do: Play peek-a-boo with your child: cover your face with your hands, then open them and say with a smile, “Found you!” Repeat several times and let them giggle.
lamb.say: You're laughing! Seeing you makes Mommy so happy, and God is happy too.

sprout.story: It was a rainy day and Xiaoyou couldn't go to the park. He pouted and was very unhappy. Mommy said, “Let's see what we can play on a rainy day!” They put on their rain boots and splashed on the balcony, listened to the raindrops on the window, and folded a paper boat. Xiaoyou laughed and said, “Rainy days are fun too!” Mommy said, “Because Jesus is with us, we can be joyful in any weather.”
sprout.ask: What made you happy today?
sprout.do: Sing a joyful song together as a family, clapping and jumping as you sing.

soldier.story: Paul and Silas were preaching the good news when they were beaten many times and thrown into prison, with their feet locked in stocks. If it were you, you would probably cry or get angry. But the Bible says that about midnight they were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening! Later Paul wrote to his friends, “Rejoice in the Lord always!” His joy wasn't because his days were going well, but because he knew Jesus was always with him.
ask: What do you think is the difference between being “happy” and having “joy”?
Is there something that hasn't gone well lately in which you could try to find joy?
soldier.do: Every night before bed this week, each person says one thing: “Today, although..., I'm still thankful for...”

youth.talk: Recently we've noticed that the mood at home often follows our moods: if work goes well we come home relaxed, and if it doesn't, even your talking sounds too noisy. That isn't fair. It is as if you were responsible for making us happy. Paul was in prison and still said to rejoice in the Lord always. What we want to learn is not to pretend to be happy, but to have a place deeper than our moods where we can stand firm.
ask: Whose mood do you think affects the atmosphere of our home most?
Do you think a Christian can be sad or angry? Does that conflict with joy?
youth.do: Parents honestly share one thing that upset them this week and how they gave it to God, and invite their child to share one as well.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for always being with us. Whether it rains or shines, please fill our home with joy. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Thermometer or Thermostat?
lessons.theme: A parent's face sets the temperature of the home

v: A cheerful heart makes good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.
A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but an aching heart breaks the spirit.

lessons.still: Think back to this morning or last night. When your family saw you, what was the expression on your face? There is no need to judge, only to look honestly. Ask the Holy Spirit to show you how much weight your face carries in your home.
teach: A thermometer and a thermostat look alike, but their functions are opposite. A thermometer only reflects the environment: when the room gets hot it goes up, and when the room gets cold it goes down. A thermostat can set a temperature: however cold the room gets, it switches on the heating and brings the room back to the setting. Many parents are the thermometers of their homes: when the children are noisy we get tense, when they cry we get irritated, when they talk back we flare up. As a result, the temperature of the home is really being set by the smallest child.

Proverbs says, “A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but an aching heart breaks the spirit.” And, “A cheerful heart makes good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.” A parent's face is the first weather forecast a child reads each day. When a child walks in from school, whether the first thing they see is a smile or a frown often decides whether they will talk to you at all. The expression on our faces is the heart's temperature leaking out.

Ask the Holy Spirit to show you: what kind of parent am I? The “conditional” type, who smiles only when the child does well? The “exhausted” type, too tired to show any expression? Or the “anxious” type, with worry underneath every smile? Seeing is not for blaming ourselves, but for admitting: my heart needs to be heated again by God's joy. A thermostat's power doesn't come from the room; it comes from being plugged into the mains. Parents' joy is the same.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parents' own hearts first, then with the children's behavior. The effects of a whole life flow from the heart, and so does the temperature of the home. When parents are led around by circumstances, they let circumstances reign; when parents are connected to the Holy Spirit, they can set the home's temperature to joy.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who gives a joyful heart, and his joy heals like medicine.
Who am I? — Am I more like a thermometer or a thermostat? Which kind of parent cools down the home: conditional, exhausted or anxious?
How should I respond? — In which moment today will I deliberately “turn up the temperature” of the home?
lessons.jesus: Luke records, “In that same hour, Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit.” He saw that God had revealed the things of the kingdom to little children, and he rejoiced and gave thanks. Jesus' joy was not driven by the cheering of the crowds; it welled up from the Holy Spirit and the Father's heart. He is the true thermostat.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for letting me see my face. I admit I am often the thermometer of the home: when the children fuss, I cool down with them and sometimes freeze the whole family. Please be the power source in my heart. Fill me with your joy so that I can set a warm temperature for this home. And heal the hearts of my children that my cold face has hurt. Amen.
acts: Ask your spouse or child to tell you honestly: “What expression do I wear most often?”
When your child walks in or wakes up today, deliberately give them a real smile first.
Find the moment that most often makes you “cool down” (for example, homework time) and pray over it beforehand.
lessons.noon: “A cheerful heart makes good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.” — Lord, make my heart cheerful, and let me be medicine for my family.

fam.key: A smiling face makes our home warm.

lamb.do: Hold your child and look in the mirror together. Make a big smile at the mirror so they can see your smile.
lamb.say: Look! Mommy is smiling and you are smiling too. It's so warm.

sprout.story: Little Penguin's home was on very, very cold ice. One day, Papa Penguin came home from work with a long face every evening, and the home seemed even colder. Little Penguin said, “Papa, you never smile, and I feel so cold.” Papa Penguin was startled, then crouched down and gave Little Penguin a big smile and a hug. Little Penguin said, “Wow, it's getting warm!”
sprout.ask: When do you think Mommy's and Daddy's faces are the warmest?
sprout.do: Play “Guess the Face”: take turns making happy, cross and sad faces for the others to guess, and finish by making the biggest smile together.

soldier.story: Do you know the difference between a thermometer and the thermostat on an air-conditioner? A thermometer only goes up and down with the room, but a thermostat can be set to a temperature and bring the room back to a comfortable level. The Bible says, “A cheerful heart makes good medicine.” One person's mood affects the people around them. Some people, when they are unhappy, make the whole family unhappy; others, when everyone is upset, can still bring warmth. Which kind of person do you want to be?
ask: In our family, who is most like a thermostat? Why?
When you are in a bad mood, how can you keep the whole family from cooling down with you?
soldier.do: Make a paper thermometer and stick it on the wall. Every dinnertime this week, mark the “temperature” of the home today together, and say what made it rise.

youth.talk: Some say parents are the weather forecast of the home: you walk in, take one look at our faces, and know whether you can talk today. We'd like to ask you one question, and please be honest: what expression do we wear most often? We guess the answer may not be pleasant, but we really want to know, because we want to be people who warm the home, not people who freeze it.
ask: When you come home, what expression do you most hope to see on our faces?
Do you think that when we're in a bad mood, we throw our feelings onto you?
youth.do: Ask your child to give the parents a score for “this week's temperature at home” from 1 to 10, and to offer one suggestion for raising it. The parents try it for a week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us a joyful heart. Please help our home to be full of smiles, so that everyone feels warm when they come home. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Though... Yet I Will Rejoice
lessons.theme: I believe: God himself is my reason for joy

v: For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!

lessons.still: One by one, hold in your heart the things in your home that are “not flourishing”: perhaps your child's grades, the family finances, a strained relationship. There is no hurry to fix them. Just say to the Lord, “Even so, I will rejoice in you.”
teach: The prophet Habakkuk saw disaster about to fall on his nation, and he listed everything that would come to nothing: “Even though the fig tree doesn't flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls.” For an agricultural society, this meant income down to zero, stores run out, and a future completely blank. In today's words, it might be: the redundancy notice arrives, the child's grades are in the red, a family member is in hospital, the savings are gone.

Then he says the boldest turning point in Scripture: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” His joy was not because of the fig tree, but because of the LORD himself. Many parents build their joy on “as long as”: as long as my child gets into a good school, as long as my husband gets promoted, as long as this check-up is clear, I will be joyful. Habakkuk teaches us to believe with “though... yet.”

Zhiwei and Yawen, who live in Auckland, have one child with learning difficulties and another who is often ill, and their work is not secure. Yawen says, “For a while I felt I had to wait until all these problems were solved before I was allowed to rejoice. Then I found that God himself is enough for my joy.” This is not giving up on effort; it is no longer letting the results of our effort sit on the throne of our hearts. Today, write your own “though... yet” declaration.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift of viewpoint, from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal. Earthly fruit has seasons of poor harvest, but God never changes. When parents' joy is rooted in God, children learn that our family's happiness doesn't depend on everything going smoothly but on a faithful God.
q: Who is God? — God is the God of my salvation, and even if everything comes to nothing, he is still the reason for joy.
Who am I? — On which “as long as” is my joy built?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: though ___, yet I believe ___, and I will rejoice in God.
lessons.jesus: Hebrews says that Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame.” There was nothing to be glad about on the cross, but Jesus saw the redemption behind the suffering, and saw children brought home one by one to the Father's house. His joy rose above his circumstances and pointed to eternity.
lessons.pray: Lord, I lay before you everything in my home that is “not flourishing.” Though my children still struggle, though money is still tight, though relationships are still cracked, yet I believe you are the God of my salvation, and I will rejoice in you. Please free my joy from “as long as” and root it in you. Amen.
acts: Write your “though... yet” declaration, at least two sentences.
Read Habakkuk 3:17–18 to your spouse, and share what your own “fig tree” is.
In one thing that isn't going well today, say deliberately, “Yet I will rejoice in God.”
lessons.noon: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” — Lord, though my circumstances are hard, I still choose to rejoice in you.

fam.key: Even when things go badly, we still have God.

lamb.do: When your child cries and fusses, first hold them and rock them gently, hum a quiet hymn, and give them a smile once they are calm.
lamb.say: It's okay. God is here and Mommy is here. We're not afraid.

sprout.story: Farmer Grandpa's apple tree grew not a single apple this year, and the little chicks had run away. His grandson asked, “Grandpa, aren't you sad?” Grandpa said, “A little bit. But I still have God! God loves me and takes care of me, and he'll give me new apples next year.” And Grandpa began to hum a song.
sprout.ask: If your favorite toy broke, what could you still thank God for?
sprout.do: Play a “Though... but” chain: “Though it's raining today, but...” Each person adds one thing they can thank God for.

soldier.story: Habakkuk was a prophet who saw that his country was about to face a great disaster. He said: even if the fig tree doesn't blossom, the vines bear no fruit, there is no food in the fields, no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls (which means having nothing at all), “yet I will rejoice in the LORD.” His happiness wasn't from having lots of things, but from having God. Things can be gone, but God is always there.
ask: If your phone, games and toys were all gone, would you still be happy? Why?
What can never be taken away?
soldier.do: Each person writes one sentence of their own: “Though..., yet I can still rejoice, because God...” and sticks it on their bedroom door.

youth.talk: Habakkuk made a list, all of it bad news, and then said, “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD.” We want to admit that our joy is often built on “as long as”: as long as your grades are good, as long as work goes well, as long as nothing is wrong at home. So when things go badly, we collapse completely, and that puts pressure on you too. We want to learn from Habakkuk and let our joy take root in God.
ask: What is the one thing in your life right now that is “not flourishing”?
Do you think saying “I will rejoice” in hard times is escaping reality, or a kind of faith?
youth.do: Parent and child each write one “though... yet” declaration, swap and read them, and pray for each other's “though.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you are always here. Even when things don't go well, we can still rejoice because of you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Celebrate Together, Rejoice in the Lord
lessons.theme: Laughter and celebration are our family's strength

v: Then he said to them, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
This is the day that the LORD has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!

lessons.still: Ask the Lord, “Lord, what is there in our family today that is worth celebrating?” Wait quietly and let the Holy Spirit remind you of the little graces drowned by busyness. Write them down one by one.
teach: After the Israelites returned from exile and rebuilt the wall, the scribe Ezra read the Law to the people. As they listened, they remembered their failures and wept. But Nehemiah said, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don't be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” God wanted his people not only to repent but to celebrate.

Many Chinese families are very good at “reviewing” but not very good at “celebrating.” When a child scores ninety-five, we ask, “Where did the other five go?” When a child learns to ride a bike, we say, “Be careful not to fall.” Over time the home becomes a place with plenty of improvement but no cheering. Nehemiah's words remind us that joy is strength, and a family that often celebrates has more strength to face difficulties than a family that only picks out faults.

Today's practice: celebrate as a family. You don't need to wait for a birthday or New Year; you can celebrate very small things: little brother putting on his shoes by himself for the first time, big sister willing to share with her younger sister, Dad coming home on time today. Light a candle, cook a bowl of sweet soup, and clap and cheer together. The psalmist says, “This is the day that the LORD has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!” Every ordinary day is worth rejoicing in the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is letting truth walk out of the head and into life. People matter more than tasks: the focus of celebration is not grades but the person, not what was completed but God's grace in them. When parents lead in rejoicing, children learn to see life with joy, and to give the credit to God.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who loves his people to rejoice and celebrate, and who makes joy their strength.
Who am I? — Am I better at picking out faults, or at celebrating? When did my child last get a cheer from me?
How should I respond? — This evening, what small thing in our family will I celebrate?
lessons.jesus: The first miracle Jesus performed was turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana. The wine had run out and the feast was about to fall flat, and Jesus stepped in so that the celebration could go on. He is not a Savior who appears only in synagogues and wildernesses; he is a Lord who goes to the feast and values human joy.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that you love us to rejoice. I admit that I am often only good at reviewing my children, and seldom celebrate them. Please open my eyes to see the small graces of each day, and give me a heart willing to cheer. Let our home have not only rules but laughter, and let the joy that comes from you be the strength of our whole family. Amen.
acts: This evening hold a “mini celebration” for one small thing in your family: a song, a snack, a cheer.
Today, when your child makes a small improvement, say, “I'm so happy for you!” instead of first pointing out what's still not enough.
Invite an elderly person or a neighbor to share your snacks, as Nehemiah said, “send portions to him.”
lessons.noon: “The joy of the LORD is your strength.” — Lord, let our family today rejoice in you and be made strong in you.

fam.key: We often rejoice together in our family.

lamb.do: When your child manages something small (crawling over, clapping, saying a word), cheer loudly and clap, then pick them up and twirl them around.
lamb.say: Wow! You did it! Let's cheer for you together!

sprout.story: A shepherd had a hundred sheep, and one day one was missing. He searched and searched in the hills, and at last found the little lamb behind a rock. He put the lamb on his shoulders and went home happily, and he called his friends and said, “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!” Everyone had a party together. Jesus says there is a party in heaven for every person who comes home too!
sprout.ask: What would you like to have a little party for today?
sprout.do: Hold a five-minute “Joy Party”: play a hymn, and as a family dance, clap and spin around.

soldier.story: The Israelites came back to Jerusalem from far away and worked hard to rebuild the wall. One day everyone gathered to hear God's word, and as they listened they all wept, thinking of the things they had done wrong. But Nehemiah said: stop crying! Go and eat good food, drink something sweet, and share with those who have nothing, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” God wants us not only to admit our wrongs, but also to celebrate his grace joyfully.
ask: Do you think our family more often “reviews” or more often “celebrates”?
Is there something this week for which the whole family should celebrate you?
soldier.do: Design a “celebration card” yourself and give it to a family member who made progress this week. Write on it: “I thank God for you!”

youth.talk: Recently we've noticed that we are very good at saying “it could be better” but seldom say “I'm so happy for you.” You score ninety-five and we ask where the other five went; you do something good and we're already thinking of the next thing. But Nehemiah says the joy of the LORD is our strength. We want to change, and cheer for you more and find fault less.
ask: Is there something you've worked hard at lately that you feel we didn't notice?
How would you like us to celebrate you?
youth.do: This week parents and child plan a small celebration together. It could be for a family member, a friend or someone who needs encouragement, and the child decides how to celebrate.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us so many things to rejoice over. Please let our home often have laughter, and let us share our joy with others. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Rejoice Always, Give Thanks in Everything
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Thankfulness is the soil of joy

v: Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
The LORD has done great things for us, and we are glad.

lessons.still: Look back over this week and, as if gathering shells on a beach, pick up the moments of joy one by one. Also look honestly at which days your home was especially cold. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and let thankfulness speak first.
teach: Paul says, “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks.” These three lines belong together: joy needs the root of prayer and the soil of thanksgiving. Thankfulness is not something we do only when something good happens; it is a way of seeing, noticing in ordinary days what God has already done. The psalmist says, “The LORD has done great things for us, and we are glad.” First we see what God has done, and joy follows.

Many of us know this experience: our attention is easily caught by negative things, and ten good things often can't outweigh one bad one. So thankfulness needs practice, like a muscle. Guohao, a single father of three in Singapore, plays “Three Thanks” with his children every evening. At first no one could think of anything, but after three months the children fight to speak first. He says, “Our family hasn't become rich, but we have become happier.”

This week we learned about rejoicing in the Lord, the thermometer and the thermostat, the faith of “though... yet,” and celebrating as a family. Today, review: did the temperature of our home rise a little? On which day did it fall back to freezing, and what made it drop? There is no need to blame yourself. Just write down one habit of joy you can keep up next week, such as sharing thanks every evening or a small celebration once a week. Joy is like a basin of coals that needs wood added regularly to keep it warm.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition. Joy is not a one-time emotion but a habit that needs repeated practice. Thankfulness turns our focus from our own lack to God's grace, from the human viewpoint to God's viewpoint; letting Jesus receive all the glory starts with one sentence: “Thank you, God.”
q: Who is God? — God is the God who has done great things for us, and his grace is in our home every day.
Who am I? — Did the temperature of our home rise this week? When did I let it fall to freezing?
How should I respond? — Which specific habit of joy or thankfulness will I build next week?
lessons.jesus: Jesus told a parable of a shepherd who found his lost sheep: when he found it, he called his friends and neighbors and said, “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!” The Father in Jesus' heart is a Father who loves to rejoice with people. He invites us too to turn every grace into the whole family's joy.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for everything you did in our home this week, large and small. I will remember it all. I admit that on some days I made our home very cold, and I ask your forgiveness. Please help me to rejoice always, pray without ceasing and give thanks in everything, so that thankfulness becomes the air in our home and joy becomes our strength. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was the warmest moment in our home this week? What was the coldest?
Ask your child, “This week, did Daddy/Mommy smile more often? Were we a bit more like Jesus?”
Write down one habit of joy to keep up next week, and start it tonight.
lessons.noon: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks.” — Lord, today I will count your blessings and thank you in everything.

fam.key: Thank you, God, we are so happy.

lamb.do: At bedtime, hold your child and stroke their little hands and feet, saying “Thank you, God” at each one.
lamb.say: Thank you, God, for my little hands. Thank you, God, for my little feet. Thank you, God, for you.

sprout.story: Every night before bed, Little Squirrel put the acorns he had found that day into a little jar, one acorn for each happy thing: “This one is for the yummy fruit I ate, this one is for playing with my brother...” After a week, the jar was full! Little Squirrel said, “Wow! God gave me so many happy things!”
sprout.ask: What happy thing from this week would you like to put in the “thank-you jar”?
sprout.do: Take an empty jar as a “thank-you jar.” Each person in the family puts in a drawing or a slip of paper about something they thank God for this week.

soldier.story: Paul wrote to the church in Thessalonica: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks.” Giving thanks in everything does not mean pretending to be happy when bad things happen, but finding God's grace in each situation. It is like slowly finding the one piece that fits in a puzzle that looks very messy. Thankfulness gets easier with practice, like learning to ride a bicycle: hard at the start, then very natural.
ask: What are the three things you are most thankful to God for this week?
Was there something unhappy in which you later found God's grace?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares “three thanks this week” and “one thing I want to do next week to make our family more joyful.” Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we learned about joy and tried to smile and celebrate more at home. Honestly, a few days went well, but on a few days we turned back into the cold Mom and Dad. We'd like to hear what you think, because you feel the temperature at home best. We also want to invite you to build a habit of thankfulness together, not for homework, but to make our family warmer.
ask: Did you feel the temperature at home was different this week? Which day was most noticeable?
Would you be willing to try a thankfulness habit with us? What way do you think would be least awkward?
youth.do: Decide together as a family on a thankfulness habit for next week, for example each person sharing one thing they're thankful for at dinner, or sending one photo of thanks each day in the family chat.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us so much grace this week. Please help us always to rejoice, always to pray, and to thank you in everything. In Jesus' name, amen.

14.memT: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”

mem.t: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

sat.d: Set up a “peace corner” in your home together: a small mat or two chairs, a soft cushion, a little lamp, a card with Colossians 3:15 on it, and an hourglass or timer. Agree on the rules for using it together: anyone who is angry can come here first to calm down; when two people are quarreling they sit here together, take turns to speak and take turns to listen, and shake hands when they have finished. When it is ready, the parents demonstrate first: apologize to each other for one small quarrel this week, and then pray together as a family.

sun: At what times and in what situations does your home most often “catch fire”? At those moments, are you usually the one putting out the fire or the one adding wood?
“Let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” Was there a moment this week when you really let him be the referee?
How can you be a “peacemaker” in your group, your church or your neighbourhood? Which peace-making method will your family keep using next week?

lessons.title: Let Christ's Peace Rule
lessons.theme: Peace in the home begins with the referee in the parents' hearts

v: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

lessons.still: First set down the sounds around you: the children's noise, the phone's notifications, the to-do list in your head. Take three deep breaths and say to the Lord, “Lord, let your peace rule in my heart.” Let those words be like a hand gently resting on your churning heart.
teach: Paul says, “Let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” The word “rule” in the original carries the sense of umpire or arbiter, like the person on the sports field who blows the whistle and decides the result. Everyone has a referee in their heart. When a child spills the milk, brothers fight over a toy, or a spouse says something sharp, who blows the whistle? My anger, my pride, or the peace of Christ?

Many parents think a “peaceful home” means a “quiet home.” In fact a home with children can never be quiet all the time, and laughter, crying and quarreling are all normal. The peace Scripture speaks of is not the absence of noise but a steady Lord in the heart in the middle of the noise. A home can be very lively and very peaceful, or very quiet and full of cold war. It is like the deep sea: however the waves rise on the surface, the depths remain calm. Peace lives in the depths.

Just before this verse Paul says, “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other... even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” And right after it he says, “and be thankful.” Peace does not drop straight from heaven; it is raised between forgiveness and thankfulness. This week we will learn to let Christ be the referee of our home, with the parents letting him blow the whistle first. When the whistle in the parents' hearts is blown by someone else, the game in the home is played quite differently.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus reign. The times of most conflict at home are often when everyone wants to be the referee: parents want to judge the children, children want to judge their brothers and sisters, and spouses want to judge who is right and who is wrong. When the peace of Christ rules in the parents' hearts, the parents step down from the judge's seat and return to the place of steward.
q: Who is God? — Christ is the Prince of Peace, and his peace can rule in my heart.
Who am I? — When there is conflict at home, who is usually blowing the whistle in my heart?
How should I respond? — When conflict comes today, how will I stop first and let the peace of Christ be the referee?
lessons.jesus: Isaiah prophesied of the child who would be born: “His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.” Jesus doesn't only bring peace; he is peace. Through the cross he broke down the wall that divided people from God and people from one another, and made us one.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the Prince of Peace. I admit that the referee in my heart is often my anger and my pride, not your peace. Please rule in my heart today. When the house is noisy, let you blow the whistle first, not my feelings. Teach me to bear with others and forgive, and to be thankful, so that your peace flows from my heart to the whole family. Amen.
acts: Write Colossians 3:15 on a card and put it in the place in your home where conflict happens most.
When conflict comes today, first say silently, “Lord, you rule here,” and then speak.
This evening count one thing you are thankful for today, and go to sleep with a thankful heart.
lessons.noon: “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” — Lord, right now blow the whistle in my heart, and let your peace rule.

fam.key: Jesus' peace is in our hearts.

lamb.do: When your child is unsettled or crying, hold them against your chest and breathe slowly and deeply, letting them feel your steady heartbeat.
lamb.say: Don't be scared. Jesus is here, and Mommy is here too.

sprout.story: The children were playing soccer when they started to argue: “It's my ball!” “No, it's mine!” Then the referee blew his whistle: “Peep!” Everyone stopped to listen to him. The referee said, “Let's take turns.” And they stopped arguing. The Bible says Jesus is like a referee in our hearts. When we feel like arguing, we can stop first and listen to Jesus.
sprout.ask: When you feel like quarreling, how can you stop first and listen to Jesus?
sprout.do: Play “Whistle and Stop”: everyone walks around the living room, and when Mommy or Daddy calls “Peep!” everyone stops, takes one deep breath and says, “Jesus' peace.”

soldier.story: Paul wrote, “Let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” Here “rule” is a bit like a referee in a ball game. In a match the two teams may clash, but when the referee blows the whistle everyone has to listen to his decision. In our hearts there are often two voices fighting: one says “Hit back!” and one says “Stop first.” Paul says to let the peace of Jesus be the referee, and listen to his decision, not to anger's.
ask: What is the “quarreling voice” that most often speaks up in your heart?
When Jesus is the referee, how do you think he would judge the thing we quarrel about most?
soldier.do: Each person makes a little “whistle card” with “Let Jesus rule” on it, and takes it out to look at when they feel angry.

youth.talk: Paul says to let the peace of Christ rule in our hearts, and the original word means to act as umpire. We want to admit that when we argue at home, we are often in a hurry to be the referee, judging whether you are right or wrong, without first letting Jesus judge our own hearts. Sometimes the house is very quiet, but it is really a cold war, and that is not peace either. We want to learn real peace.
ask: What do you think “truly peaceful” and “pretending to be peaceful” each look like in our family?
When there is conflict, which voice do you most often hear in your heart?
youth.do: Parent and child together list the three situations where conflict happens most often at home, and discuss how to let the peace of Christ rule first in each of them.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you are the Prince of Peace. Please be the referee in our hearts, and give our home your peace. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Am I Putting Out the Fire or Adding Wood?
lessons.theme: Seeing how we make the fire at home burn higher

v: For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.
As coals are to hot embers, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindling strife.
Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife.

lessons.still: Recall the most recent quarrel at home and replay it in slow motion, looking at what you said and did at each moment. Ask the Holy Spirit to show you: which word was water, and which was wood?
teach: Proverbs says, “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.” And, “As coals are to hot embers, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindling strife.” Conflict at home is like fire. Fires often can't be avoided, but how big a fire gets and how long it burns often depends on whether someone keeps adding wood. And the biggest bundle of wood is often in the parents' hands, because the parents' voices are the loudest and their power the greatest.

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: what kind of parent am I? The “wood-adding” type: when the child gets louder, I get louder; when the child slams a door, I slam one too. The “gossiping” type: complaining about my spouse in front of the children, listing the children's faults to relatives, and carrying the fire from one room to another. The “frozen” type: no quarreling on the surface, but punishing with coldness and silence, so the fire becomes smouldering coals. None of these is peace; they are only different shapes of fire.

Proverbs also says, “Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife.” A table piled with delicacies eaten in tension is worse than a dry crust eaten in peace. Many families work hard to give their children better material things, but overlook the atmosphere at the table. Zhenhua, who runs a small business in Ipoh, says, “My son told me later that what he feared most was not that we were poor, but that we quarreled at mealtimes.” Seeing is the first step to putting out the fire.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride stirs up pride, and both lose; humility draws out humility, and both win. Behind adding wood there is often the self-ruled life of “I must win.” Only when parents first take the wood out of their own hands can children learn to put the fire out. Deal with your own heart first, then with the children's behavior.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who gives peace, and he values a family at peace more than a table full of feasting.
Who am I? — Am I a wood-adding, gossiping or frozen parent? When was the most recent time I made the fire burn higher?
How should I respond? — Which bundle of wood in my own hands will I put down today?
lessons.jesus: On the evening of his resurrection the disciples had locked the doors out of fear. They had all abandoned him before. Jesus came and stood among them, and his first words were not a rebuke but, “Peace be to you.” He didn't add wood to their guilt; he used peace to rekindle a relationship that had gone cold.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for letting me see the wood I have added at home. I admit that I often answer loud with loud, punish my family with cold war, and even run others down in front of the children. Please forgive me, and heal the hearts I have burned. Teach me to stop when the fire starts, so that my words become water and no longer wood. Amen.
acts: Recall the most recent quarrel and write down which bundle of wood you added (a sentence, an action or a stretch of cold war).
Today don't complain about your spouse or other family members in front of the children.
If conflict at home involves physical violence or makes people afraid, please seek help right away from a professional organization and a church pastor.
lessons.noon: “For lack of wood a fire goes out.” — Lord, today let me add no more wood, and let my words be water that puts out the fire.

fam.key: We don't add wood. We put out the fire.

lamb.do: When your child cries and fusses, deliberately lower and slow your voice and speak to them softly.
lamb.say: Let's use small voices and speak slowly. Mommy is listening.

sprout.story: On a camping night Grandpa made a fire. Xiaoan kept throwing branches into it, and the fire grew bigger and bigger until everyone stepped back in fright. Grandpa said, “Xiaoan, stop throwing!” When he stopped, the fire slowly got smaller and went out. Grandpa said, “Quarreling is like a fire too. When someone keeps saying nasty words, it's like throwing on branches. Stop throwing, and the fire will go out.”
sprout.ask: When you quarrel, which words are like “throwing branches”?
sprout.do: Cut out a “fire” from red paper. Each time someone says a kind word, cover the fire with a blue “water” paper and see whether you can cover it up.

soldier.story: Proverbs says, “For lack of wood a fire goes out.” It means that for a fire to keep burning, someone has to keep adding wood, and quarrels are the same. Big brother says, “You're so annoying!” Little sister replies, “No, you are!” Big brother gets louder: “You're the most annoying!” Every sentence is another piece of wood, and the fire gets bigger and bigger. But as soon as one person stops adding wood and says, “Okay, let's stop for a moment,” the fire slowly gets smaller. The one who stops hasn't lost; they are the bravest.
ask: When do you most often “add wood”?
Why do you think it takes courage to be the first one to stop?
soldier.do: This week, each time you notice you're about to quarrel, say “I'm not adding wood,” then step away for a moment or take a deep breath.

youth.talk: Proverbs says a contentious man is like wood on a fire. We want to admit first: in many of our quarrels at home, we were the ones adding wood. You got louder, so we got louder; you went cold, so we went cold in return; and sometimes we even complained about you in front of others. All of that made the fire burn higher. We don't want to do it any more, and we want to begin by stopping ourselves.
ask: What kind of wood do you think we add most often when we quarrel?
If you could design a “cease-fire signal,” what would you choose?
youth.do: Parents apologize to your child for one time you added wood, then agree together on a cease-fire signal, for example a pause hand sign that anyone can use.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, please help us not to add wood when we quarrel, but to speak kindly and let the fire go out. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Peace in the Storm
lessons.theme: I believe: the Lord's peace does not depend on a quiet home

v: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.
You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.

lessons.still: Imagine you are in a little boat with the wind and waves rising all around. Jesus is in the boat with you, resting calmly on a cushion. Breathe slowly, turn your eyes from the waves to him, and say to him, “Lord, with you in the boat, I am not afraid.”
teach: On the night he was betrayed Jesus said to his disciples, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you.” The world's peace is “peace when everything goes smoothly”: a steady job, obedient children, a quiet home. Jesus' peace is peace even in the storm, because its source is not circumstances but himself. When he said this, the cross was right before him, yet his heart was at peace.

Isaiah says, “You will keep whoever's mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.” The key here is “steadfast.” Shuhui, a mother working in Melbourne, looks after two small children and a sick mother-in-law, and her home has no quiet from morning till night. She says, “I used to wait for the house to be quiet before I could be calm. Later I found that I need to fix my heart on God in the middle of the noise.”

Conviction is turning this truth from something we know into something we declare: the noise at home cannot take away the peace the Lord has given me. This does not mean we don't need to deal with conflict; it means first steadying our own hearts, so that we have strength to calm the storm at home. A captain who panics in the storm cannot save a ship; a parent with peace in their heart can help the children feel safe in the storm. Today, write your “I believe.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on circumstances. The world's peace depends on circumstances; Christ's peace depends on a relationship: first at peace with God, then at peace with ourselves and others. When parents' hearts are steadfast in trusting God, they move from “the home must be quiet for me to be at peace” to “because I have peace, I can bring quiet to the home.”
q: Who is God? — God is the God who keeps those who trust in him in perfect peace, and Jesus himself gives us his peace.
Who am I? — Does my peace depend on a quiet home, or on the Lord?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: even if my home ___, I believe the Lord's peace ___.
lessons.jesus: The disciples cried out in panic in the boat: “Teacher, don't you care that we are dying?” Jesus woke, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” and the wind ceased. He could sleep in the storm because he trusted the Father completely; and when he spoke, the wind and waves obeyed. This Lord is in the boat of our family.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving me your peace, not as the world gives. I believe the noise at home cannot take away the peace you have given me; I believe you are in the boat of our family. Please keep me steadfast in trusting you, so that in my children's crying and the busyness of our home I stay steady, and become peace for my family. Amen.
acts: Write your “I believe” declaration: “Even if my home..., I believe...”
At the noisiest moment of your home today, stop and quietly recite Isaiah 26:3 before you respond.
Read John 14:27 to your spouse and share the one thing that has taken away your peace most lately.
lessons.noon: “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you.” — Lord, I believe your peace is with me today, whatever my circumstances.

fam.key: Jesus is in the boat, so we are not afraid.

lamb.do: During thunder or noise, hold your child close, pat them gently, and sing a hymn in a steady voice.
lamb.say: It's so noisy outside, but Jesus is here and we are safe.

sprout.story: Jesus and his friends were crossing the sea by boat when suddenly a big wind blew, the waves grew huge, and water splashed into the boat! His friends were terrified and shouted, “Jesus, help us!” Jesus was asleep at the back of the boat. He woke up and said to the wind and the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind stopped and the sea went quiet. Jesus said, “Don't be afraid. I'm here.”
sprout.ask: When you are scared, how can you remember Jesus?
sprout.do: Put water in a big basin and a toy boat on it. Everyone blows to make the “wind and waves,” then say together, “Peace! Be still!” and stop blowing.

soldier.story: On the night before he was arrested Jesus said to his disciples, “Peace I leave with you.” The disciples were afraid then, because they could feel that something was wrong. Jesus said that the peace he gives is different from the world's. The world's peace is: the exam is over, the homework is done, and everyone has stopped arguing, so now it is peaceful. Jesus' peace is: even if the exam isn't over yet and the home is still a bit noisy, your heart stays steady, because you know Jesus is with us.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “peace when there are no problems” and “peace with Jesus”?
What has been taking away your peace lately?
soldier.do: Each person writes one “I believe” sentence: “Even if..., I believe Jesus...” Stick it by your bed and read it before sleeping.

youth.talk: We always used to think we could only have peace once the home was quiet and everything was going smoothly. As a result we were anxious every day, because our home is almost never quiet. Jesus said his peace is not as the world gives. We want to share with you that we are learning to fix our hearts on God in the midst of the noise. We still fail often, but we want to try.
ask: At school or in life, what takes away your peace most?
Do you think it is really possible to have peace in your heart? Have you experienced it?
youth.do: Parents share a story of experiencing God's peace in a difficult time, then invite your child to share one, and pray together for each other's most unsettled thing.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for being in the same boat with us. However big the waves are, please give us peace in our hearts. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Parents Who Make Peace
lessons.theme: Start today leading the whole family in practicing reconciliation

v: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

lessons.still: Think about whether there is a stuck relationship in your home right now: between husband and wife, between you and one of your children, or between the children. Bring it quietly before the Lord and ask, “Lord, what small step can I take today?”
teach: Jesus says, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” Notice that Jesus does not say “those who love peace” but “peacemakers.” Someone who loves peace may only avoid conflict, but a peacemaker actively walks into conflict and helps a broken relationship to be joined again. This is the mark of God's children, because God himself is the God who took the initiative to reconcile with us.

Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” The words “as much as it is up to you” are very practical. At home, a parent's first peacemaking lesson is often not mediating between the children but first being reconciled with the spouse. When children quarrel, the best teaching material is watching how Mom and Dad make up after they have argued. A grandmother in Kaohsiung who helps her daughter look after the grandchildren says, “I used to tell the children not to quarrel, yet I gave Grandpa the cold shoulder for three days. How could they learn?”

Today's practice is to teach the whole family a simple “four steps to making up.” Stop: stop first and calm down separately. Listen: take turns to speak without interrupting. Own it: say “I was wrong in...” rather than “but you...” Make up: say sorry, say “I forgive you,” and shake hands or hug. The parents go first. “If it is possible” also reminds us that where there is violence or any safety concern, we protect safety first and seek professional help.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than being right. In an argument we often want to win the point and lose the relationship. Peacemaking parents are willing to put down “I am right” first and reach out a hand. Humility draws out humility. When the parents make up first, the children learn to make up.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who took the initiative to reconcile with us, and who calls peacemakers his children.
Who am I? — Am I a parent who “avoids conflict” or a parent who “makes peace”?
How should I respond? — With whom will I take the initiative to make peace today? How will I lead my children in practicing the “four steps to making up”?
lessons.jesus: Paul says, “He is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation.” Jesus did not wait for us to come to him first. He walked into the deepest rift between people and God, and broke down the dividing wall with his own body. He is the greatest peacemaker.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for taking the initiative to reconcile with me and breaking down the dividing wall. I admit that I often just want to avoid conflict, or to win the argument. Please give me the courage to make peace first today and say sorry first. And please help me to teach my children the way of making up, so that our home becomes a home of peacemakers. Amen.
acts: Today take the initiative to find your spouse or a family member and make up over some small matter, saying, “I was wrong in...”
At dinner introduce the “four steps to making up” to the whole family: stop, listen, own it, make up. Write them down and put them up.
The next time the children quarrel, walk with them through the four steps instead of deciding straight away who is right.
lessons.noon: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” — Lord, today let me be a peacemaker in our home.

fam.key: We are people who make peace.

lamb.do: When two children grab at something, crouch down and hold both of them, speak softly, and then help them take turns.
lamb.say: One at a time. We are all good friends.

sprout.story: Abram and his nephew Lot both had lots of sheep and cattle, and there wasn't enough grass, so the herdsmen on both sides began to quarrel. Abram said to Lot, “We are relatives, so let's not quarrel. You choose first where you want to go. If you go left, I'll go right.” Abram let Lot choose first, and they stopped quarreling. God was very pleased with what Abram did.
sprout.ask: When you quarrel with your brother, sister or friend, how can you be like Abram?
sprout.do: Play the “Four Steps” finger game: hold up one finger and say “Stop,” two for “Listen,” three for “Say sorry,” four for “Make up,” and finish with a clap and a hug.

soldier.story: Abram and his nephew Lot lived together, and because they had so many sheep and cattle, their herdsmen often quarreled over the grazing. Abram was the elder and could have chosen the best land first, but he said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.” He let Lot choose first, and Lot chose the richest plain. Abram looked as if he had lost out, but afterward God promised to give him the whole land. God himself looks after the person who is willing to give way first and make peace.
ask: Why was Abram willing to let Lot choose first?
Do you think giving way means losing? Why?
soldier.do: This week, if you have an argument with a brother or sister, try using the “four steps to making up,” and share how it went at dinner on Friday.

youth.talk: Jesus says blessed are the peacemakers. We've noticed that we often tell you and your brothers and sisters not to quarrel, but after we, as a couple, have an argument we often give each other the cold shoulder for days, and you never saw us make up. We want to change, beginning with ourselves. And we want to ask you: is there a relationship at school or among your friends that needs mending?
ask: Have you ever seen us make up after an argument? How did you feel?
Which step in making up do you think is hardest?
youth.do: Parents show your child the “four steps to making up” once, apologizing to each other for a real small matter. Afterward ask your child, “Is there a relationship you'd like us to go with you to mend?”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us make up. Please help us to say sorry after we quarrel, and to forgive, and to be people who make peace. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Sowing the Fruit of Righteousness in Peace
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: This week, did our home sow peace?

v: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

lessons.still: Remember the conflicts at home this week, and also whether there was any time the fire went out before it grew big. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you see the seeds you have sown, whether peace or strife.
teach: James says, “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” And, “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” Peace is not a single event but a kind of farming: every gentle word, every time we stop first, every apology is a seed sown in the home.

A farmer does not sow today and harvest tomorrow. Peace in the home is the same: you may have sown for a week and still meet a big fight between your children. Don't be discouraged; it doesn't mean the seeds are useless, only that they are still putting down roots in the soil. Please also notice James's words “without partiality”: when we deal with the children's conflicts, do we always blame the eldest first, or always protect the youngest? Partiality stops the seeds from growing.

This week we learned to let the peace of Christ rule, saw ourselves adding wood, found peace in the storm, and practiced being parents who make peace. Today, review honestly: when did I stop first? When did I add wood again? How many times did our home use the four steps to making up? Write down one peace-making action you can continue next week. The fruit of peace often appears when you aren't looking: one day you will hear your child say to their little brother, “Let's stop for a moment.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the rhythm of peace-farming. Proud parents review only how many times the children quarreled; humble parents first ask what seeds they themselves have sown. First at peace with God, then at peace with ourselves and others: that is the order of peace, and also the order of life.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who gives wisdom from above, a wisdom that is first pure, then peaceful.
Who am I? — This week, have I sown seeds of peace or seeds of strife at home? Was I partial when dealing with conflict?
How should I respond? — Which seed of peace will I keep on sowing next week?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper the disciples were still arguing about who was greatest. Jesus did not join the argument or decide who was right. He took a towel, bent down and washed their feet. With humility he sowed a seed of peace, and that seed later bore fruit in the united church.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for being with me this week as I learned about peace. I admit that a few times I added wood again, and that I was partial toward one child. Please forgive me. Thank you also for showing me the times the fire went out before it grew big; that was your grace. Please give me wisdom from above, so that I keep sowing in peace and the fruit of righteousness grows in our home. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: which conflict at home this week did we handle best? Which needs adjusting?
Ask your child, “This week when we were arguing, were Daddy/Mommy a bit more like Jesus?”
Write down one specific peace-making action for next week, for example making sure every night that no one goes to sleep angry.
lessons.noon: “The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” — Lord, let every word I sow today be a seed of peace.

fam.key: We sow peace every day.

lamb.do: At bedtime hold your child in your arms, dim the lights and sing softly so that they drift slowly off to sleep in the quiet.
lamb.say: Goodnight. Jesus' peace is with you as you sleep.

sprout.story: Xiaole planted a seed in a flowerpot and watered it every day, but for many days nothing came up. He wanted to dig the seed up to look. Grandma said, “Don't dig it up. The seed is growing roots in the soil!” A few days later, a little green shoot poked out. Grandma said, “Saying kind words is like planting seeds too. One day peace will grow.”
sprout.ask: This week, which kind word did you say that was like planting a seed of peace?
sprout.do: Each person in the family writes or draws, on a seed-shaped piece of paper, one thing they did this week to make peace, and sticks it on a “Peace Garden” poster.

soldier.story: James says, “The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” It means that peace is like farming: you have to sow, water and wait before there is a harvest. Every time you stop first instead of quarreling, every time you say sorry, every time you help two friends make up, you are sowing seeds of peace. Sometimes it seems as if sowing the seeds does no good, but they are growing roots in the soil, and one day they will bear fruit.
ask: Which seed of peace did you sow this week?
What kind of seed do you think our family most needs to sow next week?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting. Each person shares one “peace seed I sowed this week” and one “thing I want to improve next week.” Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we tried to add less wood and make up more at home, and we also showed you an apology. Honestly, once or twice we nearly quarreled again. James says peace is sown, and not harvested all at once. We'd like to hear what you've noticed, because you are the best witness: was there a bit more peace at home this week?
ask: This week, do you feel the way we handled conflict was better than before?
Was there a time when you felt we were partial toward someone while handling a conflict?
youth.do: Choose together as a family a peace habit to continue next week, such as “never going to bed angry,” saying goodnight to each other every night before sleep.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us peace. Please help us sow seeds of peace every day, so that our home grows the fruit of peace. In Jesus' name, amen.

15.memT: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

mem.t: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;

sat.d: Play three “slow” games as a family. One: Tortoise Race. Walk from one end of the living room to the other without ever stopping your feet; the slowest person to arrive wins. Two: Whisper Down the Lane. One person whispers a sentence that is passed along to the last person; see who listens most carefully. Three: Make a treat together that needs waiting, such as jelly or steamed buns, and while you wait, take turns sharing “one thing I was impatient about lately.” Finish by reciting James 1:19 together, eating your well-waited treat, and thanking God for his patience with us.

sun: At what times of day, and in what situations, are you most likely to lose your temper with your children? Before you get angry, what signals do your body and heart usually give?
This week, what did you discover that you really want underneath your anger? Is it quiet, face, control, or fear?
How will you walk alongside another parent in the group who is wrestling with anger? Which “pause” method will you keep practicing next week?

lessons.title: Swift to Hear, Slow to Anger
lessons.theme: The anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God

v: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath in and count to four; then breathe out slowly and count to six. Repeat three times. In this slowed-down breathing, say to the Lord: “Lord, teach me to listen first, then speak, and only last to be angry.”
teach: James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” The order is interesting: listening comes first, and anger comes last. Yet in many homes the order is exactly reversed. Our child opens his mouth, and before he has finished, our temper is rising. The words are already out, and only afterward do we remember to listen. James puts the order right again: first open the ears, then the mouth, and only last the fire.

Then he adds, “for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” This hits a blind spot for many parents. We often get angry in order to make our children better: raise our voice, and the child goes to do his homework; slam the table, and the child dares not talk back. It seems to work, but anger buys only fear and compliance; it cannot buy real change in a child’s heart. It is like pulling hard on a rice seedling: it looks taller, but its roots have been loosened.

The patience described here is “long-tempered,” the opposite of short-tempered. The patience that the Spirit grows is not swallowing anger by force; it is the heart being made larger, able to carry the pace at which our children grow. Anger itself is not sin, and Jesus was angry too; but when anger comes from the self-ruled life, from impatience and control, it wounds people. This week we will put the order of our home right again: listen first, speak next, and be angry last. And very often, once we have finished listening, there is no need to be angry at all.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parent’s own heart first, and then the child’s behavior. Anger is often an attempt to force God’s righteousness out by my own strength, which is putting myself on the throne. A patient parent admits: changing my child’s heart is the Holy Spirit’s work; my part is to accompany, guide and wait.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who asks us to be swift to hear and slow to anger; his righteousness is not achieved by human anger.
Who am I? — At home, is my order “listen, speak, anger,” or “anger, speak, listen”?
How should I respond? — When my child speaks today, how will I open my ears first and answer only after I have listened?
lessons.jesus: People brought little children to Jesus, but the disciples rebuked them. When Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Jesus gets angry too, but his anger protects children; it is never aimed at them. His anger served God’s righteousness.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I am often slow to listen, quick to speak, and even quicker to be angry. I thought that a shout could make my children better, but it has left them hurt and afraid. Please forgive me. Holy Spirit, make my heart bigger and grow the fruit of patience in me. Teach me to listen first, speak next, and be slow to anger, so that your righteousness may be done in our home. Amen.
acts: When your child speaks to you today, put down what you are doing, look into his eyes, and respond only after he has finished
Write on your phone or the fridge: “Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger”
If your anger often goes out of control, or you hit people or throw things, please seek professional counseling and the help of your pastor; it is a brave step
lessons.noon: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” — Lord, today open my ears first, and then my mouth.

fam.key: Listen first, speak next, be slow to get angry.

lamb.do: When your baby babbles, stop, look at him and nod; wait until he has finished “talking” before you answer.
lamb.say: I’m listening. You talk, and Mommy listens.

sprout.story: Little Rabbit could run very fast, but she always ran off before she had heard the whole message. Mommy said, “Go and fetch a carrot, but don’t get…” and Little Rabbit had already gone. She came back with a chilli pepper! Little Tortoise listened slowly to the very end of what his mother said, and brought back the right thing. Mother Rabbit laughed and said, “Swift to hear means listening all the way to the end!”
sprout.ask: What do you think it means to listen well?
sprout.do: Play “Listen Till the End.” A parent gives a long instruction, such as “touch your nose, clap your hands, then turn around once,” and the child may begin only after hearing it all.

soldier.story: James wrote, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Have you noticed that in an argument, everyone is trying to talk and nobody is listening? Big brother hasn’t finished, and little sister shouts, “No, it isn’t!” James says to turn the order around: open your ears first and hear what the other person says, then think about how to answer, and only last decide whether to be angry. Very often, once we have listened, we find there is no need to be angry.
ask: What is the hardest part of being “swift to hear”?
Has there been a time when you listened to someone and then stopped being angry?
soldier.do: This week, when an argument starts, practice “say it back”: repeat the other person’s words in your own words and check you understood before giving your own opinion.

youth.talk: James says to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger. We want to admit that at home we are often the other way round: we interrupt you before you finish, and we start scolding before we understand. We thought anger would make you change, but Scripture says the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. We want to learn again, starting with listening to you until you have said it all.
ask: When do you feel we most often get angry before we have finished listening to you?
When we are angry, how would you like us to talk with you?
youth.do: This week, set aside fifteen minutes of “listening only” time: the child may say anything, and the parents may only nod and ask questions, with no commenting and no advice.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, help us listen first, speak next, and be slow to get angry. Make everyone in our family willing to listen well to each other. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Where Does My Anger Come From?
lessons.theme: Seeing the self underneath anger that wants to be king

v: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.

lessons.still: Recall the last time you got angry with your child. Do not rush to defend yourself, and do not rush to blame yourself. Simply ask the Holy Spirit: “Lord, what did my heart really want at that moment?” Wait quietly for his light.
teach: James asks a very direct question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” We often think our anger is caused by our children: he dawdles, he talks back, he won’t listen. But James says the root of anger is inside us: something our heart wants has been blocked. The child is only the match that lights the fire; what is really flammable is the dry wood piled up inside us.

Anger is like an iceberg. Above the water are the shouting, the slammed door and the cold face; below the water are a lot of “I wants”: I want quiet, I want to be on time, I want to keep face, I want my child to do it my way. Deeper still are fears: fear that my child will fall behind at the start, fear that others will say I cannot raise children, fear that I am a failed parent. Junjie, an engineer in Kuala Lumpur, discovered that every time he lost his temper with his son in front of relatives, he was really afraid of being seen as a father who cannot manage his child.

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on this: what kind of angry parent am I? The “volcano”: erupts at the slightest touch, quick to come and quick to go, but leaves ashes everywhere. The “pressure stove”: keeps holding it in and holding it in, then blows up completely over some small thing. The “face-saver”: especially quick to flare at the child in front of other people. Only when we see the “I want” beneath the anger can we hand it to God and let Jesus reign in that place.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life is the root of the fall, and also the root of anger. When an “I want” is blocked, the self-ruled life gets angry; when I hand my “I want” to God, the self-emptied life brings peace. Humility is laying down power and returning to my proper place: my child is not my masterpiece, and I am not the king of the home.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who searches hearts; he gently lets me see the desires beneath my anger.
Who am I? — Am I a volcano, a pressure stove, or a face-saver? What “I want” most often lies beneath my anger?
How should I respond? — Which “I want” am I willing to hand over to God today?
lessons.jesus: One village would not welcome Jesus, and James and John were so angry that they asked for fire to come down from heaven and consume them. Jesus turned and rebuked them, saying, “You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are.” He helped his disciples see the heart behind their anger, and reminded them that he came to save people, not destroy them.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for showing me the root of my anger. I admit that my anger is often not for my children’s good, but because I want quiet, I want face, I want control, and underneath there are so many fears. Please forgive my self-ruled life and heal those fears. I hand these “I wants” to you. Reign in my heart. Amen.
acts: Write down the last three times you were angry, and for each write one sentence: “What I really wanted then was…”
Find out which type of angry parent you are, tell your spouse or spiritual companion, and ask him to pray for you
When you notice you are about to get angry today, ask yourself silently: “What do I want right now?”
lessons.noon: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” — Lord, let me see my own heart, and I hand my “I wants” to you.

fam.key: When you feel angry, look at your own heart first.

lamb.do: When your child cries angrily, crouch down and put the feeling into words: “You’re angry because you wanted that toy.” Then give him a hug.
lamb.say: You’re angry. Mommy knows. Mommy is here with you.

sprout.story: Little Elephant wanted to play with the blocks, but his big sister was playing with them. Little Elephant was so angry that he knocked the blocks over with his trunk. Mommy crouched down and asked, “Why are you angry?” Little Elephant said, “Because I want to play too!” Mommy said, “So you are angry because you want something very much. We can say, ‘May I play with you?’” When his sister heard that, she shared some blocks with Little Elephant.
sprout.ask: When you get angry, what do you usually want?
sprout.do: Draw an “Angry Little Volcano”: underneath the volcano, draw what makes you angry, such as “want to play,” “want to eat,” or “want attention.”

soldier.story: James asked, “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” He said they come from the “wants” in our hearts. Think of the last time you were angry. Maybe your brother took your things, or Dad told you to turn off the computer. It looks as though it was because of the other person, but really it was because you wanted something and could not have it. It is like an iceberg: only a little shows above the water, and a huge part is hidden below. James and John, two of Jesus’ disciples, once got so angry that they wanted fire to come down from heaven on a village, but Jesus rebuked them and helped them see their own hearts.
ask: The last time you were angry, what did you really want?
When Mom and Dad are angry, what do you think they really want?
