soldier.do: Make an “iceberg card”: at the top write what you did when you were angry, and underneath write what you really wanted, then share it with Mom and Dad.

youth.talk: Lately we have been wondering: when we lose our tempers with you, is it for your good, or for ourselves? James says that fights come from the desires inside us. We have found that many times we were angry because we wanted quiet, or wanted to keep face, or were afraid your future would not turn out well. None of this is your fault. We want to say sorry to you.
ask: Have you ever felt that we were angry because of our own stress, and not because you did something wrong?
When you get angry yourself, what is usually underneath?
youth.do: A parent shares one “I want” that lay beneath their anger and apologizes to the child for that outburst; invite the child to share one of their own icebergs too.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, when we get angry, help us look at our own hearts first and tell you what we want, instead of losing our temper. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: God Is Patient with Me
lessons.theme: I believe: those whom God has been patient with can be patient with their children

v: The LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.

lessons.still: Think about how long God has waited for you: waited for you to turn back, waited for you to grow up, waited for you to drop some old habit. Quietly feel his patience toward you, and say to him: “Lord, thank you for never giving up on me.”
teach: On Mount Sinai Moses asked to see God’s glory, and God passed before him and proclaimed his own name: “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.” This is the fullest self-introduction God gives in the Old Testament. Right after “merciful and gracious” come the words “slow to anger.” Patience is written into God’s name. He is not forcing himself to hold back his anger; patience is simply his nature.

And he said this just after Israel had made the golden calf. They had only just left Egypt and had seen the Red Sea divide, yet they turned around and worshiped an idol. God had a thousand reasons to be angry, but he chose to show patience. Paul also says that he, the “chief of sinners,” obtained mercy so that “in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience.” Every one of us is a living witness to God’s patience.

Conviction begins here: I do not tolerate my children by willpower; first I admit how God has been patient with me. When I think of how many years God has waited for me, I can wait more easily for my child to learn to tidy his toys, to be on time, to manage his feelings. Children grow at their own pace, just as God waits for me in his own time. Today, write down your “I believe”: I believe God is patient with me, so…
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the human timetable to God’s timetable. A parent’s impatience often comes because the child has not grown up according to our timetable. When a parent first sees how God has been patient with him, “Why can’t he do it yet?” turns into “God waited for me like this too.”
q: Who is God? — God is merciful, gracious and slow to anger; in me he has shown all his patience.
Who am I? — What has God been patient with in my life the longest?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God is patient with me, so I am willing to wait for my child to grow slowly in ______.
lessons.jesus: The disciples could not heal a boy with an evil spirit, and Jesus sighed, “How long shall I bear with you?” But his next words were, “Bring him here to me.” Jesus gets tired too, and he sighs, but his sigh did not turn into giving up; it turned into a hand stretched out to rescue. That is patience.
lessons.pray: LORD, you are merciful and gracious, slow to anger. Thank you for showing all your patience in me, and for waiting for me so long. I believe that those whom you are patient with can be patient with their children. Help me remember how you waited for me, so that I too can wait for my children to grow in your time. Amen.
acts: Write your “I believe” declaration: “I believe God is patient with me, so…”
Recall one thing God has been patient with you about the longest, write it in your journal, and offer thanks
Find one thing your child is slower to learn, and say to him today: “That’s all right. We’ll take it slowly, and I’m with you.”
lessons.noon: “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger” — Lord, you are patient with me like this; please make me patient with my children like this.

fam.key: God waits for us, and we wait for others.

lamb.do: When your child is learning to walk or to feed himself, don’t rush to help; wait patiently beside him, and give him a big hug when he manages it.
lamb.say: Take your time. Mommy is waiting. You can do it.

sprout.story: A little chick was learning to walk and kept falling down. He said, “I’m so silly! I can’t learn!” Mother Hen said, “Don’t hurry. When you were small you couldn’t even stand, and I waited a long time for you. Now you can stand, can’t you? I will keep on waiting for you.” The chick tried once, twice, three times, and at last he could walk steadily! Mother Hen said, “God waits patiently for us to grow, too!”
sprout.ask: What are you learning that you can’t quite do yet?
sprout.do: Play “Slow Cup Stacking” as a family: each person takes a turn stacking one paper cup, and if it falls you start again, and everyone says, “That’s all right, take your time!”

soldier.story: After the Israelites left Egypt they saw God divide the Red Sea with their own eyes, but not long afterward they made a golden calf and worshiped it. God was very sad, yet when he introduced himself to Moses, he said: I am merciful, gracious and slow to anger. Think about it: if your friend betrayed you, would you still say, “I won’t be quick to get angry with you”? God is that patient. Every time we make a mistake, God is patiently waiting for us to come back.
ask: Has God waited a long time for you in something?
If God is this patient with us, who can we be a little more patient with?
soldier.do: Each person writes one “I believe”: “I believe God is very patient with me, so I am willing to be patient with ______,” and sticks it on their desk.

youth.talk: We have been reading Exodus lately. Even after Israel worshiped the golden calf, God still called himself “slow to anger.” We thought about ourselves: God has waited many years for us, and we still have old habits we are changing even now. Yet with you, we often expect you to learn something at once and get angry when you don’t. That isn’t fair. We want to start by remembering how God has waited for us, and learn to wait for you.
ask: In what area do you think we are most often impatient with you?
Who or what are you most impatient with yourself?
youth.do: Parents and child each write one “I believe” declaration, and share one personal experience of “God was very patient with me.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being so patient with us and waiting for us to grow. Help us to be patient with our family too. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Pause, and Make Peace Before Sunset
lessons.theme: Practice the family “pause plan” today

v: The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense.
“Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
and don’t give place to the devil.

lessons.still: Picture the moment today when your home is most likely to catch fire: after school, homework time, supper, bedtime. Hand it to the Lord and pray ahead of time: “Lord, at that moment, remind me to pause.”
teach: Proverbs says, “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense.” Patience is not only a feeling; it is also discretion, wisdom thought out in advance. Firefighters do not learn how to put out a fire at the scene of the fire; they rehearse long beforehand. A parent’s patience also needs preparing: before the anger comes, decide what you will do. If we only remember to be patient when the fire has already reached our throat, it is often too late.

Today’s practice is the family “pause plan.” One: recognize the signals. Before you flare up, your body tells you first: your heart beats faster, your fists clench, your voice gets louder. Two: say it out loud. “I’m very angry right now, and I need a five-minute pause.” Three: leave the scene. Go to the balcony, the bathroom or a room, breathe deeply and pray. Four: come back and make peace. When you are calm, return and talk it through well, and apologize if you need to. When parents model it first, children learn. A pause is not running away; it is not letting anger speak for you.

Paul says, “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil.” He does not say we may never be angry; he says not to let anger spend the night, and not to “give place to the devil.” Anger kept overnight ferments into bitterness. So the last step of the pause plan is to make peace before bed. Never deal with anger by hitting, scolding, shaming, threatening or giving the silent treatment; and if your anger often goes out of control, please seek professional help.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than the issue. In anger we often hurt a person over a matter. A pause gives the Holy Spirit room to work; rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head. Making peace before sunset makes the relationship matter more than being right, and lets Jesus still reign over this home at bedtime.
q: Who is God? — God gives discretion that makes us slow to anger, and reminds us not to let the sun go down on our wrath.
Who am I? — What signal does my body most often give before I get angry? Do I have a habit of letting anger spend the night?
How should I respond? — How will I introduce the pause plan to my family today, and use it the first time I need it?
lessons.jesus: Peter writes that Jesus, “when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” When Jesus faced insults he did not let anger speak for him; he entrusted himself to the Father. His pause was not weakness, but a deeper trust.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving us discretion that makes us slow to anger. Help me truly use the pause plan today: when anger comes, to recognize the signal, say it out loud, step away, and come back to make peace. Keep our family from letting anger spend the night, and from giving place to the devil. When I fail, give me the courage to apologize first. Amen.
acts: At supper, introduce the four-step “pause plan” to the whole family, and write it down and put it up at home
Choose a “pause corner” at home; it could be the balcony or a chair in a room
Tonight before bed, make sure no family member goes to sleep angry, and go to apologize first if you need to
lessons.noon: “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” — Lord, remind me to pause today, and help me make peace before sunset.

fam.key: Pause when you are angry, and make peace before bed.

lamb.do: When you feel your patience running out, put your child down somewhere safe, take a few deep breaths, then come back and hold him.
lamb.say: Mommy needs one deep breath. I’ll be right back to hug you.

sprout.story: When Little Lion got angry he would roar loudly and scare all his friends away. Papa Lion taught him a trick: “When you are angry, close your eyes first and breathe deeply three times, like blowing out a candle: whoo, whoo, whoo.” Little Lion tried it, and the fire in his heart grew smaller. Before bedtime, Little Lion even went to his friend and said, “I’m sorry. I was too fierce today.”
sprout.ask: When you are angry, how can you “blow out the candle”?
sprout.do: Practice “candle breathing” as a family: hold up one finger as the candle, breathe in deeply, blow it out slowly, and repeat three times.

soldier.story: Paul says, “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath.” It means that feeling angry will happen, but don’t let it turn into hurtful words or actions, and don’t go to sleep still angry. It is like milk left out too long, which goes bad; anger left until the next day turns into bitterness that is much harder to deal with. So our family needs a “pause plan”: when you are angry, first say “I need a pause,” go and cool down, then come back and talk well, and always make peace before bed.
ask: Which step do you find hardest when you are angry?
If someone tells you, “I need a pause,” how will you respect that?
soldier.do: Make yourself a “pause card” with your own ways to calm down, such as deep breathing, drinking water or drawing, and keep it in your school bag or pocket.

youth.talk: We want to share a new family rule with you, and it is one that we must keep first: when you are angry, you can say “I need a pause,” step away for a while, and come back to talk when you are calm. In the past we often said hurtful things in the heat of anger, and even let bad feeling drag on for days. Paul says not to let the sun go down on our wrath, and from today we want to make peace before bed, every time.
ask: Do you think the “pause plan” will work in our family? What needs adjusting?
What is the most effective way for you to calm down?
youth.do: As a family, decide on the pause rules, such as how long a pause may last, where to go, and who comes back first to talk; the parents promise to keep them first.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, help us pause when we are angry, calm down before we speak, and always make peace before we sleep. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Wait Like a Farmer
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: patience is waiting at the pace of a child’s growth

v: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.

lessons.still: Picture a farmer standing at the edge of his field, looking at the seedlings that have just sprouted. He doesn’t hurry them or pull at them; he simply waters and waits. Think back over this week: where were you like this farmer? Where were you rushing to pull up the seedlings? Ask the Holy Spirit to walk with you as you look.
teach: James says, “Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.” A farmer understands patience best. He does not dig up the seeds every day to see whether they have grown, and he does not get angry and tug at a seedling because it is short. He knows that the seed has been sown, the water has been given, and what is left is to wait for the season. Children’s growth has seasons too: some children bloom early, and some ripen late.

There is a Chinese story about “pulling up the seedlings to help them grow.” A farmer, finding his seedlings too slow, pulled each one up a little, and went home pleased, saying, “I helped the seedlings grow taller!” The next day, the whole field of seedlings had withered. Many parents’ anger is really that pulling hand: impatient that a child learns slowly, changes slowly, grows up slowly. Patience is drawing that hand back and trusting that God makes the seed sprout and grow, even though we may not know how.

This week we learned to be swift to hear, to see the root of our anger, to receive God’s patience, and to practice the pause plan. Today let us review honestly: how many times did I get angry this week? Fewer than last week? Which time did I pause successfully? Which time did I pull at the seedlings? And remember that patience is not only for our children but also for ourselves: parents need seasons to change, too. Write down next week’s adjustment, and keep waiting.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition themselves take patience. The fruit of the Spirit does not ripen overnight; a parent’s change and a child’s growth both take time. Keep your focus on Jesus, the Lord who makes the seed sprout and grow, not on your own impatience and not on your child’s speed.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who sends the early and late rain and makes the seed grow; he has his own time.
Who am I? — In what matter was I like a patient farmer this week? In what matter was I rushing to pull up the seedlings?
How should I respond? — Next week, in what matter will I deliberately wait at my child’s pace?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had been with his disciples for three years when Philip said, “Show us the Father.” Jesus answered, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip?” There was sadness in his voice, but no giving up. He kept teaching and kept waiting, until the Holy Spirit came and the disciples finally grew up.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me through my anger this week. I admit that several times I rushed to pull up the seedlings and was impatient with my child. Please forgive me, and heal my child’s heart. Thank you also for the times I paused successfully; that was your grace. Make me like a farmer who sows, waters, and then waits peacefully for your season. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: how many times did each of us get angry this week? Which pause worked? Which needs adjusting?
Ask your child: “This week, when Dad/Mom was angry, was it any different? Was it more like Jesus?”
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as praying before starting homework time
lessons.noon: “Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth” — Lord, today let me wait for my child as patiently as a farmer.

fam.key: Grow slowly, and God will help.

lamb.do: Look together at a plant or at a photo of your child when he was smaller, and gently stroke his head.
lamb.say: You grow slowly, we wait slowly, and God will help you grow.

sprout.story: A farmer planted rice, and every day he went to look at it and thought it was growing so slowly. One day he couldn’t help pulling every rice plant up a little, saying, “I’ll help you grow taller!” The next day all the rice had dried up. His son said, “Daddy, rice has to grow slowly. You can’t pull it!” Then the farmer knew he must wait patiently.
sprout.ask: What do you think the farmer should have done?
sprout.do: Take out the beans you planted this week (or plant a new one), measure together how tall it has grown, and say, “Grow slowly, we’ll wait for you!”

soldier.story: James says a farmer must wait patiently for the precious fruit of the earth until the early and late rains come. In ancient China there was a farmer who thought his seedlings were growing too slowly, so he pulled each one up a little, and they all withered. This is the story of “pulling up the seedlings to help them grow.” Learning new things is like this too: sometimes progress is slow, but if we keep trying, with God’s help we will slowly grow. Mom and Dad are learning too, so don’t be in a hurry to pull up your seedlings.
ask: This week, was there something you were more patient about than before?
What would you like Mom and Dad to give you a bit more time with?
soldier.do: Family meeting: each person says one “time this week I was very patient” and one “thing I want to be more patient about next week,” with Mom and Dad going first.

youth.talk: All this week we have been learning patience, and trying out the pause plan. To be honest, a few times it worked, and a few times we lost our tempers with you again. We found that our impatience is often because we feel you should grow up faster and understand faster. James says to wait like a farmer, and we want to learn to respect the pace of your growth, and we want to hear what you observed this week.
ask: This week, did you feel any change in the way we got angry?
In what matter do you feel we most need to give you more time?
youth.do: As a family, decide which patience practice to continue next week, and ask the child to be the “observer” who reports on Friday whether the parents managed it.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for waiting patiently for us to grow. Help us to wait patiently for one another and to grow up slowly together. In Jesus’ name, amen.

16.memT: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;

mem.t: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

sat.d: At breakfast, each person draws a slip of paper with a family member’s name on it, and must keep it secret. All day long you are that person’s “secret angel”: quietly pour him a glass of water, put his shoes away, leave a little card with a smiley face on his pillow. Young children can be helped by Mom or Dad. At supper the whole family guesses: “Who is my secret angel?” After the reveal, each person says: “Thank you for being kind to me.” Finally read Ephesians 4:32 together and pray holding hands.

sun: This week, at what moment did you most want to blame, yet chose kindness instead? What happened?
Think back to your own childhood: when you made a mistake, how did the adults respond? How does that response shape the way you respond to your children today?
To which family (or which friend of your child) will you take the initiative to show an act of kindness next week?

lessons.title: Be Kind to One Another
lessons.theme: Kindness is goodwill that reaches out first, and its source is that God forgave us first

v: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Be still, and think of the first family member who comes to mind this morning. Say slowly before the Lord: “Lord, as you have treated me, teach me to treat him.” Let those words rest for a moment.
teach: The word for kindness in the original carries the sense of “fitting, gentle, beneficial to others,” like a well-worn coat that fits the body: it doesn’t scrape or prick. Kindness is not passively refraining from losing your temper; it is goodwill that reaches out first. You see your child is tired, so you offer a glass of water before he asks. You see your spouse overwhelmed, so you take half of the dishes.

In verse 31, Paul first lists a “demolition list”: bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry and slander. In many families that list is played out at the supper table every day. Then he says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other.” Kindness does not grow in a vacuum; it is the new seedling planted in the heart after the old things have been cleared away.

The most important part is the last line: “just as God also in Christ forgave you.” The source of kindness is not our good temper but the cross. When parents remember how God has been kind to them, they are better able, at the moment the milk is spilled or the homework is forgotten, to choose kindness instead of scolding.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Kindness is the most “visible” of the nine fruits of the Spirit, and it always flows toward our “2.” A self-ruled parent first asks, “Does he deserve it?”; a self-emptied parent first asks, “How has God treated me?” Only when we are reconciled with God can kindness flow out; Jesus is our example and the Holy Spirit is the source of the fruit.
q: Who is God? — In Christ, God has forgiven me, and he has always been kind to me. Where have I recently experienced his kindness?
Who am I? — This week, what do I most often say at home: “what is good for building others up,” or the words on the list in verse 31?
How should I respond? — To which family member will I reach out with one concrete act of kindness today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was nailed to the cross, in agony and mocked by the crowd, the first words he spoke were: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” His kindness was not politeness shown in good times, but forgiveness flowing out of the deepest hurt. We can be kind to our family because he was kind to us first.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving me in Christ, again and again being kind to me. I admit that at home I often speak words of bitterness and anger; please take them out of my heart. Holy Spirit, grow the fruit of kindness in me, so that every word I speak today builds up my children and gives grace to those who hear. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Copy Ephesians 4:32 on a note and put it up in the kitchen or beside the bathroom mirror
Before you speak today, ask yourself: is this “good for building others up”?
Take the initiative to do one small thing for a family member that he did not ask for
lessons.noon: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other” — Lord, remind me right now that as you are kind to me, I should be kind to my family.

fam.key: God is kind to me, so I am kind to others.

lamb.do: When you change your baby’s diaper or wash his hands, slow down, look gently into his eyes and softly stroke his cheek.
lamb.say: You are precious. God loves you so gently, and so do Mommy and Daddy.

sprout.story: Little Rabbit ran so fast that he bumped into Squirrel and knocked over all the nuts Squirrel had worked hard to gather, rolling everywhere. Little Rabbit was frightened, sure that Squirrel would shout at him. But Squirrel said, “That’s all right, let’s pick them up together!” The two good friends laughed as they picked. The Bible says to be kind to others, which means treating people with a gentle and good heart, because God treats us that way too.
sprout.ask: If someone accidentally breaks your things, how can you be kind to him?
sprout.do: Play “Pick Up the Nuts”: scatter some balls or toys on the floor, pick them up together as a family, and each time you pick one up say, “That’s all right, I’ll help you!”

soldier.story: Ephesians 4 is like a list for tidying a room: first throw out the bad things (bitterness, anger, shouting and screaming, talking badly about others); then put in the good things (kindness, compassion, forgiveness). Paul says we do this because God in Jesus has already forgiven us. Think about it: if God counted up every wrong thing we did, we would be punished so much that we could not stand up. But God chose to be kind to us, so we can choose to be kind to others.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “kindness” and “being polite”?
Which person at home can you say a word “good for building others up” to today?
soldier.do: Make a “kind words jar”: today each person finds a chance to say one building-up word to a family member, writes it on a slip of paper and drops it in the jar, and at the weekend you read them together.

youth.talk: Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth.” Today many people think that having a sharp tongue is funnier and more real. Mom and Dad have to admit that at home we sometimes speak harshly, and even make jokes about your weaknesses, thinking it didn’t matter. When we read this passage today, we realized that God cares a great deal about how the people in a family speak to each other.
ask: Among your friends, which is more popular, a sharp tongue or kindness? Why?
Is there any way Mom and Dad talk that makes you feel very uncomfortable?
youth.do: Parents invite the child to be the “speech reminder” this week: whenever he hears the parents say something harsh, he gives a secret signal, and the parents promise not to get angry and to correct themselves at once.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always being kind to us. Help us today to say good words and do good things, and to be gentle and kind to everyone at home. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Kindness Leads to Repentance
lessons.theme: When my child fails, do I respond with condemnation or kindness?

v: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,

lessons.still: Recall the last time your child did something wrong: his face, your tone, the temperature in the air. Ask the Holy Spirit to walk you through it again; only look, and don’t hurry to defend yourself.
teach: Paul asks a sharp question: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” We often think a person must repent first in order to deserve kindness; but Scripture says it is God’s kindness that leads people onto the road of repentance. Kindness comes first, repentance after.

This is a mirror for parents. When our child fails a test, lies, or hits his brother, our first reaction is often to raise our voice and put on a stern face, thinking he will change only if he feels bad enough. What the child learns is often not repentance but hiding: next time hide it better, and you won’t get scolded. It is like the sun and the north wind in the old story: the winter sun makes a traveler take off his coat on his own more surely than the wind does.

Titus says that God saved us “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy.” We too received kindness first and learned obedience afterward. This does not mean no discipline is needed; it means that the undertone of discipline must be kindness: first let the child know “I still love you,” then walk with him through the consequences and the mending of the relationship.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Today is a day of “revelation”: the Holy Spirit shows us what kind of parents we are. A proud parent gives love only after the child admits fault; a humble parent gives love first, and then walks with the child to confess. Deal with your own heart first: is my strictness for my child’s life, or for my own face?
q: Who is God? — God uses the riches of his goodness, forbearance and patience to lead me back. Which part of his kindness moves me most?
Who am I? — When my child fails, am I the “condemn first” parent, the “cold shoulder” parent, or the “kindness first” parent?
How should I respond? — The next time my child does wrong, what will be the first sentence I say?
lessons.jesus: After Peter denied his Lord three times, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” That was not the look of a judge, but a love that let Peter go out and weep bitterly. After the resurrection, Jesus lit a charcoal fire on the shore and prepared breakfast before he asked, “Do you love me?” He was kind first, and restored afterward. This is exactly the pattern we must learn with a child who has failed.
lessons.pray: Lord, you lead me to repentance with kindness, yet I often push my child to confess with condemnation. Shine your light on me, and let me see the pride and fear hidden behind my strictness. Teach me, when my child fails, to let him know first that he is loved, and then to walk gently with him back. Amen.
acts: Write down the first thing you said the last time your child did wrong, and then write the version you wish you had said
Today when your child does something wrong, crouch down first, look into his eyes, and say: “I still love you.”
Say to a child you have been harsh with: “I was too fierce that day. I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “The goodness of God leads you to repentance” — Lord, let my kindness also become the way back for my child.

fam.key: God’s love helps me to be better.

lamb.do: When your child falls or cries, pick him up first, and speak softly to him only after he has quietened.
lamb.say: It’s all right. I’m here, and God is here too.

sprout.story: Lele the little bear knocked over Mommy’s flowerpot, and soil was scattered everywhere. He was so scared that he hid under the bed. Mommy Bear found him, and did not shout, but hugged him and said, “Mommy still loves you. Shall we tidy up together?” Lele crawled out from under the bed and said, “Mommy, I’m sorry!” He took the little broom and carefully swept the soil away.
sprout.ask: Why was Lele willing to come out and say sorry?
sprout.do: Act it out: one person is Lele and one is Mommy Bear, and practice saying “I still love you” and “I’m sorry.”

soldier.story: On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter said three times in the courtyard, “I don’t know him!” Just at the third time the rooster crowed, and Jesus turned and looked at Peter. That look was not a scolding, but it made Peter remember what Jesus had said, and he ran out and wept bitterly. Later, after Jesus rose again, he cooked fish for Peter by the lake and gently restored him. Peter was not changed by being scolded; he was changed by Jesus’ love.
ask: Which do you think makes a person change from the heart: being scolded, or being loved?
Have you ever done something wrong and been treated gently? How did you feel?
soldier.do: Write a “kindness card” to a brother, sister or classmate who has made you angry lately, and write: “I forgive you. We’re still friends.”

youth.talk: Mom and Dad want to be honest: in the past, when you made mistakes, we often scolded first and put on a stern face, thinking that was how you would remember. When we read today “the goodness of God leads you to repentance,” we realized that God does not treat us like that. We are not pretending you did nothing wrong; we want to learn to stand on your side first, and then face the problem together.
ask: When you have done wrong, what do you most want Mom and Dad to say or do first?
Has there been a time when being scolded made you want only to hide things?
youth.do: Parents find a quiet time to apologize to the child for one time they were too harsh in the past, and ask: “Next time, how could I do better?”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us even when we do wrong. Help us to be willing to say sorry when we are wrong, and help us to treat those who do wrong with love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Father Ran and Embraced Him
lessons.theme: I believe: God’s kindness is greater than my child’s failure

v: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.

lessons.still: Imagine you are the son walking home from far away, in worn-out clothes, with a confession speech all prepared in your heart. Then you see your father running toward you. Stay quietly in this picture for one minute.
teach: In the story of the prodigal son, the most surprising thing is not that the son turned back, but the father’s reaction: “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” In that culture, it was undignified for an elderly father to run in public; but this father didn’t care about his face. He cared only that his son had come home.

The son had prepared a speech, but he had said only half of it when the father interrupted him and ordered the robe, the ring and the sandals. The robe stood for honor, the ring for status, and the sandals for the fact that he was not a servant but a son. The father’s kindness was not “I’ll let you off this time,” but restoring him to his place in the house. Many parents forgive their children, and then for a long time afterward withdraw trust and warmth; the heavenly Father is not like that.

Today is a day of conviction. We want to turn our thinking from “my child must first prove himself before he deserves a pleasant look from me” to “God’s kindness is greater than my child’s failure, and greater than my own failure.” This is not naivety but faith: believing that God’s kindness can really change people, including our children and ourselves.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the human view to God’s view, from temporary failure to eternal identity. My child’s mistakes are temporary, but he is an inheritance God has entrusted to us, and that is eternal. People matter more than issues, and relationships matter more than face: better to lose a little face than to lose my child’s heart.
q: Who is God? — The heavenly Father ran when he saw the prodigal. How does this God see me today when I stumble?
Who am I? — After my child does wrong, do I withdraw warmth and trust for a long time, so that he feels he is only a “servant”?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declarations: I believe God’s kindness…; I believe my child…
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself told this story, and he told it to the Pharisees who looked down on sinners. Jesus is himself the revelation of the heavenly Father’s kindness: to the woman caught in adultery he said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” Kindness and truth are joined together in him.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for running to embrace me while I was still far off. I believe that your kindness is greater than my failure, and greater than my child’s failure. Take away the pride in my heart that wants my child to prove himself first, so that like you I may welcome a returning child with an embrace and restore him to his place in the family. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe God’s kindness…; I believe my child is…; I believe our family…
Think: are you still “keeping account” of a mistake your child made recently? Decide today to strike that entry out
Give your child a sign of “restoration”: a hug, a small treat he likes, or a task you trust him with again
lessons.noon: “While he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him” — Father, thank you for running to me; teach me also to run to my child.

fam.key: No matter what, the heavenly Father welcomes me home.

lamb.do: Play “Home Hugs” with your child: let him crawl or walk toward you from the other side of the room, and open your arms to welcome him and hold him tight.
lamb.say: You’re back! I’m so happy. I love you so much.

sprout.story: A younger son took his father’s money and went far away, and spent it all, until at last he was so hungry that he fought the pigs for food. He thought, “I will go home and say sorry to Daddy.” He was still far away when his father saw him, ran straight to him and hugged him tight, put beautiful new clothes on him, and held a big party!
sprout.ask: How do you think the father felt when he saw his son come back?
sprout.do: As a family, act out “Daddy runs to hug,” and afterward eat a little treat together to celebrate a “welcome-home party.”

soldier.story: Jesus told a story: the younger son asked for his share of the property, went far away and wasted it, and when it was all gone he had to feed pigs. He thought he would go home and be just a servant. But his father saw him from far away, ran to him and hugged him, and gave him a robe, a ring and sandals. The robe showed honor, the ring showed that he was still part of the family, and the sandals showed he was not a servant but a son. The father did not only forgive him; he made him a son again.
ask: If you were the younger son and saw your father running to you, how would you feel?
Why do you think the father didn’t scold him first and forgive him afterward?
soldier.do: Draw the robe, the ring and the sandals, and beside them write: “The heavenly Father lets me be his child.” Put it up above your desk.

youth.talk: We have heard the story of the prodigal son many times, but today Mom and Dad noticed something: the father did not put his son on “probation,” and did not say, “We’ll see how you behave.” Honestly, sometimes we forgive you, and then for several days afterward we are still cold, or we bring up old accounts. We want to learn from the heavenly Father: when we forgive, we really let you come back to your place in the family.
ask: How long do you think it takes in our family, after a mistake, to “get back to normal”?
Do you believe God’s kindness to you is greater than anything you have done wrong? Why is it sometimes hard to believe?
youth.do: Parents and child each write one “I believe” declaration about how God sees our failures, and read them to each other at supper.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being like that good father who always welcomes us home. When we do wrong, help us to be willing to come back to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Is There Anyone I Can Show Kindness To?
lessons.theme: Kindness goes out looking; go and do it today

v: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”

lessons.still: Be still and ask the Lord: “Lord, in our home and near our home, who still needs to be shown kindness?” Let a name or a face come up, and write it down.
teach: After David became king he asked an unusual question: “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” In those days a king usually wiped out the descendants of the former dynasty, but David went looking for them. He found a young man lame in both feet, hiding in a remote place and calling himself a “dead dog”: Mephibosheth.

David did not wait for Mephibosheth to come and plead; he sent for him. And he gave more than a little relief: he restored the land, and said, “You will eat bread at my table continually.” The highest peak of kindness is not charity but acceptance: giving that person a place at your table.

This is kindness in practice: not giving grudgingly when a child comes begging, but going out to look. Which child at home is most often overlooked? The quiet second child, or the oldest who is always being compared? Which elder in the extended family is seldom visited? Today, like David, ask: “Is there anyone I can show kindness to?” and then go and do it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In the eight steps of change, practice follows conviction. Kindness is not a feeling but an action; it does not wait for chances, it looks for them. Relationships matter more than things: David was willing to give back the land in order to have a person accepted again. To let Jesus reign is to let his kindness pass through our hands.
q: Who is God? — God is like David: he came looking for me while I was hiding, and invited me to eat at his table. How have I experienced such acceptance?
Who am I? — Am I a parent who takes the initiative to look for chances to show kindness, or one who helps only when someone asks?
How should I respond? — Who will I take my child to show kindness to today? What will we do?
lessons.jesus: People brought little children to Jesus, and the disciples, thinking it a nuisance, tried to send them away, but Jesus was angry with the disciples, and then “took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” To the ones who seemed least important in adult eyes, Jesus took the initiative and reached out. He shows us that kindness is giving a place to those who are most easily overlooked.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for finding me, as David found Mephibosheth, and for letting me eat at your table. Today open my eyes to see the people at home and nearby who most need kindness; and give me and my children a heart willing to act, not only to say good words but also to do good, so that people feel your acceptance at our family table. Amen.
acts: Together with your child, list three “people we can show kindness to”: one at home, one among relatives, one a neighbor or classmate
Choose one person today, and take your child along to give a small treat, a card or a phone call
At supper tonight, set aside a little extra time for the child at home who is most often overlooked, and ask about his day
lessons.noon: “You will eat bread at my table continually” — Lord, thank you for letting me sit at your table; let my table also be a place where others receive grace.

fam.key: I go looking for people I can help.

lamb.do: Hold your child and together pass a toy to another person at home, and then clap together.
lamb.say: We share together. This is kindness.

sprout.story: King David had a good friend named Jonathan. Jonathan had a son named Mephibosheth, whose feet were hurt so that he could not walk, and he hid far away. King David sent someone to find him, and said to him, “Don’t be afraid! You can come and eat at my table every day!” Mephibosheth was so happy. He had never imagined that a king would love him so much.
sprout.ask: Whom would you like to invite to our home to eat or play with us?
sprout.do: Put one extra place or a little bowl on the table, and say, “This is a place for someone who needs love.” Then pray for one person.

soldier.story: After David became king, he asked, “Is there anyone left in my good friend Jonathan’s family? I want to be kind to him.” Someone said that Jonathan had a son who was lame in both feet. David sent for him and brought him to the palace, gave him back all his grandfather’s land, and let him eat with the king every day. Mephibosheth had done nothing, yet he received all this, because David remembered his friendship with Jonathan, and remembered God’s kindness too. David did not wait for people to beg; he went to look for them himself.
ask: In your class, is there a classmate like Mephibosheth, often left out?
What do you think is the difference between “going to look for someone” and “helping only when asked”?
soldier.do: This week choose a lonely classmate at school or at church, and take the initiative to invite him to play, to eat lunch together, or give him a small card.

youth.talk: The first thing David did after becoming king was not take revenge, but ask, “Is there anyone I can show kindness to?” To be honest, Mom and Dad are usually busy with our own things and seldom go out to look for people who need help, and sometimes we don’t even notice who at home is in a low mood. Today we want to learn from David together: ask first, then go and do it.
ask: Is there someone around you whom everyone ignores but who really needs a friend?
If our family were to show kindness to someone together, who could it be? How could we do it so the person doesn’t feel pitied?
youth.do: As a family decide on one act of kindness, with the child planning the details and the parents supporting, to be done within this week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for welcoming us to your table, like King David. Help us today to find someone who needs love, to be kind to him, and to let him know that you love him. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Put On the Clothes of Kindness
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Was I more kind like Jesus this week?

v: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.

lessons.still: As if tidying a closet, recall what you “wore” at home this week: impatience, coldness, or kindness and compassion. Ask the Holy Spirit to go through them with you one by one, not to condemn, only to see.
teach: Paul uses “putting on clothes” to describe the new life: “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance.” Dressing is something we do every day, and we choose it ourselves. We do not put on clothes once for a lifetime; kindness too is something we choose to put on again every morning.

Notice the order: first “God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved,” and only then a heart of kindness. We do not work at kindness in order to be loved; because we are already loved, we are able to put kindness on. A mother in Kuala Lumpur raising two children alone said, “I was often too tired to be gentle. Then I found that I must first let God hold me, and then I have the strength to hold my children.”

This week we have learned that kindness is goodwill that takes the initiative, a power that leads people to repentance, greater than failure, and something to go out and look for. Today let us review honestly: at which moments did I put on kindness? At which moments did I change back into my old clothes? The review is not to beat ourselves up, but so that tomorrow morning we can choose more clearly what to put on.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the rhythm of growing life. A humble parent is willing to ask the child, “This week, was I more like Jesus?” Humility draws out humility: when the parent admits first, the child learns to admit as well. Love is the bond of perfection, and only within love does kindness not turn into people-pleasing.
q: Who is God? — God calls me “holy and beloved.” How does this identity help me choose kindness every day?
Who am I? — At what moment this week did I put on kindness? At what moment did I change back into my old clothes?
How should I respond? — Next week, in which time of day when kindness is easiest to lose (leaving in the morning, homework, bedtime), what specific adjustment will I make?
lessons.jesus: The prophet Isaiah describes Jesus: “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick.” Jesus never kicks a person who is down. As you look back on your failures this week, he treats you the same way: he doesn’t break you or quench you, but gently lifts you up and gives you a clean set of clothes.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for calling me holy and beloved. Looking back over this week, I see the moments when you helped me be kind to my children, and I also see the moments when I was impatient, cold, or said hurtful things. Please forgive me, and heal the family members I have hurt. Tomorrow morning, remind me to put on kindness again, and to love them by your love. Amen.
acts: Talk as a couple for ten minutes: what was the kindest moment in our home this week? At what time of day was kindness most lacking?
Ask your child: “This week, was Dad/Mom more gentle and kind like Jesus? Was there anything that made you sad?” Only listen; do not defend yourself
Write down one adjustment for next week, such as: “Every morning before leaving, hug my child first before hurrying him.”
lessons.noon: “A heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance” — Lord, today once more I choose to put on kindness.

fam.key: Every morning, I put on kindness.

lamb.do: When you dress your child, say one good word as you put on each piece: “gentle,” “love,” “kind.”
lamb.say: We put on our clothes, and we put on love.

sprout.story: Every morning Xiaoqi had to put on her clothes, socks and shoes. One day Mommy said, “Today we also put on a piece of clothing we can’t see, called ‘kindness.’” Xiaoqi asked, “How do I put it on?” Mommy said, “When you say good words to others and help them, you have put it on.” That day, Xiaoqi shared her favorite stickers with her little brother, and she felt as if she were wearing a very beautiful piece of clothing.
sprout.ask: This week, did you put on the “clothes of kindness”? What did you do?
sprout.do: Play the “dressing” game: each person pretends to put on a piece of clothing and, while doing so, tells one kind thing they did this week.

soldier.story: Paul says that every day Christians “put on” good character, like putting on a uniform: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, and over it all, love. The interesting thing is that clothes don’t jump onto you by themselves; you have to choose them and put them on. Weiming in Singapore says that each morning when he puts on his school uniform, he says in his heart, “Lord, today I want to put on kindness too.” One day he really held back from scolding the classmate who kept taking his eraser, and he even lent him one.
ask: This week, at what moment at home did you put on kindness? At what moment did you forget?
Do you think Mom and Dad were more like Jesus this week? You can be honest.
soldier.do: Ten-minute family meeting: each person says one “time I was shown kindness this week” and one “area I want to be kinder in next week.” Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we have thought together about kindness a great deal. Mom and Dad must admit first that on several rushed mornings we shouted again, and once when you were in a bad mood we did not ask properly. We don’t want to pretend we’ve done well; we truly want to hear your view, because what you see in us may be truer than what we see in ourselves.
ask: This week, did you feel our family was a little kinder? Where could you see it?
If we could change only one thing next week, which would you like Mom and Dad to change?
youth.do: Parents listen carefully to the child’s feedback, choose one thing to write on the fridge as next week’s adjustment, and invite the child to write down one of his own too.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us learn kindness this week. Some things we managed, and some we forgot. Remind us every morning to put on kindness and to love one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

17.memT: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

mem.t: ‘Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.

sat.t: Family Day: The Whole Family Does Good
sat.d: As a family, choose someone to do good for: the security guard in your building, the cleaning lady, an elderly neighbor who lives alone, or the owner of a shop you often visit. In the morning make a simple treat together or buy a box of fruit, and let each child draw a thank-you card that says, “Thank you, and God loves you.” In the afternoon deliver it as a family: the older children do the speaking and say thank you, and the younger ones hand over the cards. Back home, sit together and share: “What was their face like when they received it? How did my heart feel?” Finally recite Galatians 6:9 together and pray for that person.

sun: This week, in which “no fruit visible” matter did you most want to give up? What kept you sowing?
Whom do your children most often see you doing good for? What kind of “goodness” will they learn from you?
Next week, to which family or person would you like to lead your whole family in doing one good deed?

lessons.title: Do Good, and Do Not Lose Heart
lessons.theme: Goodness is love lived out; what is sown will surely be reaped

v: Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.still: Picture a field that has just been turned over, the soil still damp, with nothing yet to be seen. Sit for a while at the edge of this quiet field and say to the Lord: “Lord, you see every seed I have sown.”
teach: Among the fruit of the Spirit, “kindness” and “goodness” are often put side by side. If kindness is the gentle heart, goodness is the hand that turns that heart into action. Goodness is not only “not doing wrong”; it is taking the initiative to do what benefits others: cooking a pot of congee for a sick neighbor, going through the questions once more with a child who is doing homework late into the night, remembering an elder’s birthday.

Paul uses sowing and reaping: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” Parents sow every day at home: a word of praise, a time of company, a meal cooked with care, a prayer before eating. These seeds are buried in the child’s heart; for a time nothing shows, but they are growing. In the same way, a sarcastic remark or a broken promise is also a seed.

So Paul says, “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” Many parents lose heart, not because they don’t want to do good, but because they cannot see the fruit: the child still talks back, the spouse is still distant, and all the giving seems to have sunk without a trace. God’s promise is “in due season”: the time of harvest is in God’s hands, and the responsibility for sowing is in ours.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Goodness is not a plan for doing good deeds; it is the fruit that flows naturally from a life abiding in the Lord. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on whether the fruit appears at once; sow by following the Holy Spirit, and leave the time of harvest to God.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who, “in due season,” surely brings a harvest, and he remembers every seed I have sown.
Who am I? — These days, what kind of seed have I sown most at home? In what matter do I most want to lose heart and give up?
How should I respond? — Which “seed of goodness” will I sow at home today?
lessons.jesus: Peter describes Jesus: he “went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil.” Jesus’ whole life was a life of doing good, yet he was often misunderstood and rejected, and even his close disciples did not understand him. He did not stop because of this; he kept sowing all the way to the cross. The morning of the resurrection proved that not one seed he sowed was wasted.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for seeing every unnoticed act of giving at home. I admit that I often lose heart and want to give up because I cannot see the fruit. Holy Spirit, grow the fruit of goodness in me, so that I keep sowing, not by my own enthusiasm but by your strength. I believe that in due season you will bring a harvest to our family. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write down one thing you have been doing for a long time but whose fruit you cannot yet see, and pray over it: “Lord, I leave the time of harvest to you.”
Do one good deed at home today on your own initiative, and do not mention it; let only God know
Say to a family member: “Thank you for what you keep on doing. I see it.”
lessons.noon: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up” — Lord, give me strength today to keep sowing.

fam.key: Do good, and don’t give up.

lamb.do: Together with your child, put a bean or a seed into a small cup of soil, and holding his hand, water it gently.
lamb.say: We plant the seed, and God will make it grow.

sprout.story: Aming the little farmer planted a seed in the soil and watered it every day. On the first day, nothing. On the second day, still nothing. Aming wanted to give up. Daddy said, “Don’t lose heart. The seed is secretly growing in the soil!” Aming kept on watering. After many days, a little green shoot popped out of the soil! The Bible says doing good is like this too: don’t give up, and God will make it grow.
sprout.ask: What good thing can you do today, like planting a seed?
sprout.do: As a family, plant a mung bean or red bean in a cup, water it together every day, and see when it sprouts.

soldier.story: Paul says doing good is like farming: you reap what you sow. Plant watermelons and you won’t get apples; plant kindness and you won’t get a bad temper. But after the seed is sown, it takes a while to sprout. Xiaojie in Penang carried his grandmother’s shopping every day for several months, and she seemed to say nothing. One day, Grandma shared at church, “My grandson is the best gift God has given me.” Only then did Xiaojie know that his good deeds had been growing all along.
ask: Have you ever done something good, and it seemed that no one saw it, and you wanted to give up?
What do you think “in due season we will reap” means?
soldier.do: Make a “sowing record chart”: each day this week write down one good thing you did, and on Friday look together as a family at how many seeds you sowed.

youth.talk: Paul says, “Let’s not be weary in doing good,” and he knew that doing good often makes people tired and that many times there is no reward. Mom and Dad feel this too: sometimes we give a lot, yet it seems that no one cares. It may be the same for you at school: you help classmates and do the most work on the group project, and in the end nobody says thank you. In those times, should we keep going?
ask: Have you ever done something good and felt used or unseen? What did you think then?
What do you think is the biggest difference between a Christian doing good and anyone else doing good?
youth.do: Parents share one thing they persevered in for a long time and only later saw fruit from, then invite the child to share one thing he currently wants to give up on, and pray for each other.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us do good. Help us not to give up; even when nobody sees, you see. Let all the good seeds we have planted grow. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Parents Who Passed By on the Other Side
lessons.theme: When I see a need, do I stop, or do I see it and go around?

v: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.still: Think back over today or yesterday: was there a family member’s need that you saw, but were too busy and “passed by on the other side”? Ask the Holy Spirit to gently bring that picture before you.
teach: In the story of the Good Samaritan, the priest and the Levite are not bad men. They may have been hurrying to serve at the temple, or afraid of becoming unclean, or simply tired. The text says that they “saw him” and then “passed by on the other side.” What should startle us is not that they did not see, but that they saw, and had a seemingly reasonable reason to go around.

Parents today often “pass by on the other side” as well. A child wants to tell about school, and we say “mm” while looking at our phones; a child says in tears that classmates have left her out, and we say, “Don’t think too much, go and take your bath.” We are busy with important things, such as work, housework and even church service, and we walk past the wound in our child’s heart.

But the Samaritan “saw him, he was moved with compassion”; he went to him, poured on oil and wine, bandaged, set him on his own animal, took him to an inn, paid, and promised to return. Goodness is a chain of concrete actions, and it costs something: time, money, a disrupted plan. Today ask the Holy Spirit to shine light: at home, who is the one lying by the roadside? And which of the passers-by am I?
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; do not neglect a person because of a task. A self-ruled parent centers on his own schedule, and the child’s needs become an interruption; a self-emptied parent is willing to have his plans interrupted, because the person in front of him is the “2” God has entrusted to him. Goodness begins with seeing and takes shape in stopping.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who “saw him and was moved with compassion”; he has never passed by on the other side of me.
Who am I? — At home, am I more like the Samaritan who stopped, or like the priest and the Levite with very good reasons to go around?
How should I respond? — Whose need at home will I stop for and walk over to today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself is the true Good Samaritan. We fell into the hands of the robbers of sin and hurt and were beaten half to death, and he, unafraid of being made unclean, came to our side, bound up our wounds himself, paid the whole price, and promised to return. He said, “Go and do likewise.” He did it for us first, and only then invited us to do it.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I admit that at home I often “pass by on the other side”: I see my child’s need, but use busyness as an excuse to go around. Thank you that you have never done this to me. Give me eyes that see, a heart that is moved with compassion, and hands willing to stop. Let me stop for my family once today. Amen.
acts: When your child speaks to you today, put down your phone, turn around, and listen to the end while looking into his eyes
Ask a family member: “Is there something that has been hard for you lately that I haven’t noticed?”
Write down the reason you most often use to “go around,” and confess it to God
lessons.noon: “But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion” — Lord, let me see today, and stop.

fam.key: When I see a need, I stop and help.

lamb.do: When your child reaches up to be held, stop what you are doing, crouch down, pick him up, and give him a long hug.
lamb.say: I see you. I’m here.

sprout.story: A man was walking along the road when bad men beat him up, and he lay on the ground, hurting badly. The first man who came by looked at him and walked away; the second man came by and also walked away. Then the third man came. He stopped, put medicine on the hurt man, bandaged him, and took him to an inn to rest. Jesus says we should be good neighbors like this man!
sprout.ask: If you saw a child fall down and cry, what would you do?
sprout.do: Play the “Kind Helper” game: one person pretends to fall, and the others take turns being the helper, “bandaging” him with a toy bandage or a towel.

soldier.story: Jesus told a story: a man was beaten half to death by robbers and lay by the road. A priest came by, saw him, and walked on the other side of the road; a Levite did the same. Finally a Samaritan came, a man whom the Jews of that time looked down on most, and he stopped, bandaged the wounded man, took him to an inn, and paid for it. Jesus asked: who was a neighbor to that man? The answer: the one who was willing to stop and help.
ask: Why do you think the priest and the Levite didn’t stop? What might they have been thinking?
At school or at home, is there a need you saw but pretended not to see?
soldier.do: This week be a “stopping person”: each day notice one person who needs help, stop and help him, and tell Mom and Dad in the evening.

youth.talk: What saddens Mom and Dad most in this story is that the priest and the Levite were both “very spiritual people,” yet they walked past the wounded man. Sometimes we are like that too: busy with work and church matters, and when you were in a bad mood we did not stop to ask. We want to say to you that if you have ever felt that we “passed by on the other side,” you are right, and we want to change.
ask: Do you feel our family is too busy, so busy that no one really stops to care for each other?
In your world, who is the one “lying by the roadside” whom everyone goes around?
youth.do: Parents and child agree on a “stop signal”: when the child really needs to be heard, he only has to say the signal, and the parents put down what they are doing and listen with full attention for ten minutes.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for being the best Good Samaritan; you did not leave us behind. Help us to be willing to stop when we see others who need help. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: We Are His Workmanship
lessons.theme: I believe: God has already prepared good works for our whole family to walk in

v: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.still: Quietly look at your hands. They have cooked meals, held children, and also clenched into fists. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I am your workmanship, and these hands are yours too.”
teach: Paul says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.” The word “workmanship” can also be translated “masterpiece,” like a poem or a carefully carved work of art. We are not saved by doing good; once saved, we become God’s masterpiece, and doing good is not an achievement we strive to earn but the natural beauty this work displays.

Even more wonderful, these good works are what “God prepared before that we would walk in them.” It is like parents preparing breakfast for a child, who need only sit down and eat; God has already prepared good works along our path each day: a greeting a neighbor needs, an affirmation a child needs, a cup of hot tea a spouse needs. Our responsibility is not to invent good works, but to see them and step into the ones God has prepared.

This also changes the way we look at our children: they are God’s workmanship, too. The child who always messes up his room, the child who cannot sit still, are masterpieces God is still carving. Jesus said, “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The purpose of the whole family doing good is not that others praise our family, but that people see the heavenly Father.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. If I do good in order to be seen and praised, that is the self-ruled life; if I do good so that people see the heavenly Father, that is the self-emptied life. A change of viewpoint: from “I must be a good person” to “I am God’s work, and let him do good through me.”
q: Who is God? — God is the craftsman and father who made me with care and has prepared good works for me.
Who am I? — Do I often see my child as a “problem” rather than as “a work God is carving”? Whose glory am I doing good for?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declarations: I believe I am God’s workmanship…; I believe my child is…; I believe that today God has already prepared…
lessons.jesus: After washing his disciples’ feet, Jesus said, “I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” His goodness was not a speech; it was crouching down, taking up a towel, and washing dirty feet. When he did good, he did not seek people’s praise, only that the Father’s will be done and the Father be glorified.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making me in Christ Jesus; I am your workmanship. I believe you have already prepared good works for me and my family; I believe my children are also masterpieces you have carved with your own hands. Open my eyes to see the good works you have prepared today, so that the good deeds of our whole family may lead people to give glory to you. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe I am God’s workmanship…; I believe my child…; I believe God has prepared today…
Say to each child: “You are God’s masterpiece,” and name one place where you see God at work in him
Before you leave home today, pray: “Lord, let me see the one good work you have prepared for me today.”
lessons.noon: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them” — Lord, let me step into the good works you have prepared today.

fam.key: I am God’s masterpiece, and I do good things.

lamb.do: Gently hold your child’s little hands and feet, kiss them one by one, and slowly say the name of each part.
lamb.say: Your little hands and feet were made by God, and God made them so well.

sprout.story: An old potter took a lump of clay and slowly shaped it, slowly turned it, and made a beautiful vase. He said, “This is my favorite piece!” The Bible says each one of us is a work God has made, and God likes us very much. God has also prepared many good things for us to do: carry things for Mommy, smile at a friend, share toys with others.
sprout.ask: What good thing has God prepared for you to do today?
sprout.do: Using clay or dough, each person makes a small work, and when it is done says, “I am God’s work!”

soldier.story: Ephesians says we are God’s “workmanship,” which means something like God’s masterpiece. Like a painter painting a picture or an engineer designing a great bridge, God made you with great care. And God made you for a purpose: to do good. You don’t have to rack your brain to find these good works; God has already put them along your path every day. Jiaen in Vancouver noticed that the old lady next door had to carry out heavy trash every Wednesday, and he thought, “This may be the good work God prepared for me!” From then on he went to help every Wednesday.
ask: Do you feel you are God’s “masterpiece”? Why is it sometimes hard to believe?
What good work do you think God has prepared for you this week?
soldier.do: Each family member writes one “I believe” declaration, such as: “I believe I am God’s workmanship, and God has prepared good works for me.” Stick it on your bedroom door.

youth.talk: Sometimes you may feel you are not good enough: your grades, your looks and your talents don’t match up to other people’s. Sometimes Mom and Dad carelessly compare you with others, and make you feel that way even more. But the Bible says you are God’s workmanship, a masterpiece created in Christ. You do good not to prove you are good enough, but because you were already carefully made by God.
ask: How far is the sentence “I am God’s masterpiece” from the way you usually see yourself?
If God really has prepared some good works for you, what do you think they might have to do with your interests or abilities?
youth.do: Parents write the child a card listing three places where they see God’s handiwork in him, and invite the child to write down one “I believe” declaration of his own.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making each one of us so well. Help us to see the good things you have prepared, to do them, and to let others see your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Garments Dorcas Left Behind
lessons.theme: Doing good together as a family, so that goodness becomes the shape of our home

v: Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.
In those days, she became sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them.

Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.

lessons.still: Ask the Lord: “Lord, what do we have in our home that we can use to bless others?” Perhaps it is good cooking, a spare room, a craft or a little time. Wait quietly and let the answer rise.
teach: In the city of Joppa there was a woman disciple named Dorcas, and the Bible describes her in a single sentence: “This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.” After she died, the widows stood weeping around Peter, showing him the tunics and other garments Dorcas had made. She left no sermons and no buildings; she left clothes, one after another, worn on the bodies of the poor.

Goodness is often as concrete as this: a needle and thread, a meal, a lift. Dorcas used the craft she had. Every family has a “craft” God has given: grandparents in Taichung who can make rice cakes take their grandchildren to make them for the elderly who live alone at church; a dual-income couple in Singapore without much time invite a newly arrived family to lunch one Sunday a month. Goodness does not need to be big; it only needs to begin for real.

Hebrews says, “But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.” Goodness is a sacrifice, offering up time, strength and money. When children take part with their own hands, baking cookies together, wrapping gifts together, delivering them together, they learn more than “be a good person”; they learn “this is how our family lives.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the way of thinking and you change life; change life and you change the way you live. The best way for goodness to travel from ideas into daily life is for the whole family to do it together. Parents go first and children follow; life first, then relationships, then ministry. The experience of doing good together knits the hearts of the whole family together.
q: Who is God? — God is well pleased with the sacrifice of doing good and sharing, and he values every deed done for the least of these.
Who am I? — What “craft” or resources has God put in our family’s hands that we can use to bless others?
How should I respond? — What is the one good deed our whole family will do together today or this week? Who is responsible for which part?
lessons.jesus: On the day the five thousand were fed, what Jesus used was “a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish.” To the adults it seemed so little, “but what are these among so many?” Yet Jesus took it, gave thanks, and fed them all.
