He values the small goodness in a child’s hands, and he invites our children to hand over to him the little they have.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for valuing Dorcas’s every stitch, and for valuing the five loaves and two fish in a child’s hands. Make our family a home that does good, not only saying that we want to help others, but putting our hands to work together today. Use our small giving so that people feel your love, and so that our children come to know you through doing good. Amen.
acts: Hold a five-minute family meeting and choose one good deed to do together this week
Let each child be responsible for a part: drawing cards, wrapping, speaking, praying for the person
Complete the first step today: buy materials, phone to arrange a time, or make one card first
lessons.noon: “But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased” — Lord, today let our home offer you its small goodness.

fam.key: We do good things together as a family.

lamb.do: Let your child hold a sticker or a small cookie, and with your hand supporting his, give it together to another person at home.
lamb.say: We give to others, everyone is happy, and God is very happy too.

sprout.story: There was a lady named Dorcas who was very good at making clothes. When she saw people with nothing to wear, she stitched beautiful new clothes for them, stitch by stitch. Everyone loved her so much! Later she got sick and died, and everyone was very sad. Then Peter came and prayed to God, and God made Dorcas alive again! Everyone was so happy, because God loved this lady who helped others.
sprout.ask: What can your little hands do to help others?
sprout.do: Each person cuts out a “little garment” from colored paper, draws a heart on it, and gives it to someone at home or at church.

soldier.story: Dorcas lived in the city of Joppa, and often sewed clothes for poor widows. After she died, the widows showed Peter the clothes she had made, weeping as they looked. Peter knelt and prayed, and God raised Dorcas from the dead, and many people believed in the Lord because of it. Dorcas did nothing grand and dramatic; she simply used the craft she knew to help people, one garment at a time. God values such goodness, and through it he also lets more people know him.
ask: What “craft” do you have, such as drawing, making snacks, fixing things or telling stories, that you could use to help people?
In what way could our whole family help one person together?
soldier.do: As a family plan a “Dorcas project”: the Soldiers think up ideas, and you complete it together within this week and take photos to remember it.

youth.talk: Dorcas did not have much money and was not a famous preacher; she was simply very good at making clothes, and she used that to help people. Your generation has many skills that we don’t: editing videos, design, teaching people to use phones, playing music. Mom and Dad are thinking that perhaps what God has put in your hands is exactly what can bless people. This time we would like you to lead the whole family in doing good.
ask: What ability do you think you have that could be used to help others?
When doing good, how can we avoid it turning into “showing off” or just posting online?
youth.do: Invite the child to be the “team captain” of the family’s good deed this week, deciding who and how, with the parents supporting and driving.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving each of us different abilities. Help our whole family to do good together, like Dorcas, so that people see your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Seed Grows in the Night
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: keep sowing, and leave the harvest to God

v: He said, “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth,
and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how.
For the earth bears fruit by itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.
But when the fruit is ripe, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”
Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.
He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

lessons.still: Recall the seeds you sowed at home this week: a word, a meal, a time of company; and also remember the times you sowed badly. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and then place them all in God’s hands.
teach: Jesus said that God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, “and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how.” The sower does not need to dig the seed up each day to check whether it has grown; his responsibility is to sow and water, and then to go to sleep. The mystery of growth is in God’s hands.

One of the greatest temptations for parents is to “dig up” the child every day to inspect him: has his faith grown? has his character improved? why is he still the same after I have said it so many times? This anxiety often makes us grip tighter and tighter, and injures the tender shoot. A father of three in Taipei said, “I learned to pray after sowing, and then go to sleep.” This is not neglect; it is trust.

The psalm says, “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.” This week we learned that goodness must be lived out, must stop, is prepared by God, and is to be done as a whole family. Today we look back: which seeds did we sow? When did I pass by on the other side? What needs adjusting next week is not doubling our anxiety, but sowing more faithfully and sleeping more peacefully.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review and adjustment are not relying on yourself with the head, but relying on the Spirit with the heart. The head worries and keeps calculating whether the child has improved; the heart rejoices, believing that God is at work even in the night. Faithfulness is our part, the result is God’s sovereignty: let God be God, and let people be people.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who makes the seed sprout in the night; he is still at work when I cannot see.
Who am I? — What seeds of goodness did I sow this week? Where did I “pass by on the other side”? Do I often dig my child up to inspect him?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week? Which “no fruit visible” anxiety will I hand over to God?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” He himself is the grain that fell into the ground, three days in the darkness of the tomb, and then bore fruit by the thousands and millions. He lets us know that when things look most hopeless, God is often preparing the harvest.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me as I look back over this week. I see that some seeds were sown, and I also see that several times I passed by my family’s needs. Please forgive me, and let those good seeds grow slowly in my children’s hearts. I hand my anxiety to you; next week help me to sow faithfully and to sleep peacefully. Amen.
acts: Talk as a couple for ten minutes: what seeds of goodness did our family sow this week? At what moment did we pass by each other’s needs?
Ask your child: “This week, was Dad/Mom more like Jesus in goodness? Was there a time I didn’t stop to listen to you?”
Write down one adjustment for next week, and write a prayer about one “no fruit visible yet” matter to hand over to God
lessons.noon: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” — Lord, I hand the seeds I have sown to you; I believe you will make them grow.

fam.key: I sow the seed, and God makes it grow.

lamb.do: Take your child to see the cup of beans planted this week, let him touch the soil or the little sprout, and clap your hands together.
lamb.say: Look! God made it grow, and God makes you grow too.

sprout.story: Every night before going to bed, Xiaoyun ran to look at the beans she had planted. Mommy smiled and said, “While you are sleeping, the beans are growing too!” Xiaoyun didn’t believe it, but when she got up early next morning, she really saw a little sprout! Jesus says God’s Kingdom is like this: the good things we do are like seeds, and while we sleep, God is still making them grow slowly.
sprout.ask: Which “good deed seed” did you plant this week?
sprout.do: Go and look at the cup of beans planted this week; each time someone tells of a good deed they did this week, put a little pebble or a sticker beside the cup.

soldier.story: Jesus said: a farmer sows seed in the ground, sleeps at night and gets up by day, and the seed sprouts and grows by itself, though the farmer does not know how. First the blade, then the ear, and finally the full grain. Doing good and learning goodness are like this too: it doesn’t grow in a day, and we can’t make it grow by ourselves, but God makes it grow in places we cannot see. Our job is to sow every day.
ask: What good seeds did you sow this week? Was there a time you saw a need but didn’t stop?
Do you think Mom and Dad were more good this week? You can be honest.
soldier.do: Ten-minute family meeting: look at this week’s “sowing record chart,” and each person says one good deed they are happiest about and one thing to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we talked a great deal about goodness and doing good. Mom and Dad want to admit first that several times when you wanted to talk to us, we kept scrolling on our phones and gave you half-answers, and some of the good deeds we said we would do together we put off and haven’t finished. We are learning too. We don’t want to show you a perfect picture, but to let you see what a grown-up who truly wants to change looks like.
ask: This week, did you feel any small difference in our family when it comes to “doing good”?
Is there a good thing you have kept doing but can’t yet see fruit from? How could we support you?
youth.do: Parents first name one failure and one adjustment of their own this week, then invite the child to give a suggestion, and the family chooses one good deed to keep doing together next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us do good this week. Some we managed, and some we forgot. Let the good seeds we have planted grow slowly, and help us keep going next week. In Jesus’ name, amen.

18.memT: ‘Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.

mem.t: ‘It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

sat.d: Go as a family to a park or a riverside and pick up a few smooth stones, then take them home and wash them. Each person thinks of one time “God was faithful to our family”: provision when we moved, healing in sickness, finding a job, a little brother’s birth, Grandma coming safely home from hospital. With a permanent marker, write a keyword and the date on a stone; little ones can draw a picture. Stack the stones on a plate in the living room, and, as Samuel set up “Ebenezer,” say together: “The LORD helped us until now.” Later, when visitors or children ask, tell the story of each stone.

sun: This week, when did you especially experience God’s faithfulness that is “new every morning”?
What promise have you made to your child but not kept? What effect did it have on your child and on you?
Next week, what small action, saying what you mean and doing it, will help your children know the faithful heavenly Father better?

lessons.title: New Every Morning
lessons.theme: God’s faithfulness is not cut off by our failures

v: This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.
It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
“The LORD is my portion,” says my soul. “Therefore I will hope in him.”
The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.
It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.

lessons.still: In the early morning, while the light is still faint, or in the quiet of deep night, breathe quietly. Recall yesterday’s weariness and failures, and then say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you for giving me a new morning today.”
teach: Lamentations is a book written in the ruins. Jerusalem had been destroyed, the temple burned, the people carried off, and the prophet sat in the ashes weeping. Yet right in the middle of the darkest chapter, chapter three, he suddenly says, “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.” What he recalls is this: “It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.”

Then he says, “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” This faithfulness is the “faithfulness” among the fruit of the Spirit: saying and it counts, always the same, dependable. God’s faithfulness is not something he remembers to give now and then; it is like the sun that rises each day, appearing punctually morning after morning, without our having to behave well first.

For parents, this is a great comfort. Last night you may have shouted at your child again, or not finished reading that book with him. But this morning, God’s loving kindness is new again. We can become faithful parents not because we are so dependable, but because we have a God who is utterly faithful. His faithfulness is the source from which we learn to be faithful, and the ground on which we begin again after we fail.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. Faithfulness is not gritted out by willpower; it is the fruit of living in the faithful God. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on your own failures: receive God’s new loving kindness first each morning, and only then have strength to give your child a new beginning.
q: Who is God? — On my most failed days, the days that feel most like ruins, how is God’s loving kindness “new every morning”?
Who am I? — Do I often carry yesterday’s failures into today, so that neither I nor my children can begin again?
How should I respond? — Tomorrow morning, what is the first thing I will do on waking to receive God’s new loving kindness?
lessons.jesus: Before ascending, Jesus promised his disciples, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” The disciples had run away and denied him, yet he did not take back his promise. Jesus is the fullest display of God’s faithfulness: when he said he would die, he died; when he said he would rise, he rose; when he said he would be with us, he has not left us for a single day.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you that your loving kindness is new every morning. I admit that I often live today with yesterday’s failures and guilt, and often look at my children by yesterday’s mistakes. Let me come each morning to receive your mercy first, and then take this new loving kindness to love my family. Great is your faithfulness, and I will look to you. Amen.
acts: Tomorrow morning, before you pick up your phone, read Lamentations 3:22–23 once
Say to your child today: “Yesterday is over. Today we begin again.”
Write down one thing in which God has been faithful to your family in the past, and tell it to your children this evening
lessons.noon: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” — Lord, thank you that your loving kindness is new again today.

fam.key: God’s love is new every morning.

lamb.do: When your child wakes in the morning, open the curtains to let the sunshine in, pick him up, and say good morning to the sun together.
lamb.say: Good morning! God’s love is new again today, and I love you.

sprout.story: Every morning, Mr. Sun gets up right on time. Whether it rained or thundered the day before, the next morning the sun still comes out. Xiaole asked Daddy, “Will the sun ever forget to get up?” Daddy said, “No, because God makes it come out every day. God loves us like the sun, too: every morning right on time, and never forgetting.”
sprout.ask: This morning when you woke up, what did you want to say to God?
sprout.do: Tomorrow when you get up, stand by the window as a family and say together: “Thank you, God, your love is new again today!”

soldier.story: The prophet Jeremiah lived in a city destroyed by its enemies. The houses had fallen, the temple was burned, and many people had been taken away. He was very sad and wept for a long time. But suddenly he remembered something: God’s loving kindness has never stopped, and it is new every morning. It is like the sun: whatever happened yesterday, it rises again today. So Jeremiah had hope again. God’s faithfulness means God does what he says and never changes.
ask: Have you ever been so sad that it felt as if everything was broken? What could you remember then?
What do you think it means for someone who has made a mistake that God’s loving kindness is new every morning?
soldier.do: This week, each morning after you get up, write down one “new thing God has given me today,” such as a new day, breakfast, or a family member’s smile.

youth.talk: Lamentations was written in the middle of ruins, and the author does not pretend everything is fine. Sometimes your life may feel like ruins too: a failed exam, a friend’s betrayal, a bad atmosphere at home. Mom and Dad have days like that, and sometimes we are even the reason you feel like you are in ruins. But the author, in the darkest place, says: God’s loving kindness is new every morning.
ask: When days are very bad, do you think saying “God is faithful” is escaping reality, or is it a kind of courage?
Is there something that, looking back, you realize God was with you all along?
youth.do: Parents share a story of experiencing God’s faithfulness in a low point, and invite the child to share one too, or pray together for the “ruins” the child is facing now.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us new love every morning and never forgetting us. For what we did wrong yesterday, please forgive us; today, help us begin again. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Let Your “Yes” Be “Yes”
lessons.theme: Am I a parent who does what I say, or one who often says it and it doesn’t count?

v: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.
LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?
He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart;
he who doesn’t slander with his tongue, nor does evil to his friend, nor casts slurs against his fellow man;
in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to help you recall the “in a little while,” “next time” and “I promise you” you spoke to your children this week. Which did you do? Which did you forget? Let them come up quietly, one by one.
teach: Jesus said, “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” It sounds simple, but for parents it is hard. We often say, “I’ll play with you in a moment,” and the whole evening goes by; we say, “I’ll take you to the park this weekend,” and when the weekend comes we are tired; we say, “If you do that again, I will…” and in the end do nothing. The children hear it again and again and slowly learn: what Mom and Dad say doesn’t necessarily count.

Psalm 15 describes the one who may dwell on God’s holy hill: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change.” Faithfulness means that the words we speak carry weight. For a child, the more consistent the parents’ promises and boundaries are, the safer and more predictable the world is. In a home where words often don’t count, children become anxious, or learn to keep bargaining, because they do not know which sentence is true.

Today ask the Holy Spirit to shine on this: what kind of parent am I? The “say yes to anything” type, who agrees just to quiet the child? The “say it and forget it” type, so busy I cannot remember my promises? Or the “threaten but never follow through” type, who says heavy words and never carries them out? We must also admit that some threats should never have been spoken. Faithfulness begins with saying a little less, and doing what we say.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Today is a day of revelation, seeing ourselves. A self-ruled parent uses promises to buy a moment’s quiet and threats to buy obedience, and words become tools of control; a self-emptied parent lets words be a guarantee of love. A humble parent is willing to say less and do more, and to apologize when he gets it wrong.
q: Who is God? — What God says, he surely brings about, and every word of his can be trusted. Where have I seen his promises kept?
Who am I? — Am I more the “say yes to anything” parent, the “say it and forget it” parent, or the “threaten but never follow through” parent?
How should I respond? — Which promise do I owe my child that I will keep today, or honestly apologize for?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to his disciples, “In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you.” He never gave his disciples empty comfort, and never said things to please them. What he said was true, so the disciples could stake their whole lives on his word. Our children also need parents they can trust.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that every word you speak is true. I admit that I often promise my children something offhandedly and forget to do it, and I also say harsh words that I never really meant to carry out. Shine your light on me, so that I think before I speak, and do what I have said. And for the promises that fell through, I will honestly apologize to my children. Amen.
acts: List the promises you have made to your child recently and not yet kept, and choose one to do today
Before saying “in a moment” today, name a specific time, such as “At eight o’clock, I’ll spend ten minutes with you”
If a promise cannot be kept, say to your child: “I’m sorry. I promised, and I didn’t do it.”
lessons.noon: “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” — Lord, let all my words today be words that can be trusted.

fam.key: Do what you say.

lamb.do: Say, “I’ll pick you up when I count to three,” count slowly “one, two, three,” and then really pick your child up and spin him around.
lamb.say: I said it, so I do it. God loves you like that, too.

sprout.story: Little Bear said to Little Rabbit, “Tomorrow I’ll bring you honey cookies to eat!” The next day it rained very hard, but Little Bear still came, holding an umbrella and a box of honey cookies. Little Rabbit was so moved: “You said it, and you really did it!” Little Bear said, “Because I’m your good friend!” God is like this too: what he says, he always does.
sprout.ask: Is there something you promised someone but haven’t done yet?
sprout.do: Play the “Say It, Do It” game as a family: each person says one small thing they can do right now, such as “I’ll get Mommy a glass of water,” and then goes and does it at once.

soldier.story: Jesus said, “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” It means that what we say should count, with no need to swear or make pinky promises, because we are people who do what we say. Jiahao in Tainan promised to help Grandpa fix his bicycle, but on Saturday his classmates invited him to play ball. He badly wanted to go, but he remembered Jesus’ words, and first helped Grandpa fix the bike, and then went to the court. Grandpa patted his shoulder and said, “You are a child who can be relied on.”
ask: Among your classmates, who is a person who does what he says? How do people feel about him?
Have you recently promised something and not done it? How could you put it right?
soldier.do: Make a “promise card”: write down one thing you promised your family this week, and when you have done it, ask a family member to sign it.

youth.talk: Mom and Dad want to be honest first: we often say “next time” and “in a moment” to you, and the next time never comes. Sometimes we even say heavy things such as “If you do that again, don’t go out,” and then it all comes to nothing. Today we realized that this makes it hard for you to believe our words, and even makes you feel that adults don’t need to be accountable for what they say. We are sorry.
ask: Do you remember a promise Mom and Dad made that was never kept? You can say it directly.
Among your friends, how important is keeping your word? What do you think of people who often cancel at the last minute?
youth.do: Ask the child to name one promise the parents owe him, and the parents keep it within this week, or sincerely explain why they cannot and apologize.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you do everything you say. Help us to be people who do what we say, and to work hard to complete what we promise others. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: If We Are Faithless, He Remains Faithful
lessons.theme: I believe: God’s faithfulness holds me and my children for a thousand generations

v: If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.”
Know therefore that the LORD your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commandments,

lessons.still: Put your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. This heart has beaten for so many years and never stopped; who is holding it up? Say quietly to the Lord: “Lord, even if I am faithless, you remain faithful.”
teach: Paul wrote to Timothy from prison: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.” This is not encouragement to be unfaithful carelessly; it tells us that God’s faithfulness is not built on our performance but on his own character. He is faithful, not because we deserve it, but because this is the kind of God he is.

Moses told Israel that the LORD your God “himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commandments.” A thousand generations is an extremely long time. Our family line may have breaks: divorce, betrayal, elders whose words did not count, promises never kept. But God’s faithfulness can begin afresh with our generation and flow down from one generation to the next.

Today is a day of conviction, and we want to turn our thinking around: from “I must be a perfectly reliable parent, or my children will not feel secure” to “God’s faithfulness holds me and holds my children.” Of course parents should work to be faithful, but a child’s ultimate security is built not on our never failing, but on the heavenly Father who never fails.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the temporary to the eternal, from my dependability to God’s faithfulness. A proud parent pretends never to break faith; a humble parent admits, “I will fail, but God will not.” Letting children place their trust in God and not in their parents is the greatest security a parent can give.
q: Who is God? — God “can’t deny himself”; his faithfulness rests on his own nature. How does this change the way I see my failures?
Who am I? — What “breaks of faithfulness” are there in my family line? Am I afraid I will pass them on too?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declarations: I believe God’s faithfulness…; I believe that beginning with my generation…
lessons.jesus: Paul says, “For however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes.’” Every promise God made in the Old Testament to Abraham, to David, to Israel was fulfilled in Jesus. When we look at the cross and the empty tomb, we know that God’s word has never failed. Jesus is the “Yes” of God’s faithfulness.
lessons.pray: Faithful Father, I believe that even if I am faithless, you remain faithful. I believe that you keep covenant and loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love you; I believe that beginning with my generation, your faithfulness will flow through our family from generation to generation. Let my children place their trust in you, and not in an imperfect me. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe God’s faithfulness…; I believe that even if I am faithless…; I believe that beginning with my generation…
Think of one “break of faithfulness” in your family line, and pray about it before God
Tell your child: “Mom/Dad sometimes can’t manage, but the heavenly Father never fails.”
lessons.noon: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.” — Lord, my hope is not in myself but in your faithfulness.

fam.key: The heavenly Father never breaks his word.

lamb.do: Play peekaboo with your child: cover your face with your hands, then open them and say, “I’m here!” Repeat several times, appearing with a smile each time.
lamb.say: I am always here, and the heavenly Father is always here.

sprout.story: Xiaoli’s daddy promised to take her to the zoo on Saturday, but suddenly he had to work overtime and could not go. Xiaoli was so disappointed that she cried. Daddy hugged her and said, “I’m sorry, Daddy can’t do it this time. But there is a Father in heaven, and what he says he can always do!” Xiaoli wiped her tears and said, “Will the heavenly Father always be with me?” Daddy said, “Yes, he has promised.”
sprout.ask: Why do you think the heavenly Father never breaks his word?
sprout.do: As a family think of one “thing the heavenly Father has promised us,” such as “He will always be with us,” and say it loudly together three times.

soldier.story: God once promised Abraham that his descendants would be as many as the stars of heaven. But Abraham waited twenty-five years, and had his son Isaac only at the age of a hundred. In between, Abraham had his own failures: he lied, he was impatient, he tried to do things his own way. Yet God did not take back his promise because Abraham was faithless. The Bible says the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and did to Sarah as he had spoken. People break faith, but God is always faithful.
ask: Do you think Abraham would have wanted to give up after waiting twenty-five years?
When Mom and Dad or a friend let you down, how does it help to think that God is always faithful?
soldier.do: Write an “I believe” card: “I believe the heavenly Father is always faithful, because…” and write an example you have experienced, then stick it on your desk.

youth.talk: To be honest, Mom and Dad will certainly let you down. We have before, and we will again. We don’t want you to think that faith means having a perfect pair of parents. Paul says, “If we are faithless, he remains faithful.” What we most hope for is not that you depend on us all your life, but that you come to know for yourself the God who will never let you down.
ask: What do you think a person’s sense of security should be built on?
When you are disappointed with adults, are you also disappointed with God? How do you think the two can be separated?
youth.do: Parents and child each write one “I believe” declaration about God’s faithfulness; parents may also apologize for a time they let the child down.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you never break your word. Even if Mom and Dad or friends cannot do it, you will. Help us to go on believing in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Faithful in the Very Little
lessons.theme: Faithfulness begins with small promises and small habits; start today

v: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?
A righteous man walks in integrity. Blessed are his children after him.

lessons.still: Ask the Lord: “Lord, in what very small thing can I show my child faithfulness today?” It may be being on time, a phone call, or a goodnight. Write it down.
teach: Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” Faithfulness does not suddenly appear at the big turning points of life; it grows out of the small things of each day. Children rarely judge whether their parents are dependable by what we said on big occasions; they look at the small things. We said we would be there at five: were we on time? We said we would tell a story at bedtime: did we remember?

Proverbs says, “Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man? A righteous man walks in integrity. Blessed are his children after him.” It is easy to say how much we love our children, but hard to show up steadily every day. A father who works in Los Angeles and often travels decided to video call his children at nine every evening on the dot, even if only for three minutes. Two years later his daughter said, “I know that at nine o’clock Daddy will be there.”

Faithfulness also includes consistent boundaries: if we say no candy today, we do not change our minds tomorrow because the child throws a tantrum; if we agree on half an hour of screen time, we keep it ourselves too. Consistency is not rigidity; it lets children know that the rules at home can be trusted. Today’s practice is simple: promise a little less, and do what you promise; take one small thing and do it very punctually and steadily.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Changing the way of thinking must go on to practice, and practice must become a repeated habit. Faithfulness is the same small thing, done again and again, steadily. When life is changed, relationships are built: a child’s security grows out of the parents’ consistency day after day.
q: Who is God? — God is faithful even in the smallest things: the sunrise, the seasons, every breath. His faithfulness is often quiet and steady.
Who am I? — In small things, would my child say that I am a dependable parent? In which small thing do I most often break faith?
How should I respond? — Which smallest thing will I choose today, to begin doing steadily?
lessons.jesus: Before he left this world Jesus said to his disciples, “I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.” He did what he said, sending the Holy Spirit to live within us. He was also faithful in small things: remembering Peter’s mother-in-law, remembering Zacchaeus’s name, remembering to light a fire by the lake and cook breakfast for his weary disciples.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you are faithful in both big things and small. I admit that I often want to do big things to prove I am a good parent, yet I fail again and again in the small things. Today help me begin with one very small thing: being on time, remembering, doing what I say. Let my children see your faithfulness in these small things. Amen.
acts: Together as a family, make a “family promise,” such as five minutes of prayer before bed every night, and keep it every day this week
For the times you have arranged today (pick-up, play, story), show up on time
Promise one less thing today that you might not manage, and say honestly: “I’m not sure I can do this, so I won’t promise it yet.”
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” — Lord, today in one small thing, let me show my child your faithfulness.

fam.key: Do what you say, even in small things.

lamb.do: Every day at the same time, soothe your child to sleep with the same song or the same sentence; begin this little ritual today.
lamb.say: Goodnight, my treasure. God watches over you, and I’ll still be here tomorrow.

sprout.story: Bobo the puppy sat at the door every evening waiting for his young master to come home from school. Wind or rain, Bobo was always there on time. As soon as his master opened the door, he saw Bobo wagging his tail to welcome him. Mommy said, “Bobo is so faithful!” The young master said, “I want to be like Bobo, and put my toys away on time every day!”
sprout.ask: What small thing can you do on time every day?
sprout.do: Choose one small thing as “my faithful task,” such as putting your shoes away every night before bed, and stick on a sticker for every day this week you do it.

soldier.story: Samuel served in the temple from childhood, and what he did each day was small things: opening the temple doors, lighting the lamp, helping the priest Eli. No one applauded, and no one paid special attention. But he did it faithfully every day. The Bible says that Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground. A child who was faithful in small things became, when grown, a prophet whom all Israel could trust.
ask: Which do you think shows better whether a person can be relied on, small things or big things?
What “small thing to do every day” could you take charge of at home?
soldier.do: Each family member takes on one small daily chore, does it every day this week, and in the evening you tick each other’s names off.

youth.talk: Jesus said that whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. Mom and Dad have been thinking: we often ask you to keep the rules, while we ourselves say we won’t bring phones to the table and then pick them up again, or say we won’t talk about homework after eight o’clock and can’t help nagging. You surely see these small things. We want to begin with ourselves, and do what we say in the small things.
ask: Which “rule” in our family do you think the adults don’t keep themselves?
In which small thing do you think you are already a very faithful person?
youth.do: As a family decide on one small rule that everyone (parents included) will keep this week, ask the child to be the monitor, and look together on Friday at how it went.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for taking care of us every day and never forgetting. Help us to do what we say even in small things, and to be people who can be trusted. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Faithful Steward
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Was I more like the faithful heavenly Father this week?

v: Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

lessons.still: Imagine the master has returned and is sitting in front of you, asking gently: “This week, how did you take care of the children I entrusted to you?” There is no need to be afraid; he is a loving master. Answer him honestly.
teach: Paul says, “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” A steward is not the master; what he manages does not belong to him. It is the same for parents: our children are not our property but an inheritance entrusted by God. What God requires of a steward is not success or perfection, but faithfulness. This frees parents from the burden of “I must bring my child up successfully.”

In Jesus’ parable, the master says to the faithful servant, “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things.” Notice that the master praises faithfulness in “a few things.” A grandmother in Singapore who looks after two grandchildren said, “I can’t give big lectures. I only cook every day and pray for them every night.” That is faithfulness in God’s eyes.

This week we learned that God’s loving kindness is new every morning, that we should do what we say, that God’s faithfulness holds us, and that we should be faithful in small things. Today let us review honestly: which promise did I keep? Which fell through? Was the me that my child felt this week dependable? After the review, with the master’s praise and grace, adjust one small thing for next week.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Parents are not the kings of the home but God’s stewards. A steward’s measure of success is faithfulness, not the child’s performance. When you review, first ask whether you have been faithful, and then whether the child has improved; deal with your own heart first, and then the child’s behavior.
q: Who is God? — God is the loving master who values my faithfulness in “a few things” and is glad to praise me.
Who am I? — Was I a faithful steward this week? Which promise did I keep? Which fell through?
How should I respond? — In which small matter will I adjust next week, so that my child can trust me more and know the faithful heavenly Father better?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished!” He had completed everything the Father entrusted to him, leaving nothing undone. Scripture says he was “faithful to him who appointed him.” Jesus is the most faithful Steward and Son. When we look back at our own unfaithfulness, we can rest in the work he has already completed, and set out again.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for entrusting my children to me and letting me be your steward. Looking back over this week, I see that I kept some promises, and I also see several times when what I said did not count. Please forgive me, and heal the disappointment in my children’s hearts caused by my unfaithfulness. Next week help me to be more faithful in small things, so that my children see your faithfulness in me. Amen.
acts: Talk as a couple for ten minutes: what did we say to our children and do this week? Which promises fell through?
Ask your child: “This week, did Dad/Mom do what they said, more like the heavenly Father? Was there a time they let you down?”
Write down one adjustment for next week, and re-schedule a time to keep the promise you did not keep
lessons.noon: “It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” — Lord, I do not ask to be perfect, only to be faithful in the small things you have entrusted to me.

fam.key: God wants us to be faithful people.

lamb.do: At bedtime, soothe your child to sleep with the same song and the same sentence you have used every day this week, and finally kiss his forehead.
lamb.say: Every night this week, I was here. God is here every day, too.

sprout.story: Before going on a journey, a master gave money to three servants. Two servants worked hard and made the money grow; one servant buried the money in the ground and did nothing. When the master returned, he smiled at the hard-working servants and said, “Well done, good and faithful servant!” We can be faithful little helpers too, and finish well the small tasks Mommy and Daddy give us.
sprout.ask: This week, was there a small thing that you finished well?
sprout.do: Look at this week’s “faithful task” stickers and count them together as a family; clap for each person and say, “You are a good and faithful little helper!”

soldier.story: Jesus told a story: before he went away, a master gave his money to three servants to manage. Two servants were very faithful and managed it well; one servant hid the money. When the master returned, he praised the faithful servants and put them in charge of more. The Bible says that what matters most in a steward is faithfulness. Each one of us is God’s steward: our time, abilities, body and family are all things God has given us to care for.
ask: In what matter were you a faithful steward this week? What didn’t you do well?
Do you think Mom and Dad did what they said this week? You can be honest.
soldier.do: Ten-minute family meeting: look at this week’s “family promises” and chore tick chart, and each person says one thing done well and one thing to change next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we talked a lot about faithfulness. Looking back, Mom and Dad kept some promises, but a few fell through again, such as when we said we would go shopping with you and then changed the day because of work. We don’t want to make excuses. We want to ask how you felt, because you are the one who knows best whether we can be relied on.
ask: This week, did you feel we did what we said a little better? Which thing do you remember most?
In faithfulness, is there anything you want to adjust this week yourself? How can we help you?
youth.do: Parents first admit one thing they did not do and set a time to make it up, then invite the child to make a suggestion, and the family chooses one thing to adjust together next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being faithful to us all this week. Some things we did, and some we forgot. Help us next week to be more faithful people, who do what we say. In Jesus’ name, amen.

19.memT: ‘It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

mem.t: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

sat.t: Family Day: The Gentle Whisper Challenge
sat.d: Today the whole family plays a full day of the “Gentle Whisper Challenge”: everyone speaks at home at half their usual volume, and whoever forgets and gets loud pays a cute forfeit, such as meowing three times like a kitten. At noon, cook a simple dish together and practice dividing the work with gentle words: “Could you please pass me…?” “Thank you.” In the evening play “Whisper Down the Lane” and see how words change as they are passed along. After supper, sit together and share: “Which gentle word today made my heart feel best?” Finally recite Proverbs 15:1 together.

sun: In what situations are you most likely to use a “harsh word” this week? At that moment, what were you really afraid of or caring about?
When you were a child, what was the tone of voice the adults at home used? How has that tone shaped who you are today?
Next week, in which time of day when your voice is most likely to rise will you practice a gentle answer, and whom will you invite to watch over you?

lessons.title: A Gentle Answer Turns Away Wrath
lessons.theme: Gentle words put out the fire; harsh words light it

v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

lessons.still: First relax your shoulders and loosen your jaw, and notice where your body is tight. Breathe in and out slowly, and say to the Lord: “Lord, make my heart gentle first, and then make my mouth gentle.”
teach: Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” It is like two buckets: one of water, one of gas. When a child throws a tantrum, talks back or slams a door, it is as though a fire has started in the home. A parent’s answer decides whether we pour water or gas on the flames.

Many parents do not want to shout, but the moment the words leave their mouths the tone changes. The cause is often not the child but ourselves: we are tired, hurried, afraid of losing face, worried that the child is going astray. Verse 4 says, “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.” The same tongue can grow a tree of life, or crush a child’s spirit. A child may not remember the reasoning we gave, but will remember the tone in which we said it.

Gentleness is not ignoring right and wrong, and it is not letting things slide. The word for “gentleness” among the fruit of the Spirit is often used of a tamed warhorse: the strength is still there, but it obeys the master’s reins. A gentle parent still has boundaries and still says “no,” but says it in a way that the child does not need to defend himself. A gentle answer is not weakness; it is having strength and choosing not to hurt.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility, and pride provokes pride. A parent’s raised voice is often a reaction of the self-ruled life: I want to win, I want you to submit. A gentle answer is the choice of the self-emptied life: I don’t need to win; I want your heart. Change the way you think, and you change the way you speak.
q: Who is God? — God’s eyes are everywhere, and he hears every word I say at home. What is the tone in which he speaks to me?
Who am I? — When my child lights a fire, am I usually the parent who pours on water, or the parent who pours on gas?
How should I respond? — In one moment of conflict today, how will I lower my volume by half and give a gentle answer?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” He is the Lord of the universe, with power to command wind and waves, yet he speaks gently to the weary, to little children, to failing disciples. His gentleness is not an absence of power; it is the Almighty willing to bend down to speak.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you are gentle and humble in heart and have never spoken harshly to me. I admit that at home I often use harsh words and turn my children’s small fires into big ones. Holy Spirit, grow the fruit of gentleness in me, so that my tongue becomes a tree of life and does not crush my children’s spirits. In today’s conflicts, remind me to stop first and then answer gently. Amen.
acts: Write “A gentle answer turns away wrath” on a note and put it where conflicts happen most (the dining table, the desk, the doorway)
When you notice today that you are about to raise your voice, take a breath first and cut the volume in half before speaking
At bedtime, say one gentle word to your child: “Thank you for today. I really enjoy being with you.”
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” — Lord, right now turn my words into water, not gas.

fam.key: Gentle words make anger go away.

lamb.do: When your child cries and fusses, hold him in your arms and hum a song in a very soft, slow voice until he gradually quietens.
lamb.say: Shh… take your time. I’m here, and God is here too.

sprout.story: Little Elephant and Little Hippo were fighting over a ball. Little Hippo shouted, “It’s mine!” and Little Elephant shouted, “It’s mine!” They got louder and louder, and in the end both cried. Then Little Tortoise slowly walked over and said softly, “We can play together.” Little Elephant and Little Hippo stopped, and felt a little less angry. The three of them played ball together and had a lovely time.
sprout.ask: When you are angry, which feels better, speaking loudly or speaking softly?
sprout.do: Play the “Loud Voice, Soft Voice” game: first say loudly, “It’s mine!”, then softly, “Let’s play together,” and compare which one feels better inside.

soldier.story: Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” Imagine someone says a very fierce thing to you: your heart feels as if a fire has been lit, and you want to shout back. If you shout back, the fire gets bigger; if you answer with gentle words, the fire slowly goes out. Xiaolin in Penang had her homework ruined by her little sister. She wanted to scold her, but took a deep breath and said, “I’m very sad. Can you help me fix it?” Her sister cried and said sorry, and the two of them glued the homework back together.
ask: Do you think answering with gentle words is brave or timid? Why?
At home, whose words most often “set you on fire”? How could you answer?
soldier.do: This week be a “fire-fighter”: whenever someone at home is loud, answer once with gentle words, and in the evening tell the family how many fires you put out.

youth.talk: Mom and Dad want to admit first: when we talk to you, we often use a harsh tone, especially about homework and phones. Sometimes we aren’t really angry with you; we are tired and hurried, but the moment we open our mouths it comes out as shouting. Proverbs says, “a harsh word stirs up anger,” and no wonder our quarrels so often leave both sides hurt. We want to learn to speak a different way.
ask: In our family’s arguments, whose tone do you think most easily makes things worse? You can be honest.
When you are very angry, how do you want others to speak to you so that you don’t get angrier?
youth.do: Parents and child agree on a “cool-down signal”: when anyone’s voice is too loud, the other can give the signal, both pause for one minute, and then continue in a calm tone.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always speaking so gently to us. When we are angry, help us not to shout but to speak softly and well. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Smallest Fire, the Greatest Forest
lessons.theme: What has my tongue set on fire at home?

v: So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

lessons.still: Think back over today or yesterday to the harshest thing you said to your child. Listen to its tone, and think of the look on your child’s face when he heard it. Ask the Holy Spirit to listen with you, to shine his light gently and not to accuse.
teach: James says, “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” One match can burn down a whole mountain. It is the same in a home. A sentence like “How can you be so stupid?”, “If I’d known, I wouldn’t have had you,” or “Look at other people’s children” may be forgotten by the speaker in a few minutes, but the one who heard it may remember it all his life. Many adults, even in middle age, can still recall word for word something a parent once said.

James goes on: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.” This pierces the hearts of many Christian parents: on Sunday we sing praise at church, and in the car on the way home we mock our children. The same mouth prays in the morning and shouts in the evening. James says, “these things ought not to be so.”

Today ask the Holy Spirit to shine on this: what kind of speaker am I as a parent? The “eruption” type, kind most of the time and out of control when angry? The “sarcastic” type, not loud, but stabbing with sour words? The “comparing” type, always speaking of other people’s children? Or the “silent” type, who punishes by not speaking? Seeing is the first step to change. “Nobody can tame the tongue,” and so we need the Holy Spirit all the more.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parent’s own heart first, and then the child’s behavior. The tongue is only the outlet; the source is the heart, for out of it flow the issues of life. From a self-ruled heart, words want to win and control; from a heart renewed by the Holy Spirit, words can build people up.
q: Who is God? — God made my child in his own image; how much does he care how I speak to his image?
Who am I? — Am I more the “eruption,” the “sarcastic,” the “comparing,” or the “silent” kind of parent?
How should I respond? — Which words that lit a fire will I take back and apologize for to my child?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was on trial, an officer struck him, and he did not curse; he said calmly, “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?” His gentleness was not cowardice; even when provoked he still ruled his tongue. No deceit was found in his mouth, and no malice.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that my tongue has lit many fires at home. With the same mouth I praise you, and then wound my children, whom you made in your own image. Please forgive me, and heal the wounds that my hurtful words have left in my children’s hearts. Renew my heart, for I know that only you can tame the tongue. Amen.
acts: Write down the sentence you most often say to your child with fire in it, and then write a gentle way to say it instead
Today find a chance to say to your child: “I once said ‘…’. That was wrong, and I’m sorry.”
Ask your spouse or a trusted friend to tell you: which tone of voice do you use most often?
lessons.noon: “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” — Lord, guard my tongue today, so that I do not light a fire at home.

fam.key: My mouth speaks good words.

lamb.do: Gently touch your child’s lips and your own, then kiss his forehead and say a blessing.
lamb.say: Our little mouths will say lovely words and praise God.

sprout.story: In the forest there was a little squirrel who spoke very carelessly. He often said, “You’re so silly!” and “You’re so ugly!” Everyone who heard him felt sad. One day Grandpa Owl said, “Little Squirrel, a bad word is like a tiny spark, and it can set the whole forest on fire!” Little Squirrel was startled, and from then on he learned to say, “Thank you!” and “You’re wonderful!” The animals in the forest all liked to be his friends.
sprout.ask: Do you know which words are “good words” and which are “bad words”?
sprout.do: Take turns as a family to say one “good word,” and each time pretend to blow out a candle, saying, “Good words put out fires!”

soldier.story: James says that the tongue, though small, is like a little fire that can burn a great forest, and like the small rudder of a ship that can turn a big vessel. One sentence like “You’re terrible” can make a classmate sad for years; one sentence like “You can do it” can help a person stand up again. James also says that it is wrong for us to use the same mouth to praise God and to curse people.
ask: Have you ever been hurt deeply by one sentence? What was it?
This week, did you say any words that “lit a fire” to a family member or classmate? How could you put it right?
soldier.do: Make a “good words list”: write ten sentences that can encourage people, and this week say at least one of them to someone each day.

youth.talk: James says that a small fire can spread to a large forest. Mom and Dad remember saying things like “Why can’t you ever learn?” and “Look at other people’s children,” which may have burned in your heart for a long time. When we said them we thought we were pushing you on, and only now do we see that we were lighting a fire. If any words have kept hurting you, we really want to hear them.
ask: Is there something Mom and Dad said that still matters to you now?
Online and on social media, do you think the fire of the “tongue” is even bigger? What do you think of sour, bitter words?
youth.do: Parents find a quiet time and ask the child to name the sentence that hurt him most; the parents do not defend themselves, but say only: “I’m sorry. That isn’t true. In our eyes you are precious.”

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us a mouth. Help us to use it to praise you and encourage our family, and not to say hurtful words. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Gentle King Comes Riding a Donkey
lessons.theme: I believe: gentleness is not weakness; it is power under control

v: “Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations.
He will not strive, nor shout, neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax, until he leads justice to victory.
“Tell the daughter of Zion, behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.”

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus riding a young donkey, slowly entering the city gate, with no warhorse and no sword. His eyes have seen you. Stay quietly in this picture, and let his gentle gaze rest on you.
teach: Many parents carry a worry: “If I am too gentle, will my child climb on top of me?” We think that strictness gives dignity and gentleness is weakness. But the King that Matthew describes is “humble, and riding on a donkey.” He is the King of kings, yet he chose a donkey and not a warhorse. It was not that he lacked power; he used power to serve, not to press people down.

Isaiah’s prophecy says, “He will not strive, nor shout, neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax.” Jesus did not need to be loud to have authority. True authority does not depend on volume. The Bible also says that Moses was “very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth,” and he was the very leader who brought a million people out of Egypt.

Today is a day of conviction, and we turn our thinking around: from “gentleness is weakness and cannot control a child” to “gentleness is power under control, authority governed by the Holy Spirit.” A gentle parent still sets boundaries and still carries out consequences, but does not shame, threaten or shout. A child will obey out of trust, and not give in out of fear.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving one’s place to grab power; humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place. A parent’s authority is given by God, not for proving that I am the boss. To let Jesus reign is to let this gentle King govern our emotions and our tone.
q: Who is God? — The King of kings chose to come riding a donkey; what does his gentleness reveal about what kind of God he is?
Who am I? — Do I believe in my heart that “if I am gentle I can’t control my children”? Where did that idea come from?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declarations: I believe gentleness is…; I believe what my child needs is…
lessons.jesus: The same Jesus once overturned the tables of the money changers in the temple; and this same Jesus then turned around and healed the blind and the lame, and received the children’s praise. His power never runs out of control; his anger was only for God’s house and the oppressed, while his gentleness reached every weak person. This is power under control.
lessons.pray: Gentle King Jesus, I believe that gentleness is not weakness but power governed by you. I believe that what my children need is not a loud parent but a parent they can trust. Come and be king over my emotions, so that at home I lead my children not by volume or threats but by your authority and love. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe gentleness is…; I believe my authority comes from…; I believe my child needs…
When you set a boundary today, crouch down, meet your child at eye level, and say it clearly in a steady voice without raising the volume
Think of a gentle and strong person you know, thank God for him, and learn one thing from him
lessons.noon: “Behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey” — Lord Jesus, today be the gentle King in my heart.

fam.key: Jesus is a gentle King with power.

lamb.do: Let your child sit on your lap and rock gently, pretending to ride a little donkey, while you sing a song praising Jesus.
lamb.say: Jesus is a gentle King, and he loves you so much.

sprout.story: Everyone was waiting for the king to come into the city. They thought the king would ride a tall, big horse with many soldiers. But then Jesus came, riding a little donkey, slowly walking in. The children held branches and shouted, “Hosanna!” Jesus is the greatest king, but he is so gentle and not fierce at all.
sprout.ask: Why do you think Jesus rode a little donkey and not a big horse?
sprout.do: As a family, take towels or branches and line up, and shout “Hosanna!” together to welcome Jesus, the gentle King.

soldier.story: When Jesus came into Jerusalem, everyone thought he would ride a warhorse like a general, lead an army and drive out the Romans. But Jesus rode into the city on a young donkey. This was telling everyone: I am a King, but I am a gentle King. Gentleness is not having no strength; it is like a tamed warhorse, very strong, but obeying its master’s command. Jesus had power to calm storms, drive out demons and heal the sick, yet he chose to treat people with gentleness.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “gentle” and “weak”?
Among the people you know, who is both gentle and strong?
soldier.do: Write an “I believe” declaration: “I believe gentleness is not weakness, because Jesus…” and put it on your bedroom door; this week find one chance to solve a problem with gentleness instead of force.

youth.talk: Many people think that being gentle means being easy to push around; at school, being too gentle may mean being looked down on, and it is the same at work. Mom and Dad used to think that we had to be fierce to keep you in line. But Jesus is the King of kings, and he rode into the city on a donkey. We have begun to wonder: could real strength be the strength to control yourself?
ask: In your school, do you think gentle people are respected or bullied? Why?
How do you think Jesus’ gentleness differs from what people call a “nice guy”?
youth.do: Parents and child each write one “I believe” declaration about gentleness and strength, and may read together the passage about Jesus entering Jerusalem and talk about his choice.

fam.pray: Jesus, thank you that you are a gentle King. Help us to be like you, strong and also gentle, not bullying anyone and not afraid to do what is right. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Speech Seasoned with Salt
lessons.theme: Practice today: tone, choice of words and posture that carry grace

v: Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.
By patience a ruler is persuaded. A soft tongue breaks the bone.

lessons.still: Ask the Lord: “Lord, at what moment today will I most need your salt when I speak?” It may be waking the children, urging homework, or bedtime. Note that moment down and hand it to him in advance.
teach: Paul says, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt.” Salt gives food its flavor without taking over the food’s own taste; too little salt, and the dish is bland; too much, and it is hard to swallow. Good words are the same: honest but not stabbing, principled but warm. “Go and do your homework” and “When your homework is done, shall we go for a walk together?” mean the same thing, but taste completely different.

Proverbs says, “A soft tongue breaks the bone.” It is a startling picture: the hardest bone broken by the softest tongue. Many parents find that what shouting a hundred times could not do, crouching down, looking into the child’s eyes and saying it softly once, does. Gentle words have a wonderful power: they pass through the child’s armor of defense and reach straight to his heart.

Today’s practice has three small steps. One: lower your body, crouch or sit so that you are at the child’s eye level. Two: slow your speech and lower your volume. Three: say a connecting word first, and then the request, for example, “I know you still want to play. You’re having so much fun, aren’t you? In five minutes we need to put the toys away.” A single father in Kuala Lumpur tried it for a week and said, “My voice isn’t hoarse any more, and my son is more willing to listen.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is the key step in change, and gentleness must travel from the way we think to the tone we use. People matter more than tasks: putting away toys is a task, and the child’s heart is a person. Do not hurt a person just to get a task finished. Speak with the heart, relying on the Spirit, and your words carry grace; urge with the head, relying on yourself, and only commands remain.
q: Who is God? — God always speaks to me with grace, as if seasoned with salt. How does he speak gently to me today?
Who am I? — Are my words often “too bland” (not daring to say what is true) or “too salty” (said too sharply)?
How should I respond? — At which moment today will I practice crouching down, slowing down, and connecting before requesting?
lessons.jesus: Isaiah describes God’s shepherding: “He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.” Jesus is this good shepherd. He does not drive the lambs with a whip but leads them gently; he knows which is slow and which needs to be carried. His words always carry the salt of grace.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that like a good shepherd you lead me gently and speak to me tenderly. Today put your salt in my words: honest and warm, principled and gracious. At the moments when I am most hurried, remind me to crouch down, slow down, and connect with my child’s heart first. Let my words be sweetness in my children’s hearts. Amen.
acts: When you talk with your child today, crouch down or sit down to his eye level at least three times
Rewrite one command you often use into a “connect first, request second” version, and use it today
As a family decide on some “forbidden family words” (for example “stupid” or “shut up”), put them on the fridge, and let the adults keep them first
lessons.noon: “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt” — Lord, put your grace into every word I speak today.

fam.key: I speak gently and politely.

lamb.do: Crouch down or lie on the floor so that your eyes are at your child’s level, and speak to him slowly and softly while looking at him.
lamb.say: I’m looking at you, I’m listening to you, and I love you so much.

sprout.story: Mommy forgot to put salt in the soup, and Xiaoan took a sip and said, “It has no taste!” Mommy added just a little salt, and the soup became delicious. Mommy said, “Words need salt, too! Add ‘please,’ ‘thank you’ and ‘I’m sorry,’ and your words will sound lovely.” Xiaoan thought about it and said, “Mommy, please may I have another bowl of soup, thank you!”
sprout.ask: What “salty words” will you use?
sprout.do: Make a “word soup”: take a bowl, and every time someone says a sentence with “please,” “thank you” or “I’m sorry,” they pretend to sprinkle a little salt into the bowl.

soldier.story: Paul says our speech should be seasoned with salt. Salt is amazing: just a little can make a whole bowl of soup taste good. It is the same with words: the same thing, with a little gentleness and a little politeness added, sounds completely different. “Go away!” and “I’d like to be quiet by myself for a while. Is that all right?” mean almost the same, but which one feels better? The Bible also says a soft tongue breaks the bone, meaning that gentle words are more powerful than shouting.
ask: Can you change “Hurry up!” into a sentence with “salt”?
When are you most often “too salty” in what you say?
soldier.do: As a family make a “forbidden words chart”: write three sentences everyone will no longer say, and three “salty words” to use instead, and keep it together, adults and children.

youth.talk: Paul says speech should be seasoned with salt. Mom and Dad have found that often it is not the content we get wrong but the flavor: we want to remind you about sleep and it comes out as blame; we want to show interest in your friends and it comes out as an interrogation. We want to practice asking about your feelings first, and then telling you our worries. You can teach us, too, how you can best take things in.
ask: When Mom and Dad need to remind you of something, in what way are you most willing to listen?
Do you think there are times when you yourself speak “too salty”? Especially to whom?
youth.do: Parents ask the child to rewrite the “too salty” sentence they say most often into a “salted” version; the parents use it this week, and at the weekend ask the child to give a score.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us to speak well. Help us to speak gently and politely, like soup with salt in it, so that people feel comfortable hearing us. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Restore with a Gentle Heart
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Did my speaking sound more like Jesus this week?

v: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,

lessons.still: Recall the sound of your voice at home this week: the soft moments, and the loud ones. Like listening to a recording, ask the Holy Spirit to listen with you; don’t hurry to give a score, only listen honestly to yourself.
teach: Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” This gives parents two reminders: when a child does wrong, the goal is to “restore,” not to “knock down”; and we too must take care, because we are equally weak and can lose control.

The word “restore” is also used of fishermen mending their nets and of a doctor setting a dislocated bone. To mend a net needs care, to set a bone needs a gentle hand, and too much force only makes the injury worse. Paul also says that the Lord’s servant “must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him.” The purpose of discipline is restoration, so its method must also be gentle.

This week we learned that a gentle answer puts out the fire, that the tongue can light a fire, that gentleness is power under control, and that words should be seasoned with salt. Today let us look back honestly: at which moments did I restore my child with gentleness? At which moments did I shout, sneer, or turn cold? If there is any violence or threat at home that makes people afraid, please do not bear it alone; seek your pastor and professional help. The review is so that next week we set out more gently.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review and adjustment are for repeated growth, not for self-blame. A humble parent dares to ask his child, “This week, did my speaking sound more like Jesus?” When a parent first admits that his tone has hurt, the child learns to admit too; humility draws out humility, and the home becomes a win-win.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who restores me with gentleness, and never mends me by shaming me.
Who am I? — When my child did wrong this week, was my aim to “restore” him, or to “knock him down” and let off my own steam?
How should I respond? — In which moment next week when I am most likely to lose control, what specific method will I use to remind myself to be gentle?
lessons.jesus: After the risen Jesus had eaten breakfast with Peter by the lake, he asked him, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He did not bring up old accounts, or list Peter’s three denials in front of everyone; he gently asked three times, “Do you love me?” and then said, “Feed my lambs.” This is restoring with a gentle heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for restoring me with gentleness again and again. Looking back over this week, I see moments when I was gentle, and I also see many harsh words I should not have said. Please forgive me, and heal the places where my children were pierced by my words. Next week help me remember that discipline is to restore, not to knock down, and let me take care of myself too and lean on you. Amen.
acts: Talk as a couple for ten minutes: what was the temperature of our words at home this week? Which moment was gentlest? Which moment was most out of control?
Ask your child: “This week, did Dad/Mom speak more gently? Which sentence made you saddest?” Only listen; do not defend yourself
Write down one adjustment for next week, such as: “Before I start urging, crouch down and take three deep breaths.”
lessons.noon: “You who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” — Lord, today let my discipline be restoring, not knocking down.

fam.key: When we do wrong, we help each other gently.

lamb.do: When your child makes a mess, hold his little hand and slowly tidy up together, and finish with a hug.
lamb.say: That’s all right. We’ll fix it together. I love you.

sprout.story: Little Lamb Mie-Mie did not listen and ran out of the sheepfold, and got stuck in the bushes, crying in fear. The shepherd found him, and did not get angry and scold him, but carefully pushed the branches aside, held Mie-Mie in his arms, and slowly took him home. Mie-Mie leaned against the shepherd and felt so safe. Jesus is that good shepherd, and when we do wrong, he gently brings us back.
sprout.ask: This week, did you do something wrong and get gently helped?
sprout.do: As a family act out “the shepherd finds the lamb”; whoever plays the shepherd uses the gentlest voice to say: “I’ll take you home.”

soldier.story: Paul says that if someone does wrong, we should “restore” him with a gentle heart. Restoring is like mending a torn fishing net, or a doctor putting a dislocated arm back in place: it must be done carefully and gently, for too much force only hurts more. Zixuan in Johor Bahru saw his little brother take his snack, and wanted to tell on him loudly, but then he asked gently, “Are you very hungry? Next time tell me, and I’ll share.” His brother shyly gave the snack back and said sorry.
ask: This week, did you use gentle words to help someone who did wrong?
Do you think Mom and Dad spoke more gently this week? You can be honest.
soldier.do: Ten-minute family meeting: each person says the gentlest sentence of this week, and one “too salty” sentence they want to drop next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we practiced speaking gently. Mom and Dad must be honest: there were a few times we broke down again, especially at night when we were very tired and you were on your phone. We found that we often want to “correct” you and forget to “restore” your heart. We would like to hear your feedback, even if it is not pleasant to hear, because we really want to change.
ask: This week, was there a time when the way we spoke made you more willing to talk with us?
If you do something wrong, how do you want us to talk with you so that it is “restoring” and not “knocking down”?
youth.do: Parents listen carefully to all of the child’s feedback, pick one adjustment and write it down, and invite the child to choose one person he wants to treat more gently.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for gently bringing us back when we do wrong. Help us next week to treat our family with gentle words too. In Jesus’ name, amen.

20.memT: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

mem.t: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

sat.t: Family Day: Our Family’s Fruit Tree
sat.d: Prepare a large sheet of paper and draw a big tree together, writing “Remain in the Lord” on its roots. Cut out nine fruits in different colors and write on them love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Take turns drawing a fruit and saying where you have seen it in a family member these past weeks, for example: “I saw Mom being very patient this week.” Then stick the fruit on the tree. Finally, choose together the “fruit we most want to grow”, hold hands around the tree, and thank God for the fruit he has grown in your family over these three months. Hang the tree in the living room.

sun: Over these thirteen weeks of the “Life” stage, which week’s truth changed you most? What concrete difference have you seen at home?
Among emotions, words, phone and time, which one most often rules over you? What attempt at self-control did you make this week?
After doing the family health check, which family would you like to invite to walk the next stage with you, or which change in your family will you share with your group?

lessons.title: Ruling Your Spirit Is Greater Than Taking a City
lessons.theme: The hardest city to conquer is your own heart
