v: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.
Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.

lessons.still: Be still and notice your heart right now: is it hurried, tired, troubled or calm? Don’t rush to change it. Simply say to the Lord, “Lord, I can’t govern this heart. Please come and rule it.”
teach: Solomon said, “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.” In ancient times, capturing a city was a general’s greatest achievement. Yet Scripture says there is something harder and greater than taking a city: ruling your own spirit. Many parents are capable at work. They can lead a team and solve difficult problems, but at home they are defeated by a spilled bowl of rice or unfinished homework.

Another proverb says, “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.” A city with no walls lets the enemy walk in at any time, and its people live in constant unease. A parent whose emotions have no boundaries makes children live in that same unease: they never know whether Dad will come home in a good mood or a bad one, or whether Mom will explode in the next second.

Self-control is the last fruit of the Spirit, like a wall that encircles the other eight. It includes control of our emotions, our words, our phones and our time. It does not come from gritting our teeth and suppressing ourselves, but from letting the Holy Spirit be master of the heart. Ruling your spirit does not mean I “conquer” myself; it means I hand the keys of my heart to Jesus.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life wants to sit on the throne, yet our own heart is the hardest thing to control. The self-emptied life does not mean destroying yourself; it means letting Jesus reign in your heart: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” The effects of a whole life flow from the heart. Guard the heart, and you guard the family.
q: Who is God? — God is the Lord who can rule my heart, and his power is greater than my emotions.
Who am I? — Is my heart more like a city with walls, or a city “broken down and without walls”? Do my children feel safe around me?
How should I respond? — Among emotions, words, phone and time, which “key” will I hand to Jesus first today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness, and when he was hungry the devil told him to turn stones into bread. He had the power to do it, yet he answered, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” His self-control was not a lack of power, but power held in obedience to the Father. He is the perfect example of ruling one’s own spirit.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for overcoming temptation in the wilderness for me. I admit that I often cannot govern my own heart, and that when my emotions rise, they break down the peace of our home. Please let the Holy Spirit grow the fruit of self-control in me. Be the master of my heart, build walls around it, and let my children feel safe with me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
acts: Write down the moments when you most easily “lose the gate” (for example, coming home from work, leaving in the morning, bedtime), and pray over them
Today, in a moment when emotion is about to boil over, stop first and say, “Lord, I give you my heart.”
Copy Proverbs 16:32 onto a card and keep it in your wallet or phone case
lessons.noon: “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.” — Lord, please come and rule my heart right now.

fam.key: Let Jesus rule my heart.

lamb.do: When your child is upset or crying, hold him close and take slow, deep breaths yourself first, so he can feel your calm.
lamb.say: Slowly now, breathe in, breathe out. Jesus is with us.

sprout.story: Little Lion was so strong he could push over trees, but whenever he got angry he roared and bit at everyone, and all the animals were afraid of him. Mother Lion said, “The truly mighty lion is the one who can stop even when he is angry.” Little Lion tried it. When he felt angry, he stopped first and counted one, two, three, then asked God for help. Soon the little animals were saying, “Little Lion is amazing! He can rule himself!”
sprout.ask: When you are angry, how can you help yourself stop?
sprout.do: Practice “Lion, stop and wait”: everyone pretends to be an angry little lion and roars, then all stop together, count one, two, three, take a deep breath and say, “Jesus, help me.”

soldier.story: In ancient times, the most important thing about a city was its wall. Without one, enemies could rush in at any time. Solomon said that a person who does not rule his own spirit is like a city without walls. He also said that someone who can rule himself is greater than a general who captures a city. Winning many levels in a game does not make you the strongest. The real hero is the one who can rule himself when he is angry, when he wants to be lazy, or when he wants to keep playing on his phone.
ask: Which do you think is harder: ruling your own heart, or defeating an enemy? Why?
When do your “walls fall down” most often, so that you cannot control yourself?
soldier.do: Draw a castle and write on its walls the things you want Jesus to help you guard, such as “anger”, “phone” and “words”. Put it up in your room.

youth.talk: Solomon said that ruling your spirit is greater than taking a city. We want to be honest with you: we ask you to control your temper, your phone and your time, yet we often fail ourselves. We say harsh words when we are angry, and once we pick up our phones we cannot stop. We have no right to ask this only of you. This week we want to learn self-control together, not by pressing you with rules, but by all of us letting Jesus be master of our hearts.
ask: Do you think self-control limits your freedom, or protects it? Why?
Among emotions, words, phone and time, which do you find hardest to control?
youth.do: Parents first name the one thing they most need to control, then invite the child to name one. Agree to remind and pray for each other this week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you are stronger than we are. When we are angry and want to lose our temper, please help us stop and let Jesus take care of our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Who Rules Over Me?
lessons.theme: Phone, time and habits: am I the master or the slave?

v: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are expedient. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything.
Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

lessons.still: Open your phone’s screen-time report and look at yesterday’s number. Don’t rush to blame yourself. Simply bring that number to the Lord and ask, “Lord, where has my time gone?”
teach: Paul said, “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are expedient. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but I will not be brought under the power of anything.” Phones, binge-watching, shopping, work, even exercise and ministry are not sins in themselves. The question is whether I am using them or they are using me. Whatever I cannot let go of has begun to reign over me.

Many parents tell their children to use their phones less, while answering messages at the dinner table and scrolling late into the night. When our children want us to play and we say “in a minute” with our eyes still on the screen, they learn not the rules we speak but the example we show: even grown-ups can’t put it down. When children are asked what they most want their parents to change, the answer is often: use your phone less.

Paul also said, “redeeming the time.” To redeem means to buy back what has been taken away. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: what kind of parent am I? The “always online” type, the “bringing work home” type, the “can’t stop before bed” type, or the “hiding in the screen when emotions rise” type? Seeing what rules over me shows me where to buy my time back.
lessons.light: 321 Light: To let Jesus reign is to let nothing else reign in the heart. People living the self-ruled life think they are enjoying freedom, but they are in fact ruled by their desires. People living the self-emptied life hand everything to Jesus and receive true freedom. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: relationships matter more than things, so don’t miss your child for the sake of a screen.
q: Who is God? — God is Lord of time, and he has entrusted each day to my care.
Who am I? — Among phone, work and entertainment, which one is “ruling” me? Which kind of parent am I most like?
How should I respond? — From which stretch of time will I “redeem” lost hours for my family today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ life was extremely busy, with crowds pressing on him constantly. Yet Scripture records, “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” He was not ruled by the needs of the crowd, nor led around by fame. He was master of his time because he first gave his time to the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I am often ruled by my phone, my work and many other things. It looks like freedom, but I cannot let go. In front of my children I say one thing and do another. Shine your light on me and show me what reigns in my heart. Help me to redeem my time, giving it first to you and then to my family. Amen.
acts: Check yesterday’s screen time, write down the three apps you used most, and confess it honestly to God
Today, choose a stretch of time in front of your family (for example, dinner until bedtime) and put your phone in a drawer
Ask your child, “When do you think Dad or Mom looks at the phone most?” and thank him for being honest
lessons.noon: “I will not be brought under the power of anything.” — Lord, today only you reign in my heart.

fam.key: I am the master, not the slave of my phone.

lamb.do: When you play with your child, put your phone in another room, look at him with full attention, and play with blocks or sing songs together.
lamb.say: Right now I am only looking at you. You are the most important.

sprout.story: Little Monkey had a toy that glowed. He played and played with it, and would not even stop to eat. When his friends called him, he did not hear. Soon his eyes were tired and his tummy was hungry, and his friends had gone away. Mother Monkey said, “A toy is for you to play with. Don’t let the toy be your boss.” Little Monkey put the toy down and went climbing trees with his friends. What fun!
sprout.ask: What is something you love so much that it is hard to stop?
sprout.do: Make a “rest basket” together as a family. At mealtimes and bedtime, everyone puts phones and tablets in the basket and says together, “Now it’s family time!”

soldier.story: Paul said, “I will not be brought under the power of anything.” To be under the power of something is to be controlled and tied up by it. Games, videos and phones are not necessarily bad, but if you keep thinking about them, cannot put them down, or argue with your family over them, then they have become your boss. Haoran in Sydney noticed that every day he turned on his game as soon as he got home from school and was impatient even when his family spoke to him. He decided to finish his homework and play with his little sister first, and only then play for half an hour. He found he was much happier.
ask: Do you think something is “ruling” you?
Do you think Mom or Dad is ruled by anything? You can say so honestly.
soldier.do: Make a “Who’s the Boss?” checklist as a family: each person writes down the one thing they find hardest to put down, and this week records daily whether they were its master.

youth.talk: Mom and Dad often nag you about too much phone time, but to be honest, we are often tied to our phones ourselves: we reply to messages at meals, scroll short videos before bed, and look at the screen while you are talking to us. Paul said, “I will not be brought under the power of anything.” We want to face ourselves first, and to hear your view rather than simply set rules for you.
ask: Who in our family do you think is most ruled by their phone? You can say it straight.
What are the best and the worst effects of your phone on your life?
youth.do: Look at each other’s daily screen time as a family. No criticism, just sharing. Then each person chooses one stretch of time to cut back this week, with parents going first.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us fun things and for giving us our family. Please help us not to be ruled by phones and games, and let Jesus be the King in our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Grace Teaches Us to Live Self-Controlled
lessons.theme: I believe: self-control is the fruit of the Spirit, not my willpower

v: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;
For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

lessons.still: Think of something you have resolved to change again and again, and failed every time. Don’t blame yourself any more. Simply set it before the Lord and say, “Lord, I can’t do this by myself. I need your grace.”
teach: When many parents hear the word “self-control”, they think of gritting their teeth and relying on willpower. But Paul says, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age.” What teaches us self-control is not rules but grace. Self-control is not a burden we strain to carry; it is fruit that grows after we are loved.

Think of a child who is loved and a child who is frightened. The frightened child behaves in front of adults but loses control once they leave. The loved child has a settled heart and can more readily choose well on his own. We are the same: the more we know we are accepted in Christ, the less we need a phone, food, shopping or an angry outburst to fill the emptiness inside.

Paul also says, “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” Self-control is something God “gave” us. We don’t produce it ourselves. Today is a day of conviction, so we turn our thinking around: from “I must try harder to control myself” to “I will remain more deeply in the Lord and let the Holy Spirit grow the fruit of self-control.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head. The heart brings joy, while the head brings worry. Self-control that depends on willpower turns into anxiety and control, and presses children in the same way. Self-control that depends on the Spirit brings peace and freedom, and our children can learn it from us.
q: Who is God? — God gives a spirit of power, love and self-control, and his grace teaches me himself.
Who am I? — Do I often rely on willpower, blame myself when I fail, and demand the same of my children?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe” declaration: I believe self-control is …; I believe God has already given me …
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was arrested, Peter drew his sword and struck, but Jesus said, “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” He held all power and chose not to use it. This self-control was not weakness but complete trust in, and obedience to, the Father. His self-control accomplished our salvation.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I believe self-control is the fruit of the Spirit, not my willpower. I believe you have already given me a spirit of power, love and self-control. I admit that I often rely on myself, blame myself when I fail, and ask the same of my children. Let me remain more deeply in your grace, so that self-control grows naturally from a loved heart. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations: I believe self-control is …; I believe what God has given me is …; I believe my child can also …
Think of something you keep failing to change by willpower. Today start with prayer instead: “Lord, let your grace teach me.”
Tell your child, “We control ourselves not because we are afraid of being scolded, but because God loves us and helps us.”
lessons.noon: “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” — Lord, I receive the self-control you have given me.

fam.key: God helps me control myself.

lamb.do: Give your child a small cookie and say, “Let’s pray first, then eat.” Hold his hand and say a one-line prayer, then eat happily together.
lamb.say: We wait a moment, thank God, then eat. Well done!

sprout.story: Little Penguin wanted to eat the whole box of candy at once. He tried to hold back by himself, but the harder he tried, the more he wanted them. Papa Penguin said, “Shall we ask God to help?” Little Penguin closed his eyes and prayed, “God, please help me eat just one.” He ate one and shared the rest with his friends. Little Penguin found that controlling himself with God’s help was much easier than trying alone.
sprout.ask: What would you like to ask God to help you control?
sprout.do: Play the “Wait a Moment” game: put one small snack in front of each person, count to ten together, pray a thank-you prayer together, then eat together.

soldier.story: Paul told his student Timothy, “God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” Self-control means being able to rule yourself. Paul said it is a gift God “gave” us, not something we have to force out by ourselves. Just as a phone needs charging, we also need to “recharge” with God every day, so that we have strength to control our temper, our mouth and our playing time.
ask: Have you ever tried very hard to change something by yourself and kept failing?
What difference do you think there is between “relying on God’s help” and “gritting your teeth alone”?
soldier.do: Write an “I believe” sentence: “I believe God will help me control …”. Read it every morning and pray about it.

youth.talk: Many people think being a Christian means a pile of rules and constant self-suppression. Mom and Dad used to ask this of you too, as if self-control meant “you may not”. But Scripture says it is God’s grace that teaches us to live self-controlled. We are beginning to understand that real self-control is not being controlled; it is knowing we are loved, so we don’t need other things to fill the gap.
ask: What does “self-control” sound like to you: a chain, or freedom?
When you are in a bad mood, what do you most easily use to fill the gap? Does it really help?
youth.do: Parents and child each write an “I believe” sentence about self-control and grace, and share one thing they are learning to hand over to God. If there is any habit you find hard to break free from, remember you can ask a trusted adult or pastor for help.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us and helping us. Please give us strength to control our temper, our mouth and our playing time. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Set a Watch Before My Mouth
lessons.theme: Emotions, words, phone and time: practicing self-control as a family

v: Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.
Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from troubles.

lessons.still: Rest your hand lightly on your lips and be quiet for a moment. Say to the Lord, “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” Then think: when will the moment come today at home that most needs your self-control?
teach: David prayed, “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” He was a mighty warrior-king, yet he knew the place he most needed guarded was his mouth. Proverbs says too, “Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from troubles.” Many family troubles begin not with big events but with one word we failed to hold back.

Self-control needs practical methods, just as a city wall needs gatekeepers. For emotions: when anger rises, step away for a minute, drink some water, breathe deeply, say a short prayer, and then come back to talk. For words: before saying what you are thinking, ask three questions. Is it true? Is it helpful? Is it the right time? For phone and time: set “screen-free times” and “screen-free places” at home, such as the dinner table and the bedroom.

The best way to practice self-control is to do it together as a family. Children don’t learn self-control because we demand it, but because they watch how we practice it. One mother in Taipei, caring for elders above and three children below, put her own phone into the family “rest basket”. She said, “What my children noticed first was the moment I put my phone down.” Start today, with one small rule and an example that the adults set first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps of change are information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, adjustment, repetition and multiplication. After information, revelation and conviction comes practice, and then repetition. Self-control is not a one-time resolve but a choice made again every day. When parents practice it first, children follow. This is change from the inside out: life first, then daily living, then relationships.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to “set a watch before my mouth”, and he gladly stands guard at my weakest place.
Who am I? — Among emotions, words, phone and time, which one do I most need God to guard?
How should I respond? — Which small rule of self-control will our whole family set today? How will I be the first to keep it?
lessons.jesus: Peter described the suffering Jesus: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” Even when most provoked, Jesus guarded his mouth. His self-control came from entrusting himself to the Father. He did not need to defend himself, because he had given himself to his heavenly Father.
lessons.pray: LORD, set a watch before my mouth and keep the door of my lips. I admit that I often say things I regret when I am upset, and waste time with my phone that I should be spending with my family. Today please help me to stop first when anger rises, to think before I speak, and to put down my phone in front of my family. Let my self-controlled life lead my children to learn self-control. Amen.
acts: As a family, make a “self-control agreement”, for example: no phones at the dinner table, no arguing after 9 p.m., and a one-minute pause when angry
Today, at a moment when you want to say something harsh, first ask yourself: Is it true? Is it helpful? Is it the right time?
Tonight, parents put their phones in the “rest basket” first and spend at least fifteen minutes doing something with their child
lessons.noon: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” — Lord, today be the guard of my mouth.

fam.key: Our whole family learns to control ourselves together.

lamb.do: Play “One, two, three, stop!” with your child: clap and dance together, and when you say “stop”, freeze together, then burst out laughing.
lamb.say: Stop and wait, well done! Jesus helps us.

sprout.story: In Little Rabbit’s home they played a “Little Door Angel” game. Whenever someone wanted to say something unkind or lose their temper, they first put a finger on their lips and said, “Shh, guard the door!” Then they thought, and spoke kindly instead. One day Little Rabbit was very angry and about to shout, when he remembered. He put his finger on his lips and said, “Shh, guard the door!” Then he said slowly, “I’m very angry. Can I have a hug?” Mom hugged him right away.
sprout.ask: When you are angry, how can you “guard the door”?
sprout.do: Practice “Shh, guard the door!” together as a family: put a finger on your lips, take a deep breath, then say something kind.

soldier.story: King David was very good at fighting wars, yet he prayed, “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” He knew the mouth was harder to control than any enemy. Self-control needs methods. When angry, leave for a minute, breathe deeply and pray. Before speaking, ask three questions: Is it true? Is it helpful? Is it the right time? With phones and games, agree on the time beforehand and stop when it is up.
ask: Which of the three questions before speaking is hardest for you?
What “self-control agreement” can our whole family make together?
soldier.do: As a family, write three points for “Our Family’s Self-Control Agreement”. Everyone signs it and it goes on the fridge. Start keeping it today.

youth.talk: David was a warrior, yet he prayed for God to guard his mouth. Mom and Dad have found that what we most need to guard is often our own mouths and phones. We would like to set a few self-control agreements for our home with you. They aren’t only for you; the whole family keeps them, including us. You can suggest rules you think are fair, and we will discuss them together.
ask: Which “self-control agreement” does our family need most? Which one do Mom and Dad most need to keep?
Does “pausing for a minute first” when angry work for you? What other methods work better for you?
youth.do: Discuss and set three “self-control agreements” as a family, with the child writing them down. Parents commit to keeping them first, and agree that the child may remind them.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us. Please guard our mouths so that we speak kind words, and help us control our temper and our playing time as we learn together as a family. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Looking Back to See the Fruit
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: reviewing the Life stage and inviting the whole family to a health check

v: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

lessons.still: Open your notes from these thirteen weeks, or simply recall these months, as if looking back through a photo album. Ask the Holy Spirit to walk with you page by page: where has there been change? Where are you still struggling? Say quietly to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for working all along.”
teach: From Week 9 until today we have walked through the “Life” stage. We began by learning that parents must first remain in the Lord: finding strength in weariness, laying down the burden of perfectionism in rest, becoming a new creation in Christ, and not passing old wounds on. Then, week by week, one fruit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Paul said, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” These thirteen weeks have been learning to walk by the Spirit at home.

Today we do a “family health check”, like a yearly physical. It is not meant to frighten us, but to help us see clearly and care for ourselves well. Husband and wife together, or a single parent with a spiritual companion, read through the thirteen themes and give each a score from one to five. Don’t compare yourselves with others, only with yourselves three months ago. Then circle one improvement you are most grateful for, and one area where you most need God’s help.

After the check, invite your children to take part: “In these months, do you think Dad and Mom have become more like Jesus? Which fruit have you seen most often? Which do you most hope we will grow?” Their answers may move us or sadden us. But remember Paul’s words: “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” The change does not end today. In the next stage, we will bring life into the rhythm of home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. These thirteen weeks are the foundation of the whole family’s training: when parents’ lives are renewed, family life will change. Review, adjustment, repetition and multiplication: today’s health check is the review and adjustment, and sharing the grace you have seen with another family is multiplication.
q: Who is God? — Looking back over these thirteen weeks, what good works has God begun in me? What kind of God is he, who is determined to complete what he starts?
Who am I? — In the family health check, what improvement am I most grateful for? Which fruit do I most need God’s help with?
How should I respond? — For the next stage, which corrective action will I take, and with whom will I share which grace?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” These thirteen weeks began and end with this sentence. None of the fruit is squeezed out by our effort; it grows naturally as we remain in Jesus. He is the one who began it, and he will be the one to complete it.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking with me through these thirteen weeks. I have seen you doing a good work in me, and I have also seen how much weakness is still in me. Thank you for not giving up on me, and that you will complete the work you began. Let me and my family keep remaining in you and bearing more fruit of the Spirit, and let us share the grace we have experienced with another family. Amen.
acts: Do a family health check: score the thirteen themes of Weeks 9–21 (remaining in the Lord, strength, rest, new creation, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control) from one to five, and circle the one you are most grateful for and the one that most needs help
Husband and wife (or a single parent with a spiritual companion) talk for twenty minutes, and ask the children, “In these months, have Dad and Mom become more like Jesus?”
Write down one corrective action for the next stage, and the name of one family you would like to share this journey with
lessons.noon: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” — Lord, thank you for not giving up on me. Please keep working in my home.

fam.key: Remain in Jesus and we will bear fruit.

lamb.do: Hold your child and look at the family fruit tree. Point to each fruit, whisper its name softly, then kiss your child.
lamb.say: You are God’s treasure. Jesus has helped our family grow so much fruit.

sprout.story: When the little sapling was first planted, it had only a few small leaves. Every day it drank water and soaked up the sun, holding tightly to the soil. After many months, the sapling grew tall and even bore red fruit! A little bird flew by and said, “Wow, you’re wonderful!” The little tree said, “I didn’t do it myself. It’s because I stayed rooted in the soil, and the rain and sunshine helped me grow.” When we stay connected to Jesus, we will bear good fruit too.
sprout.ask: In these months, what good fruit do you think has grown in our family?
sprout.do: Look at “Our Family’s Fruit Tree”. Each person points to one fruit and says who they saw it in, then everyone claps together and thanks God.

soldier.story: For these three months we have been learning the nine fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Jesus said he is the vine and we are the branches. When branches stay joined to the vine, they bear fruit naturally. Fruit doesn’t grow in a day. Some is already red, and some is still small and green. That’s all right. Paul said the good work God began in our hearts, he will surely complete.
ask: Of these nine fruits, which do you think has grown best in you? Which do you most want to grow?
Do you think Mom and Dad have become more like Jesus in these months? Which fruit have you seen most often?
soldier.do: A fifteen-minute family meeting: each person gives every family member, and themselves, a “fruit award”, saying which fruit they see in that person. Then choose together the fruit the whole family most wants to grow in the next stage. Parents go first.

youth.talk: For these three months Mom and Dad have been learning to change ourselves first, before talking about changing you. We know there are still many things we do badly. Some fruit has only just sprouted, and some seems not to have grown at all. Today we want to do a “family health check”, and the most important part is hearing your honest opinion. Your answers won’t be used to start an argument. We truly want to know.
ask: In these months, what do you think is the most obvious change in Mom and Dad? What would you like us to keep working on?
If you look at our family through the nine fruits, which seems the most abundant? Which is most lacking?
youth.do: Parents and children complete the family health check together. Each writes down one change they are most grateful for and one direction they want to practice together in the next stage, and then they pray together for the family’s next step.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you are the vine and we are the branches. Thank you for helping our family bear good fruit these three months. Help us always to remain in you and bear more fruit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

21.memT: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

mem.t: LORD, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.

sat.t: Family Day: Designing Our Family’s Day
sat.d: Prepare a long strip of paper and draw a timeline from morning to night. Together, mark four moments: waking up, mealtimes, leaving home and bedtime. At each moment, everyone sticks on a note, written or drawn, saying “how we could remember God at this time”. For example: a short morning prayer on waking, a high-five blessing at the door, a song before bed. Finally, choose two small rituals that everyone agrees on, begin them next week, and stick the timeline by the front door.

sun: Which part of your family’s day is the most chaotic? What state are you usually in at that time?
Which small morning or bedtime ritual did your family try this week? How did the children respond?
Which family would you like to invite to try “one sentence in the morning, one prayer at bedtime” for a month, to encourage each other?

lessons.title: Sitting, Walking, Lying Down, Rising Up
lessons.theme: Passing on faith through the rhythm of the family’s day

v: Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one.
You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.
You shall write them on the door posts of your house and on your gates.

lessons.still: Don’t pick up your phone yet. Sit up straight, put your feet on the floor and breathe slowly three times. Say to the Lord, “Today, from the moment I rise until I lie down, every moment belongs to you.” Rest in that sentence for a while.
teach: Moses spoke to a people about to enter Canaan. They would face new land, new work and new temptations, and what Moses gave them was not a complicated plan but a simple picture: “You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” Faith is not passed on through one special conference a year, but through the ordinary rhythm of every day. A river rounds a stone not with one great flood, but by flowing day and night without stopping.

Notice the order in the passage. First, “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart”, and only then, “you shall teach them diligently to your children.” The words must enter the parents’ hearts before they can flow to the children. The four moments, rising up, walking by the way, sitting in your house and lying down, are the four joints of a day: morning, going out, the table and bedtime. In this unit we will find them again, one by one.

Rhythm is different from rules. Rules are like a fence that only tells you what you may not do. Rhythm is like a trellis for a vine, a place where life can climb. A family does not need a perfect family altar from the start. It only needs a fixed starting point: one sentence in the morning, one prayer at night. This week’s memory verse says, “In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” Let’s begin with the morning.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the mindset and you change life; change life and you change daily living. In the first twenty-one weeks, we let God first change parents’ mindsets and lives. From this week, it must land in everyday life. Change in daily living doesn’t come from gritting our teeth but from rhythm: when God’s word has a fixed place in the home, Jesus reigns there.
q: Who is God? — God told Israel to talk of his words when they sit, walk, lie down and rise up. At which moment of your family’s day does he want to appear?
Who am I? — What drives the rhythm of my family’s day right now: work hours, tutoring classes, or phones?
How should I respond? — Among rising, walking, sitting and lying down, which moment will I recover first?
lessons.jesus: Jesus grew up in Nazareth, and Scripture says he entered the synagogue “as was his custom”. His life had a rhythm: prayer in the early morning, walking with his disciples, teaching at the table, withdrawing to the mountain at night. He was not pushed along by busyness but lived by the Father’s rhythm, so even on the busiest days he remained at peace.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us each day, from rising to lying down, all in your hands. I admit that our family’s rhythm is often dragged along by busyness, anxiety and screens. Please write your word on my heart first, and let it flow through me to my children. Let our home begin with one small morning and one small night, and find again the rhythm of walking with you. Amen.
acts: Draw your family’s usual day as a timetable, and circle in red the four moments of rising, walking, sitting and lying down
Tonight choose a “morning sentence” and say it to your child when he wakes tomorrow, for example, “Good morning! Today is a new day God has given us.”
Before leaving home, high-five your child and say, “God be with you!”
lessons.noon: “and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” — Lord, right now I am on the way, and I want to remember you.

fam.key: Rising or lying down, God is in our home.

lamb.do: In the morning, as you pick up your child, stroke his face and say “good morning” slowly. At night, as you lay him in bed, stroke his face again and say “good night”. Use the same actions and the same tone every day.
lamb.say: Good morning, God loves you. Good night, God watches over you.

sprout.story: Every morning Xiaole was woken by the alarm clock, while Mom hunted for socks and called out, “Hurry up! We’ll be late!” One day Mom got up a little earlier. She sat by Xiaole’s bed, stroked his head and said, “Good morning, Xiaole! Today is a new gift from God.” Xiaole rubbed his eyes and smiled. That morning everyone still had to leave the house, but it felt as if a little more sunshine had come in.
sprout.ask: What do you like Mom and Dad to say to you when you wake up?
sprout.do: Practice the “Wake-up Pat-a-Pat”: pat your head and say “Thank you, God, for a new day”, pat your tummy and say “Thank you, God, for breakfast”, pat your feet and say “God goes with me”.

soldier.story: Moses was about to say goodbye to the people of Israel. He did not tell them to hold one big gathering a year. He said that God’s words should be in their homes all the time: say them when you sit at home, when you walk on the road, when you lie down to sleep and when you get up in the morning. They should even be written on the door frames. Why? Because what we do and say every day shapes the kind of person we become. Just as we brush our teeth every day to keep them healthy, we remember God every day so that our hearts grow closer to him.
ask: At what time of day is it easiest for you to remember God? At what time is it easiest to forget?
If we wrote one sentence on our door frame, what would you want it to say?
soldier.do: Make a “door-frame card” that says “God is with us”. Stick it on the inside of the front door, and this week touch it each time you leave and say the words.

youth.talk: To be honest, our mornings are often in “battle mode”: rushing, searching for things, hurrying each other along. In the evenings we each hide in our rooms with our phones. Recently Mom and Dad read how Moses said God’s words should be talked about when we sit, walk, lie down and rise up. We don’t want to become a super-spiritual family overnight. We just want to ask you: is there some small way for our family to remember God for one moment each day?
ask: When is the most “rushed” moment in our family’s day? How do you feel then?
If we added one very small spiritual habit that isn’t awkward, what would you suggest?
youth.do: Ask your child to help design a “not awkward” morning or bedtime habit. Parents do it for a week first, and at the weekend ask the child how it felt.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you are with us when we get up and when we lie down. Please go with us to school and to work, and keep us safe as we sleep at night. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Proclaim Loving Kindness in the Morning, Faithfulness Every Night
lessons.theme: What does my family proclaim in its mornings and nights?

v: It is a good thing to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, Most High,
to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night,
with the ten-stringed lute, with the harp, and with the melody of the lyre.
For you, LORD, have made me glad through your work. I will triumph in the works of your hands.

lessons.still: Recall the first sentence spoken in your home this morning, and the last sentence before bed last night. Don’t rush to judge. Simply ask the Holy Spirit to listen with you: was there any trace of God’s voice in those two sentences?
teach: The heading of Psalm 92 is “A song for the Sabbath day”. The psalmist says, “to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night.” A day has two doors: morning opens the door and night closes it. When we open the door, we proclaim God’s loving kindness: today you are loved, and you can go out with confidence. When we close it, we proclaim his faithfulness: today God did not leave us, and we can sleep in peace.

Yet in many homes the mornings and nights proclaim something else. The morning proclaims anxiety: “Hurry up! We’re going to be late again!” The night proclaims disappointment: “Why isn’t your homework finished yet?” Shufen, a single mother in Kuala Lumpur, once recorded her own voice one morning and was shocked when she listened. In fifteen minutes she had said “hurry up” eleven times and “I love you” not once.

Today is not for condemning ourselves, but for letting the Holy Spirit shine his light: what kind of parent am I? One who opens the door with hurrying and closes it with blame, or one who opens it with loving kindness and closes it with faithfulness? A child’s first impression of God often begins with the first and last sentences he hears at home each day. Those two sentences matter far more than we think. They are like bookends, holding the child’s day between them, and whatever happens in the middle, the child will read it through those two sentences.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Focus on Jesus, not on circumstances. If the morning’s focus is on the timetable, anxiety will lead the home. If the focus is on God’s loving kindness, busyness remains but the heart has an anchor. Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head: the heart brings joy, the head brings worry.
q: Who is God? — His loving kindness cannot be fully proclaimed in any morning, nor his faithfulness fully counted in any night. Where did you see his loving kindness today?
Who am I? — Does my family’s morning proclaim loving kindness or anxiety? Does our night proclaim faithfulness or disappointment?
How should I respond? — What will I say as my first sentence tomorrow morning, and my last sentence before bed tonight?
lessons.jesus: On the morning of his resurrection, the first thing Jesus said to weeping Mary was to call her name tenderly. He did not rebuke his disciples for their weakness; he lit a charcoal fire on the shore and prepared breakfast. Jesus filled the beginning of the day with loving kindness, and he longs to begin every morning in our home the same way.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for greeting me with loving kindness every morning and guarding me with faithfulness every night. I admit that the mornings in my home are often full of hurrying and the nights full of blame. Shine your light on me and change me, so that my mouth first proclaims your loving kindness and faithfulness, and my children hear your voice in mine. Amen.
acts: Tomorrow morning record fifteen minutes of the sounds at home on your phone, listen to it yourself, and count how many times you say “hurry up” and how many times “I love you”
Tonight at bedtime, tell each child one “faithful thing God did today”, for example, “You came home safely today, and God protected you.”
Write “loving kindness in the morning, faithfulness every night” on a piece of paper and stick it by the bathroom mirror
lessons.noon: “to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night” — Lord, in the middle of this busy moment I also remember your loving kindness.

fam.key: In the morning say God loves me; at night say God watches over me.

lamb.do: In the morning, when you draw back the curtains, hold your child and look at the light outside, and say a thank-you. At night, before turning off the light, hold him and look at the night outside, and say good night.
lamb.say: The sun is up, God loves you. The moon is up, God is with you.

sprout.story: Every morning, when Grandfather Sun came up, the little birds in the garden began to sing, “Tweet tweet, God loves us!” Every night, when Sister Moon came out, the little owl softly said, “Hoo hoo, God is with us.” One bird sang the morning and one owl sang the night, and the whole garden heard God’s love from morning to night.
sprout.ask: Would you like to be the little bird in the morning or the owl at night? What will you say?
sprout.do: Play the “Little Bird and Owl” game. In the morning, flap your wings like a bird and say “God loves me”. At night, blink your eyes like an owl and say “God is with me”.

soldier.story: Psalm 92 says we should proclaim God’s loving kindness in the morning and his faithfulness at night. Loving kindness is God’s goodness to us, and faithfulness is God doing what he says. Zhiming in Singapore once did badly in an exam and hid in his room that evening. His dad knocked and came in. He didn’t scold him, but said, “You’re very sad today, but God has been with you all along. He promised never to leave you, and today he kept that promise.” Zhiming cried a little, then slept very peacefully.
ask: What difference do you think there is between “loving kindness” and “faithfulness”?
In what way was God good to you today, or true to his word?
soldier.do: Keep a “Loving Kindness and Faithfulness Diary”. This week, each morning write one thing that shows “God loves me”, and each night write one thing that shows “God watches over me”. Share them with your family on Friday.

youth.talk: Recently I noticed something that made me uncomfortable. In our home, the thing I say most in the morning is “hurry up”, and the thing I say most at night is “haven’t you finished yet?” I think I have been starting your day with anxiety and ending it with pressure. That is not what I want to give you, and it is not what God wants to give you either. I want to try to change, but I need your help.
ask: How does my tone in the morning and at night make you feel? You can be honest.
What do you wish you could hear before leaving in the morning or before going to sleep at night?
youth.do: Ask your child to be the “tone reminder”. This week, whenever a parent says something hurried in the morning, the child may quietly say “loving kindness”, and the parent must say it again in a different way.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us every morning and watching over us every night. Please help our mouths always to speak of your goodness. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: I Lay Down and Slept; I Awakened
lessons.theme: I believe: the family’s rhythm is trust, not control

v: But you, LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.
I cry to the LORD with my voice, and he answers me out of his holy hill. Selah.
I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for the LORD sustains me.
He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber.
Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

lessons.still: Imagine putting everything you cannot let go of today into a basket, one thing at a time, and handing it into the Lord’s hands. Then sit for a while with empty hands and say to him, “You never slumber, so I can rest.”
teach: Psalm 3 was written when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. The worst kind of pain had struck his home: his son had betrayed him and was hunting him down. By all accounts he should have lain awake that night. Yet David wrote, “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for the LORD sustains me.” He didn’t sleep because the problem was solved, but because he knew who was keeping watch. He said God was “a shield around me”, and “the one who lifts up my head”. On the night his family was broken, his eyes did not stay on Absalom; they stayed on God.

Many parents cannot hold to a morning and evening rhythm, not because they are lazy but because they are afraid: afraid their children will fall behind, afraid the work will never be done, afraid that if they stop they will lose ground. So they grab time in the morning, catch up at night, and even in bed think about tomorrow. Psalm 121 says, “he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” Since God does not slumber, parents do not need to stand guard twenty-four hours a day. A passenger on a plane does not need to stare at the cockpit to feel safe. We do our part, and we hand the whole journey to the true Captain.

So the spiritual rhythm of a home is not just one more ritual added on; it is a declaration of trust. Stopping to pray in the morning declares, “Today does not depend on me.” Stopping to give thanks at night declares, “Today God watched over us.” Behind the rhythm is trust. Today, write your “I believe”: I believe God keeps watch while we sleep; I believe that stopping to meet with God is not a waste of time.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the human viewpoint to God’s, from “there isn’t enough time” to “time is given by God”. Parents living the self-ruled life think they are the family’s watchman and so cannot stop. Parents living the self-emptied life know God is the keeper, so they can work within his rhythm and rest within it too.
q: Who is God? — He is the keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps. How does your heart feel when you think of that?
Who am I? — Do I keep a rhythm because I trust, or do I keep rushing because I am afraid?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe that while we sleep God …; I believe that stopping morning and evening to meet with God is …
lessons.jesus: When the storm was raging, Jesus was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. The frightened disciples woke him, and he rose, rebuked the wind and the sea, and all became calm. He could sleep because he trusted the Father completely, and he could wake because he ruled the storm completely. All our mornings and nights are in the hands of this Jesus.
lessons.pray: Lord, I believe that you neither slumber nor sleep. I admit that I often think the home depends on me to hold it up, so I am anxious in the morning, tired at night and awake in the small hours. Today I give the watchman’s post back to you. I believe that stopping to meet with you is not a waste but trust. Teach me to rise in your rhythm and to lie down in your rhythm. Amen.
acts: Write two “I believe” declarations and stick them by your bed: “I believe God keeps watch over this home while we sleep.” “I believe stopping morning and evening to meet with God is not a waste of time.”
Tonight before bed, write down the thing you most worry about tomorrow, put it in your Bible, and say, “Lord, I give this to you.”
When you wake tomorrow, before getting out of bed, say, “I awakened, for the LORD sustains me.”
lessons.noon: “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for the LORD sustains me.” — Lord, right now I am not holding myself up. I trust that you are keeping watch.

fam.key: God never sleeps, so I can sleep in peace.

lamb.do: As you settle your child to sleep, rest a hand gently on his chest, pat slowly in time with his breathing, and softly hum a hymn.
lamb.say: Sleep in peace. God watches over you all night.

sprout.story: In Penang, Grandma was putting her little granddaughter Anan to bed. Anan said, “Grandma, there’s thunder outside and I’m scared!” Grandma said, “Anan, do you know? God never sleeps! While we sleep, he keeps his eyes wide open all night, watching over us.” Anan asked, “Doesn’t he get tired?” Grandma smiled and said, “God doesn’t get tired, because he is God.” Anan hugged Grandma and slowly fell asleep.
sprout.ask: If God is watching over you all night, do you feel a little less afraid?
sprout.do: Play the “Night Watchman” game. Everyone pretends to sleep while one person is the “night watchman”, walking quietly around. At the end the watchman says, “God is a better watchman than me!”

soldier.story: King David had to flee in the night from his own son Absalom, who wanted to kill him. It was the saddest and most dangerous night of his life. Yet he wrote a psalm that says, “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for the LORD sustains me.” He wasn’t unafraid, and not everything was solved, but he knew God was a shield around him. Another psalm says the God who keeps us “will neither slumber nor sleep”. Just as a night security guard patrols a building so the residents can sleep in peace, God is the best watchman for our home.
ask: Are there times at night when you feel afraid or cannot sleep? What are you usually thinking about?
What do you think “God is a shield” means?
soldier.do: Make a “shield card”. Draw a shield, write “God protects me” inside it, and keep it by your pillow. This week hold it as you pray before bed.

youth.talk: Have you ever kept scrolling on your phone at bedtime because the moment you stop, your mind starts thinking about tomorrow’s exam, your friends, the messages you haven’t answered? Mom and Dad are the same. At bedtime we often think about work and money. Recently I read how David, on the night his son was hunting him, could still say, “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for the LORD sustains me.” I wonder where his peace came from.
ask: What most occupies your mind at bedtime? Does your phone help you relax, or does it make it harder to sleep?
What connection do you think there is between trusting God and sleeping well?
youth.do: Try it for a week as a family: fifteen minutes before bed, leave the phones charging in the living room, each write down one thing to hand to God, and then go to sleep.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you never sleep and keep watch over our home all night. We give you our fears, and tonight we will sleep in peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Lay It Out in the Morning, Give Thanks at Night
lessons.theme: Start today: three minutes in the morning, three minutes before bed

v: Give ear to my words, LORD. Consider my meditation.
Listen to the voice of my cry, my King and my God, for I pray to you.
LORD, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.

lessons.still: Picture tomorrow morning at home: who wakes first? Who is hardest to get out of bed? Ask the Lord to walk into that picture with you, and ask him, “Tomorrow morning, what do you want me to do first?”
teach: This week’s memory verse is David’s morning prayer: “LORD, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” To “lay out” originally carried the sense of arranging in order, like a priest in the early morning setting out the offering and the wood one piece at a time on the altar. A morning prayer need not be long. It only lays the day out before God. To “watch expectantly” is to go out with anticipation, to see how God will answer today.

The Huang family in Singapore has four children, and their mornings were chaos from half past six to a quarter past seven. They tried a “three-minute morning”: the whole family stands in a circle by the door, Dad reads one verse, each child says one thing to hand to God today, Mom sums it up in a one-sentence prayer, and then everyone high-fives and goes out. Three minutes, no hymns, no sermon, but the children said, “When I go out the door, my heart is not so panicked.”

At night there is the “three minutes before bed”, which can be remembered with three words: thank, tell, pray. Thank: name one thing you thank God for today. Tell: say one thing that made you sad or worried today. Pray: parents pray a short prayer of blessing over the children. A family’s rhythm is not about doing a lot but about doing it every day. Three minutes every day is better than an hour once and then stopping. With small children, use actions and songs. With older children, listen more and speak less. The format can adjust to your family, but when that fixed moment goes missing, everyone will miss it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Among the eight steps, “practice” turns conviction into daily life. Don’t wait until the whole family is ready and the schedule is clear. Begin with the smallest step, today. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: when parents first meet God in their own mornings, the family’s mornings will change.
q: Who is God? — He is the God who hears our voice in the morning. Do you believe he cares about every small thing in your home this morning?
Who am I? — What most often blocks our morning and evening rhythm: time, emotions, or my own failure to keep going?
How should I respond? — Start the “three minutes before bed” tonight, and try the “three-minute morning” tomorrow. Who will lead it? Where will we do it?
lessons.jesus: Scripture says that Jesus rose “early in the morning, while it was still dark”, and went out to a deserted place to pray. The night before, he had healed the sick of a whole town, and the next day his disciples searched everywhere for him. Jesus’ strength was not squeezed out of busyness but flowed from meeting the Father in the early morning. He invites us to begin our days the same way.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for rising before dawn to pray, and for showing me the power of the morning. I admit that I am often pulled away by my phone and my to-do list the moment I open my eyes. Today I will begin: laying out my day before you in the morning, and giving thanks to you at night. Help me not to seek perfection but only to come every day, and let my children experience your presence in these small three minutes. Amen.
acts: Tonight, at your child’s bedside, do your first “three minutes before bed”: thank, tell, pray and bless
Tomorrow, get up ten minutes before your children, spend five minutes laying your day out before God, and then wake the children
Choose a fixed place at home for the “three-minute morning” gathering, such as the front door, the dining table or the living-room sofa
lessons.noon: “In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” — Lord, accept what I lay before you today, and I wait for your answer.

fam.key: Give the morning to God; thank God at night.

lamb.do: Build a fixed bedtime routine: bath, pajamas, the same hymn in your arms, a kiss on the forehead and the same blessing. If the order is the same every day, your child will feel safe because it is familiar.
lamb.say: Thank you, God, for today. Tomorrow God will be with you too.

sprout.story: Big brother Xiaokai and little sister Xiaoqing have “Three Fingers Time” every night. Holding up the first finger, they say one thing they thank God for today. Holding up the second, they say one thing that made them sad today. When they hold up the third, Mom prays for them. One day Xiaoqing said, “Second finger: I fell down today.” Mom hugged her, and together they gave her knee to God. Xiaoqing said, “Third finger time is my favorite!”
sprout.ask: What would you like to say with your first finger today?
sprout.do: Play “Three Fingers Time” tonight: thank, sad, pray, and everyone takes a turn.

soldier.story: David spoke to God every morning. He said, “In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” It means he set out what he would do that day and what he was worried about before God, like arranging building blocks one by one, and then went out waiting to see how God would respond. Jesus also often rose to pray before it was light. Talking with God in the morning is like checking the weather and taking an umbrella before leaving the house. When your heart is prepared, the whole day is steadier.
ask: If you could say only one sentence to God tomorrow morning, what would it be?
Of the three things at night, thank, tell and pray, which do you find hardest? Why?
soldier.do: Try the “three-minute morning” as a family. Stand in a circle by the door, each say one thing you will hand to God today, then high-five and go out. Soldiers can take turns as “morning captain”, reading one verse.

youth.talk: I know the words “family devotions” may sound like pressure, as if we must sit for a long time and share our thoughts. I’d like to suggest a very short version: one minute before leaving in the morning, two minutes before bed, and that’s all. You don’t need to say much each time. You can even just say, “Nothing today.” I want to try this because I need it myself, not because I want to control you.
ask: If we fixed a time for the family to stop for a minute or two, would morning or evening be more workable for you?
Is there something you’d like me to pray for you about at night, but are usually too shy to say?
youth.do: Agree a one-week trial with your child. Each night, go to his door and ask, “Is there anything you’d like me to pray for you today?” Whatever he says, pray briefly, say good night and leave.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, in the morning we give you our day, and at night we thank you for watching over us. Please be with us every day, and make us want to talk with you each day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Three Times a Day, as He Had Done Before
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: let the rhythm become a habit

v: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.

lessons.still: Quietly look back over this week’s mornings and nights, like watching a timeline. Which day began well? Which day was a muddle? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, without blame, simply with honesty.
teach: Daniel knew the decree had been signed, yet he went home, opened the windows toward Jerusalem, and “kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.” The most moving words are the last three: as he did before. He didn’t suddenly become spiritual in a crisis; it was the rhythm of decades that let him stand firm in the crisis. Taken captive to Babylon as a young man, away from the temple and his parents, he carried his rhythm of prayer into his home in a foreign land, and that rhythm went with him through several kingdoms.

This week you may have managed only two days, or you may have done one day and been swept away by life. That is all right. Mr. Zhou in Vancouver said his family’s bedtime prayers were on and off for the first three months, and in the fourth month their children began reminding them: “Dad, we haven’t prayed yet!” A rhythm is like making a path. The first few times the grass is high, but walk it for long enough and the path appears on its own. When it was interrupted they did not blame themselves or the children. The next evening they sat at the bedside again, as if nothing had happened, and began again.

The purpose of review is not to give marks but to adjust. Ask yourself three questions. Which small ritual felt most natural? Keep it. Which one got stuck? Shrink it, or change its time. Who most needs to be invited in? Your spouse, a teenager, or your own heart? Write down one adjustment for next week, as concrete as possible, such as “move the three-minute morning to after breakfast”. Remember, God values “as he did before”, not “perfect”. A family that is imperfect but keeps coming back has more power than a perfect family that does it once.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the necessary road to changing daily life. A proud parent gives up as soon as they fail, or blames the family for not cooperating. A humble parent admits weakness, adjusts the approach and tries again. Humility leads to humility: when parents are willing to adjust, children also learn not to fear failure and to start over.
q: Who is God? — He hears us in the evening, morning and at noon. At which moment this week did you experience him hearing your prayer?
Who am I? — How many days did our family keep the morning and evening rhythm this week? What got stuck most: time, emotions, or my own perseverance?
How should I respond? — Which habit will I keep next week, and which will I adjust?
lessons.jesus: On the most painful night in Gethsemane, Jesus went “as his custom was” to the Mount of Olives to pray. His everyday habit of prayer became his strength in the darkest hour. He also saw his disciples asleep, yet gently said, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” He understands our weakness.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us through this week’s mornings and nights. Some days I managed it, and some days I forgot, was tired or gave up. Do not let me be condemned by failure, but like Daniel let me come back to you again and again. Help our family walk our small rhythm into a path of walking with you. Amen.
acts: Talk for ten minutes with your spouse: this week, which part of the morning and evening rhythm felt most natural? Which got stuck? How will you adjust next week?
Ask your child, “This week, in the mornings and evenings, have Dad and Mom become more like Jesus?” Just listen, without defending yourself
Write down one adjustment for next week, for example, “Move the three minutes before bed to straight after the bath”
lessons.noon: “Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.” — Lord, it is noon now, and I want to speak with you too.

fam.key: Coming back to God every day is a good habit.

lamb.do: Think back over this week’s bedtime routine. Choose the step your child found calmest and liked most (for example, one song or one hug) and keep it fixed next week.
lamb.say: Every day we say good night to God. Well done!

sprout.story: A little caterpillar climbed to the same leaf every day for breakfast, then crawled back to the same branch to sleep. One day it rained heavily and he couldn’t find his leaf. He was very sad. But the next day the sun came out, and he crawled back to the leaf as usual. After many, many days, the little caterpillar became a beautiful butterfly! When we keep doing the same good thing every day, God slowly changes us.
sprout.ask: Of the things we did together this week every day, which did you like best?
sprout.do: Make a “Daily Sticker Chart”. Each morning or evening, after praying together, stick on one sticker, and see how many you can stick next week.

soldier.story: Daniel was a high official in a foreign land. One day the king decreed that for thirty days people could only make requests to the king and not pray to God. Daniel heard about it, yet he went home, opened his window and knelt down three times a day to pray and give thanks, “as he did before”. He was thrown into the lions’ den, but God shut the lions’ mouths. Daniel did not begin praying only that day. He had done it every day for many years. What you practice every day will help you in hard times, just as a footballer who trains every day finds his feet move by themselves in the match.
ask: Of this week’s morning or bedtime habits, which day do you think we did best?
If we changed one thing next week, what would you suggest?
soldier.do: Hold a five-minute family meeting. Parents first say where they fell short, then each child gives one suggestion, and the family chooses one adjustment for next week.

youth.talk: This week we tried small habits in the morning and evening, and honestly, I didn’t manage them every day myself. One day I was so tired that I just went straight to sleep. I want to admit that first. Daniel’s story moved me, not because he was so great, but because he did it “as he did before”. I think what our family needs is not perfection, but coming back again and again.
ask: Which part of this week’s morning and evening habits was helpful for you? Which part felt forced?
How could we adjust it so that it feels like “our family’s” and not “something Mom and Dad made us do”?
youth.do: Let your child lead the adjustment. Ask him to suggest one specific change, parents try his suggestion next week, and at the weekend you evaluate it together.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for waiting every day for us to come to you. Sometimes we do it, and sometimes we forget. Please help us talk to you every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

22.memT: LORD, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.

mem.t: Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,

sat.t: Family Day: Cooking a Meal Together
sat.d: Today the whole family prepares dinner together. Share the work by age: the youngest wash vegetables and set out the bowls and chopsticks, older children chop and cook one dish, and parents do the main dish and the cleaning. Put a “phone basket” in the middle of the table, and before eating everyone puts their phone in it. Take turns, with one child leading the prayer before the meal. During the meal, draw three homemade conversation cards (for example, “the happiest moment of today”, or “if you could invite one Bible person to dinner, who would it be?”). After the meal, tidy up together, and finish by saying, “Thank you, God! Thank you, family!”

sun: How many meals a week does your family eat together with no screens? What most often interrupts your table?
Which table conversation question did your family try this week? What did a child say that surprised you?
Which family (or single brother or sister) will you invite to your home for a meal next month, so that your table becomes a place that blesses others?

lessons.title: Breaking Bread at Home
lessons.theme: The table is the most natural family altar

v: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.still: Picture your table at home tonight, and where each family member sits. Invite the Lord to sit down too, and say to him, “Lord, our family table is your seat as well.”
teach: After Pentecost, a brand-new community appeared in Jerusalem. Luke describes their life by two places: the temple and the home. They worshiped in the temple, and at home they were “breaking bread”, taking “their food with gladness and singleness of heart”. Beyond the great gatherings at the temple, the early church was most alive around table after table in people’s homes. The gospel spread not only from the pulpit but over a bowl of soup and a piece of bread.

In the Old Testament, the altar was where people met God, and eating and drinking together before God was part of worship. Moses told the people, “There you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice in all that you put your hand to, you and your households.” The table is the most natural altar in a home. It happens every day, everyone attends, no extra time needs to be arranged, and we only need to invite God to the table.

The Wangs in Taichung both work, and only three evenings a week can they eat together. They decided to begin with those three meals: no phones at the table, a different person praying before the meal each time, and each person sharing one thing from their day. Mrs. Wang said, “The food is just as simple, but the children have started to look forward to dinner.” A family altar doesn’t have to mean sitting stiffly in the living room. It can begin at tonight’s table.
lessons.light: 321 Light: First God, then people, then tasks. If the only things on the table are “tasks”, such as homework, grades and bills, relationships get squeezed out. When God is invited to the table, people are seen again. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things: an ordinary meal full of love is better than a banquet where no one talks.
q: Who is God? — He delights in his people eating, drinking and rejoicing together before him. Have you ever felt God’s presence at the table?
Who am I? — Is my family’s table more like an altar, a refueling stop, or a convenience store where everyone eats separately?
How should I respond? — Which meals this week can I fix so the whole family eats together before God?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often served people at the table. The Pharisees criticized him, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.” To Jesus, the table was not a place only for good people but a place where grace arrives. He ate at Zacchaeus’ house, and that household was saved.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you love to sit and eat with people. I admit that our family table is often hurried, silent, or taken over by screens and grades. Come and sit at our table. Let us eat with gladness and singleness of heart, and make this table an altar where our family meets you and loves one another. Amen.
acts: Look at this week’s calendar with your spouse and circle at least three dinners that are “all together, no screens”
Tonight before the meal, ask one family member to lead a simple prayer of thanks
Leave an empty chair at the table, or put a small cross on it, to remind everyone that Jesus is here too
lessons.noon: “breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart” — Lord, at today’s lunch I also want to receive my food with a thankful heart.

fam.key: God is at our family table too.

lamb.do: Seat your child in his high chair and bring him to the table with the family. Before eating, hold his little hands, put them together, and say a short prayer of thanks.
lamb.say: Thank you, God, for our food. It is so happy to eat together.

sprout.story: One day Jesus went to eat at the house of a man called Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus was very short, and nobody liked him because he often took other people’s money. But Jesus said, “Zacchaeus, today I must stay at your house!” Zacchaeus was so happy that he prepared lots of good food. While they ate, Zacchaeus’ heart changed. He said, “I took people’s money, and I will give it back to them!” When Jesus came to dinner, Zacchaeus’ home became a better place.
sprout.ask: If Jesus came to our house for dinner today, what would you like to feed him?
sprout.do: When you set the table, put out one extra pair of chopsticks for “Jesus”, and at the meal everyone says, “Jesus, welcome to our home for dinner!”

soldier.story: When the church had just begun, the believers didn’t only meet in the temple; they often ate together at home. When they ate, they were happy and sincere and thanked God together. People nearby saw them and thought, “These people are so different!” and wanted to know their God. After that, more and more people believed. An ordinary table can show people God! It’s like a lamp in a window that everyone passing by can see.
ask: Do you think people who saw our family eating would think we are “very different”? In what way?
Which dish of ours do you like best? What memory does it bring back?
soldier.do: This week, be the “table helper”: set out the bowls and chopsticks, and once everyone is seated, remind them, “Let’s give thanks first!”

youth.talk: I want to tell you something: I know our dinners sometimes feel like an interrogation. The moment I open my mouth it’s homework, exams and tutoring. No wonder you want to go back to your room as soon as you finish. When I read that the early church took their food “with gladness and singleness of heart”, I felt what our table lacks is gladness. I want to change that, so dinner becomes a place you want to stay.
ask: Which part of our dinners makes you want to finish quickly and leave?
If we could talk about anything at dinner, what would you most like to talk about?
youth.do: Agree on one dinner this week as a “no homework questions day”: parents don’t mention grades or exams, and only chat about fun things in each other’s lives. At the end, ask your child how it felt.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for our good food, and for the family we eat it with. Please come and eat with us every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Martha’s Table
lessons.theme: Is my table busy with serving, or sitting down to listen?

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
