Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Think back to your most recent family dinner. Where were you? In the kitchen, on your phone, or at the table but with your mind elsewhere? Ask the Holy Spirit to call your name gently, as Jesus called Martha’s.
teach: Martha loved Jesus, so she received him into her house and bustled about preparing a good meal. But she was “distracted with much serving”, and in the end she could not help complaining to Jesus about her sister. Jesus did not rebuke her for cooking. He said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” The problem was not the work but a heart so filled with tasks that she forgot the One sitting in front of her.

Many parents are Martha parents: the food must be hot and the nutrition must be enough, yet they are always the last to sit down and the first to get up. There are also the supervisor parents, for whom the table becomes an interrogation room for checking grades and questioning whereabouts. And there are the absent parents, present at the table with their eyes on their phones. Mrs. Li in Johor Bahru said, “I cook four dishes and a soup every day, yet my child says that at mealtimes I’m the person he least wants to see.”

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: which am I? When our children look back on the family table, what they remember will not be how rich the dishes were but the atmosphere: were they hurried, interrogated, or listened to and welcomed? Jesus said the “good part” will not be taken away. At home, that good part may be the ten minutes when a parent puts down the spatula and sits to listen to a child. Cold food can be reheated, but the moment when a child wants to talk may not come again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head. Martha was calculating with her head: who isn’t helping, is there enough food. Mary was listening with her heart. Focus on Jesus, not on your own performance, nor on how much others are doing. Don’t hurt people for the sake of tasks. Don’t lose a heart for the sake of a table full of food.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said “Martha, Martha” twice, and his rebuke carried tenderness. How do you hear him call your name?
Who am I? — At the table, am I more like a Martha parent, a supervisor parent, an absent parent, or a listening parent?
How should I respond? — At the next meal, which “serving task” can I put down so I can sit and listen to my family first?
lessons.jesus: Jesus didn’t tell Martha to stop cooking. He invited her to come back to him first. He himself once “arose from supper” and tied a towel round his waist to wash his disciples’ feet. His service was never frantic, because he was first with the Father. The service he teaches us begins by sitting at his feet.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you see that I am distracted with much serving at home and troubled in my heart. I admit I often turn the table into a workbench, an interrogation room or a table for my phone. Call my name gently. Let me put down my anxious thoughts, choose the good part, and sit down to listen, to you and to my family. Amen.
acts: At dinner today, be the first to sit down, and don’t touch your phone until you stand up
At dinner, ask just one open question, such as, “What made you laugh today?” and then only listen, without commenting
Swap one complicated dish for a simple one, and use the time you save to sit and talk with your family
lessons.noon: “but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” — Lord, right now I put down my busyness and choose you first.

fam.key: Sit down together and listen together.

lamb.do: At mealtimes, pull your child’s high chair close to you, face him, look into his eyes, and copy the sounds he makes, “talking” with him.
lamb.say: I’m listening to you. I love everything you say.

sprout.story: Martha and Mary were two sisters. When Jesus came to their house, Martha ran about, busy cooking, serving soup and wiping the table, and the busier she got the crosser she became. Her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet, quietly listening to him tell stories. Martha said, “Jesus, tell my sister to come and help me!” Jesus said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are too busy. Listening to me is the most important thing.”
sprout.ask: Do you like it when we all chat together at mealtimes, or when everyone is busy with their own things?
sprout.do: Play the “Ears Game”. At the meal, each person tells one thing from today, and the others “prick up their ears” (making rabbit ears with their hands). When the person finishes, everyone says, “I heard you!”

soldier.story: When Jesus visited Martha’s home, Martha was busy preparing a big meal, while her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet to hear his teaching. Martha was upset and went to complain to Jesus. Jesus said, “You are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” He didn’t mean cooking was wrong, but that our hearts shouldn’t be stuffed full of tasks. It is like a schoolbag crammed so full that the most important textbook won’t fit in. If our hearts are crammed full, there is no room to listen to God and to our family.
ask: At home, are you more like Martha or like Mary? Why?
At mealtimes, how do you most want your family to listen to you?
soldier.do: This week, be the “table host”. At dinner, ask a question, such as “Where did you see God help you today?” and let everyone answer in turn.

youth.talk: Recently I noticed that I have three modes at the table: one is always busy, in and out; one keeps asking about your homework; and one eats while looking at my phone. When I read Jesus saying to Martha, “you are anxious and troubled about many things”, I felt it was about me. I’d like to ask how you feel, even if it’s hard to hear.
ask: Which mode am I in most often at the table? What do you think when that happens?
What do you think matters most for a “good dinner”?
youth.do: Ask your child to help design some “table rules”, such as who puts their phone down first and who starts the conversation. Try them as a family for a week.

fam.pray: Jesus, thank you for coming to our home. Please help us not to be too busy at mealtimes, so we can sit down and listen to each other. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Their Eyes Were Opened in the Breaking of Bread
lessons.theme: I believe: Jesus is willing to be recognized at my family table

v: They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.” He went in to stay with them.
When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
Their eyes were opened and they recognized him; then he vanished out of their sight.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”

lessons.still: Be quiet and recall: has there been a meal in your life when you especially felt loved and accepted? Stay in that picture a while and ask the Lord, “Were you there too?”
teach: On the day of the resurrection, two disciples were walking dejectedly on the road to Emmaus. Jesus came near, but they did not recognize him. All the way he explained the Scriptures, and their hearts burned, yet their eyes were still dim. It was only in the evening, at the table, that “he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them. Their eyes were opened and they recognized him.” The risen Lord was recognized at an ordinary evening meal.

This gives parents great hope. We often think children can meet God only at a special conference, a camp or a moving sermon. But God loves to open children’s eyes over ordinary home-cooked meals. A child may forget what the pastor said, but remember Dad’s sincere prayer before the meal, or the evening Mom, after a bad day, put his favorite piece of fish in his bowl. Love and faith are often not explained but tasted. The acceptance a child tastes at the table will become the flavor by which he later understands the gospel.

Today we move from knowing to conviction. Write your “I believe”: I believe Jesus is willing to be recognized at my family table; I believe the prayer before the meal is not a formality but an invitation; I believe my children will meet the risen Lord at our ordinary dinners. When our viewpoint changes, the table is no longer only a place to be filled but a place of meeting. Like the two disciples at Emmaus, who got up from the meal at once and hurried back to Jerusalem that very night with their news, a dinner with the Lord present can renew the strength of a discouraged family.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal. From the earthly side, a dinner is just eating; from heaven’s side, it is an eternal investment. Conviction leads to action: letting Jesus reign begins with letting him take the seat of honor at my family table.
q: Who is God? — The risen Jesus opened the disciples’ eyes in the breaking of bread. Whose eyes does he want to open at your family table?
Who am I? — Do I think children meet God only at “big gatherings”, and so look down on the table at home?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: about my family table, I believe …
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.” He did not only sit at table in Emmaus. Today too he knocks at the door of our home, waiting to be invited in to sit at our table.
lessons.pray: Risen Lord Jesus, I believe you are willing to be recognized at my family table. I admit that I often treat mealtimes as routine and say grace in a hurry. Today I open the door of my home and invite you in. As we break bread and eat, open each of our eyes, so that my children may recognize you in ordinary dinners. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations and stick them by the table: “I believe Jesus is willing to be recognized at my family table.” …
Slow down tonight’s prayer of thanks, and give thanks specifically for one food and the person who prepared it
At dinner, share a memory of experiencing God at a table, such as an unforgettable meal from your childhood
lessons.noon: “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him.” — Lord, today open my eyes to recognize you in ordinary things too.

fam.key: Jesus is with us when we eat.

lamb.do: At the meal, pick up a small piece of bread or a steamed bun, break it slowly in front of your child, give him a small piece, and then share it with the rest of the family.
lamb.say: We share it together, and Jesus is with us.

sprout.story: Two people were walking home, very sad, because they thought Jesus had died. A man walked along with them and told them lots of stories from the Bible. When they reached home, they asked the man to stay for supper. He took the bread, gave thanks to God, broke it and gave it to them. Wow! They looked, and it was Jesus! Jesus was alive! They were so happy, and ran at once to tell their friends.
sprout.ask: If you found that Jesus was sitting at our family table, what would you say to him?
sprout.do: At dinner tonight, let your child take a piece of bread or a cookie, break it, and share it with each family member, saying, “Jesus loves you!”

soldier.story: On the day Jesus rose from the dead, two disciples walked back to Emmaus feeling very disappointed. Jesus walked beside them, but they did not recognize him. All the way he explained the Scriptures to them, and their hearts burned as they listened. In the evening they asked Jesus to stay and eat with them. Jesus took the bread, gave thanks and broke it, and suddenly their eyes were opened and they knew it was Jesus! Jiahao in Melbourne says the first time he felt God was real was not at church but at a family dinner, when Dad prayed for a sick classmate, and the next day the classmate really did get better.
ask: Have you ever felt God was very near when we were eating at home?
Why do you think Jesus chose mealtime for the disciples to recognize him?
soldier.do: This week at every dinner, take turns saying one thing: “Where did I see Jesus today?” The adults must say one too.

youth.talk: You may feel that grace before meals is just an old habit in our family, and sometimes we say it so fast it seems like part of a routine. To be honest, I often do that myself. But I read that the disciples on the road to Emmaus recognized Jesus at supper, as he broke the bread. I started to think that maybe the place God most wants to show up in our home is not a special meeting but this table, every day.
ask: Does our grace before meals mean anything to you, or is it just a habit?
What would you suggest to make the prayer before the meal more real?
youth.do: Invite your child to lead the prayer before a meal once this week, in his own way. It can be just one sentence. Parents don’t correct or add anything, but only say “Amen”.

fam.pray: Risen Jesus, thank you for eating with us. Please open our eyes, so that every day we recognize you beside us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Children Around Your Table
lessons.theme: Start today: giving thanks, conversation and praise

v: Your wife will be as a fruitful vine in the innermost parts of your house, your children like olive shoots around your table.
Behold, this is how the man who fears the LORD is blessed.
You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land which he has given you.

lessons.still: Picture your children around the table tonight, like young olive shoots growing. For each child, whisper their name and say, “Lord, thank you.”
teach: Psalm 128 paints a picture of a blessed family: “your children like olive shoots around your table.” An olive tree takes decades to mature, and the table is where it is watered every day. Deuteronomy also reminds us, “You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God.” Thanks before the meal and blessing after it turn the dinner table into an altar. Today let’s give our family table a simple flow.

Step one is “put down”: before eating, everyone puts their phone in the phone basket, with parents going first. Step two is “thank”: the prayer of thanks can be led in turns, or each person can say a sentence beginning “I thank God for …”, or you can sing a short grace together. Step three is “talk”: open the conversation with a question. Step four is “praise”: close with one sentence after the meal, for example everyone saying, “Thank you, God, we’re full!” The whole flow takes only five extra minutes.

Prepare conversation questions like these: “What was the high point and the low point of your day?” “Who helped you today, and whom did you help?” “If Jesus went to school with you today, where would he stop?” “Whom do you most want to pray for this week?” Guohua, a single dad in Kuala Lumpur, wrote the questions on popsicle sticks and put them in a cup for his three children to draw in turn. He said, “Before, a meal was over in ten minutes. Now it often lasts forty.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is what lands conviction. We don’t wait until the whole family is spiritual before we begin. We use one simple flow and practice it every day. Parents are first to put down the phone, first to lead the prayer, first to share their own low point. Humility leads to humility: when children see parents open up, they are willing to open up too.
q: Who is God? — He is the God who gives us food and delights when we bless him once we are full. Which food you ate today reminded you of his grace?
Who am I? — Among the four steps, put down, thank, talk and praise, which is hardest for my family? Am I the one who gets stuck?
How should I respond? — Tonight, try the whole flow of “put down, thank, talk, praise” once, and see what happens.
lessons.jesus: Jesus took five loaves and two fish, “looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples”, and five thousand were fed. He looked to heaven and gave thanks before the meal, cared for every person during it, and afterward told them to gather up the pieces. His table had thanksgiving, sharing and thrift, the best example for our family table.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for letting our children gather around our table. Today I will begin: at the table I will first put down my phone, first give thanks, first listen, and bless you when we are full. Help me to persevere, so that this table becomes the warmest place in my children’s lives, and the place where they most often meet you. Amen.
acts: Prepare a phone basket by the table today, and at dinner parents put their phones in first
Write ten table conversation questions on slips of paper or popsicle sticks, put them in a cup, and draw one tonight
After the meal, say a sentence of praise as a family, such as, “Thank you, God, we’re full!”
lessons.noon: “You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God” — Lord, thank you for today’s food. I bless you.

fam.key: Put down, thank, talk, praise: eat together.

lamb.do: Each time before you feed your child, hold his hands together and sing a short grace. When he has finished, pat his little tummy and say “thank you, God” together.
lamb.say: Full tummy, thank you, God!

sprout.story: Little Bear’s family has four steps at mealtimes. First, put down: put the toys in the basket. Second, thank: hold hands and thank God. Third, talk: Little Bear says he saw a butterfly in the park today, and Papa Bear says he fixed a car today. Fourth, praise: when they have finished, everyone pats their tummies and says, “Thank you, God, we’re full!” Little Bear thinks mealtime is the happiest time of the day.
sprout.ask: What would you like to tell everyone at the meal today?
sprout.do: Tonight be the “Put-Down, Thank, Talk, Praise captain”. Before eating, remind everyone to put things down and hold hands for grace, and after the meal lead everyone in patting their tummies and saying thank you to God.

soldier.story: The psalm says a blessed home has children around the table like little olive shoots. Olive trees grow slowly, but they can live for hundreds of years and bear a great deal of fruit. The table is like the place where the little trees are watered each day. Once, Jesus took five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven and blessed them, then shared them out, and five thousand people were fed, with twelve baskets left over. Our table can be like that too: thank first, then share, and when we are full, remember to praise God.
ask: If you could make up a table conversation question, what would you ask everyone?
Do you think leaving phones off the table is a good idea or very hard to do? Why?
soldier.do: Write five table conversation questions and put them in the “conversation cup”. Each dinner this week, draw one.

youth.talk: I’d like to suggest we try a very simple dinner flow: phones aside first, then after grace take turns answering one question, and finish with a “thank you, God”. I know phones off the table may be hard for you, and for me too. I often answer work messages while I eat. So I’ll put mine away first, and if I pick it up, you can remind me.
ask: What do you think is the biggest difficulty with a dinner without phones? How could we solve it?
Would you help come up with some table questions? What kind of question would you want to answer?
youth.do: Design the phone basket together with your child (an old box decorated would do), and agree on one exception, such as “emergency calls may be answered, but say so first”.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for our food and for the family we eat with. When we are full, we want to thank you and praise you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: A Dinner of Herbs, Speech with Salt
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: the atmosphere at the table matters more than the menu

v: Better is a dinner of herbs, where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.still: Think back over this week’s family meals. Which was the warmest? Which was the tensest? Ask the Holy Spirit to look at those two pictures with you, and ask him, “Lord, what was the difference?”
teach: Proverbs says, “Better is a dinner of herbs, where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred.” Whether a family table is good depends not on how rich the food is but on whether the people at it love one another. Another proverb says, “Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife.” Many parents work hard to prepare food, then quarrel, compare and blame at the table, so the children are full but their hearts are hungry.

Paul says, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt.” Salt gives food flavor and stops it going bad. Words at the table are the same: gracious words give a home its flavor, while rough words slowly spoil relationships. In the Chen family in Singapore, three generations live together, and Grandpa was in the habit of nagging his grandson at the table. In the end the whole family agreed that at the table they would speak only three kinds of words: words of thanks, words of curiosity and words of encouragement.

This week we learned that the table is an altar, that we should not be a hectic Martha, that we can believe Jesus is recognized in the breaking of bread, and we tried put down, thank, talk, praise. Today, review honestly: how many meals did we manage? Which sentence made the table sweet, and which made it bitter? Then write down next week’s adjustments, such as fixing which meal, replacing which topic, and who will look after the phone basket. The table is a chance that comes every day. If today didn’t go well, tomorrow we can begin again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride and both lose; humility draws out humility and both win. Quarrels at the table often begin with one proud remark. If parents are willing to apologize first at the table and speak gracious words first, the atmosphere of the whole table will change.
q: Who is God? — He values love for one another above a rich feast. At which simple meal did you feel his love?
Who am I? — This week, were my words at the table more like salt seasoning the food, or like a handful of sand?
How should I respond? — Which table habit will I keep next week? Which will I adjust?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus knew Judas would betray him and Peter would deny him, yet he still sat at table with them, broke bread for them, washed their feet and spoke gently to them. At the tensest table, his words were still full of grace and his heart still full of love. He is willing to change the tone of our family table too.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for eating with us this week. I admit that sometimes my words made the table bitter, and my children were full but hurt in their hearts. Forgive me, and heal them. Teach me to speak words seasoned with salt, so that even if our table has only herbs, it is filled with love for one another. Amen.
acts: Talk for ten minutes with your spouse: which meal this week was warmest, and why? Which meals will you fix next week, and which habit will you adjust?
Ask your child, “This week at mealtimes, have Dad and Mom become more like Jesus? Was there any sentence that made you uncomfortable?” Just listen, without defending yourself
Write down one table adjustment for next week and stick it on the fridge
lessons.noon: “Better is a dinner of herbs, where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred.” — Lord, today I want to season every word of mine with love.

fam.key: A meal with love tastes best.

lamb.do: At mealtimes, say more gentle words to your child and describe the food in a soft voice: “This is a red tomato. It smells so good.” Help your child connect eating with warm voices.
lamb.say: Eating with you makes me so happy.

sprout.story: One day Rabbit’s family had only carrots to eat, but they told jokes as they ate and laughed so much. Fox’s family had a big table of delicious chicken legs, but they argued as they ate, and when they had finished nobody was happy. The Bible says that eating ordinary food together with love is far better than a feast with anger!
sprout.ask: Which family do you think had the nicer meal, Rabbit’s or Fox’s? Why?
sprout.do: At dinner tonight, each person says one kind thing to the person next to them, such as “Thank you” or “You were great today”.

soldier.story: The Bible says our words should be seasoned with salt. A soup without salt is bland, a soup with too much salt is too salty to drink, and a soup with just the right amount of salt is delicious. Speaking is like that too: if we say nothing, our family can’t feel our love; if we speak too harshly, they get hurt; and words with grace are words everyone can take in. One family agreed that at the table they would speak only three kinds of words: words of thanks, words of curiosity and words of encouragement. Their dinner became the time the whole family looked forward to most.
ask: At mealtimes this week, did anyone say something that made you very happy?
Was there any sentence that made you uncomfortable? How would you like it said next time?
soldier.do: A five-minute family meeting: each person shares “the happiest thing at the table this week” and “one thing about the table they’d like to improve next week”, with parents going first.

youth.talk: This week we tried to make dinner different, and I want to admit first that a few times I still couldn’t help nagging you at the table, or looked at my phone. I’d like to hear how you really feel. The Bible says a dinner of herbs where there is love is better than a fattened calf with hatred. I would rather our family eat more simply, but have every meal make you feel loved, not checked up on.
ask: Was there any dinner this week when you thought, “This isn’t bad”?
What is the one thing you think our family table most needs to change?
youth.do: Parents first apologize to the child for something they said wrongly at the table this week, then invite the child to decide one table adjustment for next week, such as choosing the dish once a week on a “your choice” day.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us eat together. Please help us to say kind and gentle words at the table, so that every meal in our home is full of love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

23.memT: Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,

mem.t: ‘The LORD bless you, and keep you. The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

sat.t: Family Day: A Night of Blessing
sat.d: During the day, make “blessing cards” together. Each person writes or draws a card for every other family member, with the words “I bless you …” and one good quality you see in them. In the evening, before the lights go out, the family sits together in the living room. Parents first lay hands on each child (a hand on the head or shoulder) and bless them with Numbers 6:24–26, adding the child’s name. Then invite the children to bless their parents, and finally give the blessing cards to one another. If grandparents live far away, call them by video and ask them to bless their grandchildren.

sun: Were you ever blessed by your parents or elders when you were small? How did those words (or the absence of them) shape you?
How did your child respond when you gave a bedtime blessing this week? How did you feel?
Which parent or grandparent will you share the “bedtime blessing” with, inviting them to begin blessing the family too?

lessons.title: This Is How You Shall Bless
lessons.theme: Parents are the priests of the home, entrusted by God with a blessing

v: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’ You shall tell them,
‘The LORD bless you, and keep you.
The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.
The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
“So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”

lessons.still: Be quiet for a moment and imagine God’s face turned toward you, looking at you with a smile. Don’t hurry to speak. Simply receive his gaze and say to him, “Lord, let me receive your blessing first.”
teach: God told Moses to speak to Aaron and his sons: “This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.” Then came three lines: “The LORD bless you, and keep you. The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.” At the end God said, “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.” The blessing was not the priests’ invention. God himself wrote the words and put them in their mouths.

These three lines draw closer with each one. To bless and keep is God’s provision and care. “His face to shine on you” is like the beaming smile on a father’s face when he sees his child. “Lift up his face toward you” is God turning to look at you with his full attention, and placing peace in your heart. To this day many Jewish families lay their hands on their children’s heads on Friday evening at the Sabbath and speak this blessing, one generation after another. What the child hears in that moment is not only a parent’s voice but God’s name being placed on him.

The New Testament says believers are “a royal priesthood”. At home, parents are their children’s priests: on one hand bringing the children to God in prayer, and on the other speaking God’s blessing over them. Mr. Zhang in Taipei comes home late from overtime every night when the children are already asleep, so he stands by their beds and gently lays his hand on their heads and speaks these three lines. He says, “I can’t give them much time, but every day I can leave them with God’s blessing.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus reign, and let him receive all the glory. A blessing is not the parent’s own power but “my name”: God’s name and God’s favor. Parents living the self-emptied life do not influence their children through their own eloquence or achievements, but become channels for God’s blessing to flow through, so that children hear the Father’s voice in their parents’ mouths.
q: Who is God? — He takes the initiative to give the priests the words of blessing, and promises, “I will bless them.” What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — Do I realize that I am my children’s priest? What do I most often say to my children?
How should I respond? — Tonight, how will I speak the blessing of Numbers over my children?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus ascended, “he lifted up his hands and blessed them. While he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.” The last picture he left his disciples was not of instructions or rebukes but of raised hands and a blessing. He still intercedes for us today at the Father’s right hand, and his blessing has never stopped.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making your face shine on me, lifting it toward me, and giving me peace. I admit that I often speak to my children only with demands and reminders, and seldom with blessing. Let me receive your blessing first, and let me be the priest of my home, speaking blessing over my children every day in your name. Amen.
acts: Copy Numbers 6:24–26 onto a card, keep it by your bed or as your phone wallpaper, and learn it by heart today
Tonight at bedtime, go to each child’s bed and say with his name, “___, the LORD bless you, and keep you …”
If your child is already asleep, still bless him softly. If he is not with you, bless him by message or phone call
lessons.noon: “The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.” — Lord, lift up your face toward me now, and let me bring this blessing to my children tonight.

fam.key: Mom and Dad bless me in God’s name.

lamb.do: At bedtime, gently rest your hand on your child’s head, look into his eyes, smile, and slowly speak the blessing from Numbers. Use the same gesture and the same words every night.
lamb.say: God bless you and keep you. You are God’s treasure.

sprout.story: Long, long ago, God told the high priest Aaron, “This is how you shall bless my people.” So Aaron lifted his hands and said to everyone, “The LORD bless you and keep you. May God smile on you. May God give you peace.” Everyone was so happy hearing it, because it felt as if God were smiling at each one of them. Tonight Mom and Dad will also put their hands on your head and give you God’s blessing!
sprout.ask: What do you think it looks like when God smiles at you?
sprout.do: Play “God’s Smile”. A parent says one blessing to the child and gives him a big smile. The child says “God loves you” to the parent and smiles back.

soldier.story: More than three thousand years ago, God himself wrote a blessing for the priest Aaron and his sons to use in blessing the people of Israel: “The LORD bless you, and keep you. The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.” God also said, “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.” Many families still use these words to bless their children today. Like a baton passed in a relay, this blessing has been handed down from generation to generation, and now it has reached our family.
ask: Which of these three lines do you like best? Why?
What do you think it feels like for “God’s face to shine on you”?
soldier.do: This week, learn Numbers 6:24–26 by heart. Say it together as a family each night before bed, and at the weekend try using it to bless Mom and Dad.

youth.talk: You may think it is a bit strange for Mom and Dad to say a blessing at bedtime, especially now you are older. I want to say why. In the Bible, God told the priests to bless the people with a set of words, and said, “I will bless them.” I realized that most of what I say to you is reminders, demands and worries, and I seldom speak God’s blessing over you. I’d like to begin, but I will respect your feelings and your way.
ask: What is the difference between being blessed and being reminded?
If I were to bless you, which way would you find easiest to accept: face to face, by message, or a written card?
youth.do: With your child’s agreement, bless him once in a way he is comfortable with. If he doesn’t want it face to face, send a message with Numbers 6:24–26 and his name.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for smiling at us every day. Please bless us and keep us, and let us sleep in peace tonight. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Blessing and Cursing from One Mouth
lessons.theme: Are the words I speak to my children blessing or cursing?

v: With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

lessons.still: Think back over what you have said to your children these past few days, especially when you were angry or tired. Ask the Holy Spirit, like a gentle sound engineer, to replay those words for you. Don’t rush to defend yourself. Simply listen.
teach: James says, “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing.” Many parents sing wholeheartedly at worship on Sunday, then at home say to their children, “How can you be so stupid!” “You’re just lazy!” “If I’d known, I wouldn’t have had you.” We don’t think of these as curses, but to a child they are a verdict on who he is.

Proverbs says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” Children treat their parents’ words as a mirror that shows them who they are. If parents often say “you’re just careless”, the child decides he is a careless person. If parents often say “I see how hard you are trying”, the child slowly grows into a hardworking person. After Esau lost his father’s blessing, he “cried with an exceedingly great and bitter cry” and begged, “Do you have just one blessing, my father?” Inside every child is a longing for a parent’s blessing.

Meiling, a single mother in Ipoh, says the sentence she heard most as a girl was “You’re a drain on the family.” She vowed never to say that to her daughter, yet on one tired day the same words slipped out. In that moment she saw that curses are inherited from generation to generation, unless someone stops before God. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: what kind of parent am I? One who blesses often, or one who is unknowingly cursing?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parent’s own heart first, then the child’s behavior. Cursing words usually flow from a wounded, weary, self-ruled heart, because the child embarrasses me or makes me lose control. When a parent brings their own heart to the cross to be healed, blessing can flow from the mouth. Pride provokes pride; humility draws out humility.
q: Who is God? — He made my child in his own image. How does he regard every sentence I say to my child?
Who am I? — What label do I most often put on my child? Do those words include any curses I heard myself as a child?
How should I respond? — For which sentence do I need to apologize to my child, and what blessing will I replace it with?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptized, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Jesus had not yet begun to preach or done any miracle, yet the Father’s blessing came first. His identity was built on the Father’s blessing, not on his performance. He is willing to heal the curses we heard growing up and rename us in the Father’s voice.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that my mouth holds both praise and cursing. I have wounded my children with sharp words and stuck labels on them that do not belong to you. Forgive me, and heal me of the words I heard as a child that still affect me today. Cleanse my lips, so that what I say to my children is what you said to Jesus: you are my beloved, and I am pleased with you. Amen.
acts: Write down the three negative labels you most often put on your children, and next to each write a matching blessing
Today find a chance to say to your child, “I used to say you were ___. I was wrong. What I see is …”
Pray about the most hurtful sentence you heard as a child, hand it to God, and ask him to heal it
lessons.noon: “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.” — Lord, guard my mouth today, so that only blessing comes out.

fam.key: My mouth will speak words of blessing.

lamb.do: As you dress your child or change his diaper, speak blessing as you go, for example, “Your little hands are so strong. God made you wonderfully.”
lamb.say: You are God’s special creation. I really like you.

sprout.story: One day Little Chick Jiji knocked over the water bowl, and Mother Hen said angrily, “You silly chick!” Jiji was so sad that he kept his head down all day and felt he really was silly. In the evening Mother Hen hugged Jiji and said, “Mommy was wrong. You’re not silly. You’re a good chick God made, you just had an accident.” Jiji lifted his head and smiled. The words we say can make someone put their head down, or lift it up.
sprout.ask: What do people say that makes you very happy? What makes you very sad?
sprout.do: Play “Head Up, Head Down”. A grown-up says a sentence. If it is a blessing, the child lifts his head and smiles. If it is unkind, he puts his head down. At the end the family only says “head up” words.

soldier.story: Isaac was old and ready to bless his elder son Esau, but his younger son Jacob got in first and took the blessing. When Esau came back and found out, he wept aloud: “Do you have just one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, my father.” A grown man crying that bitterly shows how much he longed for his father’s blessing. The Bible says death and life are in the power of the tongue. A word can be like a seed that grows courage in someone, or like a nail that leaves a hole in their heart.
ask: Is there a sentence you still remember because it made you very happy or very sad?
What “nail words” do you think our family says most? What “seed words” could replace them?
soldier.do: Make a “seed words jar”. Each day, everyone writes one blessing or word of encouragement for someone else and puts it in the jar. At the weekend, open it and read them together.

youth.talk: I want to be honest with you. I know that sometimes I say very heavy things to you, such as “You’re so irresponsible” or “What will become of you if you go on like this?” I said them out of anger and worry, but I now understand those words may have left deep marks in you. James says that blessing and cursing coming from one mouth ought not to be so. I want to apologize to you properly.
ask: Is there something I said that still bothers you? Would you be willing to tell me?
What words do you wish I would use to describe you?
youth.do: Parents write a short letter, apologizing specifically for one thing they said wrongly, and listing three good qualities from God that they see in their child. Leave it on the child’s desk.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us mouths. Please help us not to say hurtful words, but only kind words of blessing, so that our family is happy to hear them. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Jacob’s Hands
lessons.theme: I believe: my blessing carries God’s promise

v: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn.
He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day,
the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.”

lessons.still: Imagine a warm pair of hands resting on your head. They are the Father’s hands. Stay quietly in this picture and let his blessing fall on you first, before you prepare to become hands that bless others.
teach: Before Jacob died, Joseph brought his two sons to him. The old man, with failing eyes, stretched out his hands and laid them on his grandsons’ heads, praying to “the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day”, to “bless the lads”. Hebrews records this scene and says Jacob blessed “by faith”. He could not see his grandsons’ faces clearly, but he could see God’s promise clearly.

Jacob’s blessing had three elements that parents can learn from. First, he told what God had done in his life: “fed me all my life long to this day”. A blessing includes testimony. Second, he linked the boys to the family’s faith: “let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac”. A blessing includes identity. Third, he spoke over their future: “Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.” A blessing includes hope. Testimony, identity and hope are the skeleton of a good blessing.

Grandpa Lin in Tainan is over eighty and has believed for less than ten years. He says, “I used to give my grandchildren red envelopes. Now I want to give them a blessing.” Each time they visit, he lays his hands on their heads and says in Taiwanese, “May Jesus protect you, and may you become a person who fears God.” Today, write your “I believe”: I believe my blessing is not empty words, because God says, “I will bless them”; I believe my blessing will bear fruit in my children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction is the key to change. If parents think a blessing is only pleasant words, they won’t keep it up. If they are convinced that God himself has promised to bless, they will speak it every day until the children are grown. The “3” in 235, becoming spiritual parents to your children, begins by laying hands on them and blessing them, passing the baton of faith to the next generation.
q: Who is God? — He is “the God who has fed me all my life long to this day”. Looking back over your life, where has he shepherded you?
Who am I? — Do I believe that the blessing I speak over my children carries God’s promise?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration, and write a blessing for your child using “testimony, identity, hope”.
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the one who fulfills the promise. The multitude Jacob blessed finally reaches all nations through Jesus. He brings blessing to us not because we deserve it, but because on the cross he took the curse in our place. So in him we can boldly bless our children.
lessons.pray: God who has fed me all my life long to this day, I believe you will shepherd my children too. I believe the blessing I speak in your name is not empty words, because you have promised to bless them. Let me be like Jacob: even when my eyes cannot see the future clearly, I lay my hands on my children by faith and hand your blessing on to the next generation. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations, for example: “I believe God will bless my children.” “I believe my blessing will bear fruit in my children.”

Write a personal blessing for each child using “testimony, identity, hope”, such as: “God has always kept our family; you are a child God loves and who belongs to him; may you grow up to bring people peace.”
Tonight, lay hands on your child and bless him with this blessing
lessons.noon: “the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads” — Lord, bless my children too.

fam.key: God’s blessing is passed down from one generation to the next.

lamb.do: Let your child look at family photos. Point to Grandpa and Grandma, say their names, then lay your hand on your child’s head and bless him.
lamb.say: God kept Grandpa and Grandma, Mom and Dad, and God will keep you too.

sprout.story: Grandpa Jacob was old, and his eyes could not see well. His son Joseph brought his two little grandsons to see him. Grandpa Jacob stretched out both his hands, one on the younger boy’s head and one on the older boy’s, and said, “God has looked after me all my life, from young to old. May God look after you and bless you too!” The two little boys felt how warm Grandpa’s hands were, and they knew that God was their God too.
sprout.ask: What blessing would you like Grandpa and Grandma to say over you?
sprout.do: Today call or video-call your grandparents and ask them to say a blessing over you, and say one for them too: “God bless you!”

soldier.story: When Jacob was very old and near the end of his life, Joseph brought his sons Ephraim and Manasseh to see him. Jacob crossed his hands and laid them on his two grandsons’ heads to bless them. First he told how God had shepherded him all his life. Then he said these boys belonged to the family of Abraham. Finally he blessed them to grow into a multitude. The blessing had three key points: testimony (what God has done for me), identity (who you are) and hope (what you will become). Like a letter with an opening, a middle and an ending, a good blessing has a skeleton too.
ask: If you were to bless a younger brother, sister or friend, what testimony, identity and hope would you speak?
What do you think is worth handing down in our family from generation to generation?
soldier.do: Using the three lines of “testimony, identity, hope”, write a blessing for one family member and read it to him in person tonight.

youth.talk: In his old age Jacob could not see well, yet he still reached out to bless his grandsons, and Scripture says he did it “by faith”. I have been wondering what is worth handing down in our family. It is not the house or the savings, but how God led our family through hard times. I want to tell you those stories, and I also want to hear your hopes for your own future, so that my blessing is not empty words but close to who you are.
ask: What things do you think God has done in our family’s history that stand out to you?
What hopes or worries do you have about your own future?
youth.do: Parents share one “testimony of God in our family”, then ask the child about one hope for the future, and finally bless that hope with a short prayer.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for looking after Grandpa and Grandma, Mom and Dad, and us. Please pass your blessing down from one generation to the next, until it reaches us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Hold Them in Your Arms and Bless Them
lessons.theme: Start today: three bedtime questions and the laying on of hands

v: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

lessons.still: Picture tonight at your child’s bedside, the light low and him about to fall asleep. Ask the Lord, “Lord, what does he most need to hear from me tonight?” Wait a moment, and note the sentence that comes to you.
teach: People were bringing little children to Jesus, and the disciples, thinking it a waste of time, rebuked them. When Jesus saw it, he “was moved with indignation” and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Then he did three things: he “took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” Holding is closeness, laying on hands is passing something on, and blessing is words. These three actions are exactly the pattern for a bedtime blessing.

Bedtime is when a child’s heart is most open in the whole day. You can open the conversation with “three bedtime questions”. First: “What are you thankful to God for today?” Second: “What made you sad or worried today?” Third: “What would you like me to pray about?” After listening, pray briefly, and then lay hands on him and bless him. The Zheng family in Singapore has three children, and Dad and Mom take turns. Each child gets about three to five minutes, and no one is left out.

For the blessing you can use the blessing from Numbers, or say your own, for example: “___, you are a child God loves. The LORD bless you and keep you. May you sleep sweetly tonight, and tomorrow be strong and courageous, a person who brings others peace. I bless you in the name of the Lord Jesus. Amen.” For little ones, you can pat and sing. With teenagers, first ask, “May I put my hand on your shoulder and bless you?” Respect their wishes. Laying on hands can be just a light touch on the shoulder.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. A bedtime blessing is not a technique but a relationship: parents put down the phone and the housework and give their full attention to the child for a few minutes. Practice should be small and daily. Three minutes every night is better than an hour now and then. This is how parents build what belongs to God in their children’s hearts, day by day.
q: Who is God? — Jesus was indignant when the disciples blocked the children. How precious children are to him! What new thing does this show you about God?
Who am I? — What often “blocks” my children from coming close to me and to God: my busyness, my phone, or my moods?
How should I respond? — Tonight, do “three bedtime questions plus the laying on of hands” with each child, and note their answers.
lessons.jesus: Even in the busiest stretch of his ministry, Jesus stopped to hold children. He didn’t say “Wait until I’m finished”, and he didn’t just wave. He held them, laid hands on them and blessed them, one by one. His cherishing of children is the best reason for us to stop at the bedside before sleep.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for taking little children in your arms and blessing them. I admit that, because of busyness and weariness, I have often rushed my children’s bedtime. Tonight I want to learn from you: to stop, to hold, to listen and to bless. Through my hands, put your love and peace in my children’s hearts. Amen.
acts: Tonight, do the “three bedtime questions” with each child: what are you thankful for, what made you sad, what shall we pray about?
Write a blessing on a small card and keep it by the bed. Lay hands on your child and bless him, saying his name
If your child is older or away from you, send a message of blessing with his name and Numbers 6:24–26
lessons.noon: “He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” — Lord, tonight bless my child through my hands.

fam.key: Tell three things at night, then receive a blessing.

lamb.do: Hold your child in your arms and rock him gently, sing a simple hymn, then rest your hand on his head and bless him with the same words each night. Kiss his forehead and lay him in bed.
lamb.say: The LORD bless you and keep you. Good night, my treasure.

sprout.story: Lots of moms and dads brought their little children to see Jesus, and the disciples said, “Go away, go away! Jesus is busy!” But Jesus said, “Let the children come to me!” He picked up the little ones one by one, laid his hands on their heads and said, “God bless you!” The children were so happy, because Jesus loves children best of all. Tonight Mom and Dad will hold you and bless you, just like Jesus.
sprout.ask: What would you like to thank God for today? Is there anything that made you sad?
sprout.do: Play “Three Fingers at Bedtime” tonight: thank God, something sad, ask Mom and Dad to pray. At the end, Mom and Dad lay their hands on your head and bless you.

soldier.story: Some people brought little children to Jesus, and the disciples thought the children would bother him and sent them away. When Jesus saw it, he was actually angry! He said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Then he took the children in his arms and laid his hands on them to bless them. In Jesus’ eyes, children are not a nuisance at all. They are important. One elementary school boy said his favorite time is not playing games but every night when Dad sits on his bed and asks, “How was your day?” and then prays for him.
ask: Of the three bedtime questions, which is hardest to answer? Why?
What would you like Mom and Dad to bless you with at bedtime?
soldier.do: Tonight, you ask Dad or Mom the “three bedtime questions” first, and then they ask you. Finally bless one another.

youth.talk: I know you’re older now and may not need me to tuck you in. But the picture of Jesus taking children into his arms and blessing them moved me. I’d like to pause at your door every night, ask whether you’re all right, and speak a blessing over you. You can just say “fine”, and I won’t push you. If you’re willing, I’d like to put my hand on your shoulder and pray. If not, that is completely all right.
ask: When someone asks “How was your day?” at bedtime, does it help you relax, or does it feel like pressure?
What kind of blessing would feel comfortable and not awkward to you?
youth.do: This week, each night pause for a minute at your child’s door: ask one question, listen to one answer, and say one blessing. Respect your child’s boundaries and don’t force him to share.

fam.pray: Jesus, thank you for loving children, and for loving us. Please hold us tonight and bless us, so that we sleep sweetly. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Do Not Let the Sun Go Down on Your Wrath
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: going to sleep reconciled and blessed

v: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
Stand in awe, and don’t sin. Search your own heart on your bed, and be still. Selah.
Offer the sacrifices of righteousness. Put your trust in the LORD.
Many say, “Who will show us any good?” LORD, let the light of your face shine on us.
You have put gladness in my heart, more than when their grain and their new wine are increased.
In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me live in safety.

lessons.still: Look back over each night of this week. Which night did you go to sleep at peace? Which night did you go to bed with anger or regret? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and gently ask, “Lord, what anger have I not yet handed to you?”
teach: Paul says, “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath.” In ancient times sunset marked the end of the day. God knows that family members will get angry with each other, so he doesn’t say “never be angry”. He gives a deadline instead: don’t carry anger into the night. The biggest enemy of a bedtime blessing is often not too little time but anger still in the heart, either we are still angry with our child or our child is still angry with us.

Psalm 4 says, “Search your own heart on your bed, and be still.” It also says, “In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me live in safety.” Bedtime is a good time to review the day. The He family in London has a rule: if there has been a quarrel during the day, before bed they must say “I’m sorry” and “I forgive you” before the blessing. Dad says, “Sometimes I’m the one who speaks first, and that is the hardest and most important part.”

This week we learned that parents are the priests of the home, that we shouldn’t curse with our mouths, that we bless by faith, and that we practice three bedtime questions and the laying on of hands. Today, review honestly: for how many nights did we bless our children this week? Which night felt most natural? Which night did we skip because of anger or busyness? What shall we adjust next week? Perhaps move the blessing earlier, make the words fit each child better, or first deal with the matter that has not yet been reconciled. Remember, a blessing after reconciliation is the most powerful.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to your place. Parents often think apologizing first means losing, but humility overcomes pride. When a parent says “I’m sorry” first, the child learns not the parent’s weakness but the road to reconciliation. Don’t hurt people for the sake of a matter. Don’t let a small thing carry anger through the night.
q: Who is God? — He is the God of “you alone, LORD, make me live in safety”. On which night this week did you experience the sleep he gives?
Who am I? — Did I go to bed with anger this week, or let my child go to bed feeling wronged?
How should I respond? — What will I keep of next week’s bedtime blessing, and what will I adjust? What else needs reconciling first?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was nailed to the cross, before the sun went down he prayed for those who nailed him, asking the Father to forgive them. He did not carry anger into death, but ended that day with forgiveness. Because of him, we can go to sleep each day with a forgiven heart, and bless our family with a forgiving heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us through every night this week. I admit that on a few nights I lay down angry and let my children go to sleep feeling hurt. Forgive me, and give me the courage to speak first and make peace. Let every night in our home end with us lying down to sleep in reconciliation and blessing. Amen.
acts: Talk for ten minutes with your spouse: on how many nights this week did you do the bedtime blessing? Which night moved you most? How will you adjust next week?
Ask your child, “This week at bedtime, have Dad and Mom become more like Jesus? How do you like me to bless you?” Just listen, without defending yourself
If anything is still unreconciled, say “I’m sorry” tonight before bed, and then bless your child
lessons.noon: “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” — Lord, before sunset today, help me to lay down my anger.

fam.key: Before sleep, make peace first, then receive the blessing.

lamb.do: If you raised your voice at your child during the day, hold him at bedtime, say sorry in a gentle voice, pat him softly and bless him. Even a little one can feel his parents’ tone.
lamb.say: Mommy (Daddy) was too loud just now. I’m sorry. I love you, and God loves you.

sprout.story: Little Elephant and his big brother quarreled over a toy in the daytime. At bedtime Little Elephant turned his back on his brother and couldn’t sleep at all. Mother Elephant came over and said, “The Bible says not to go to bed angry.” Little Elephant thought for a while, turned over and said, “Brother, I’m sorry.” His brother said, “I’m sorry too. I forgive you.” Mother Elephant laid her long trunk on their heads and blessed them, and the two little elephants soon fell asleep.
sprout.ask: Are you angry with anyone today? Shall we make peace before bed?
sprout.do: Play “Making-Up Hugs” at bedtime. If anyone quarreled today, say “I’m sorry” and “I forgive you” to each other, then hug.

soldier.story: Paul said, “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath.” It means that anger will happen, but don’t let it stay overnight. Anger is like trash that hasn’t been taken out. After one night it smells, and after a week the whole house is uncomfortable. One family has a rule: if there is a quarrel in the day, before bed they must say “I’m sorry” and “I forgive you”, and then Mom and Dad bless everyone. They say that next morning, everyone feels lighter.
ask: Was there a night this week when you went to bed angry or sad?
Which do you find harder: saying “I’m sorry” or saying “I forgive you”?
soldier.do: A five-minute family meeting: each person names one time “this week at bedtime when you felt warmest”, and suggests one thing that could improve the bedtime blessing next week.

youth.talk: This week I tried to bless you every night. Some nights I managed it, and on some nights, because we had just quarreled, I didn’t come. Afterward I thought that those were exactly the nights that most needed a blessing. Paul says not to let the sun go down on your wrath, and I want first to say sorry for those nights. From now on, even if we quarrel, I will come and knock on your door before bed, not to argue again but to make peace.
ask: Was there anything about the way I blessed you this week that felt uncomfortable? Was there something you actually liked a little?
If we have quarreled, how would you like me to come to you before bed?
youth.do: Parents first apologize for one night this week when they went to sleep without making peace, then ask the child to suggest one change that would make the bedtime blessing more comfortable, and do it next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for protecting us every night. Please help us not to go to bed angry, but to make peace first and then receive your blessing together. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

24.memT: ‘The LORD bless you, and keep you. The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’

mem.t: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

sat.d: The evening before, finish the housework and homework. Gather round the table, light a candle, and let Mom and Dad say, “This is the Sabbath God has given us. Together we will rest and together we will worship.” Today there are no tutoring classes, no talk of grades and little screen time. Go for a walk in the park or by the sea, play a board game, take an afternoon nap. In the evening each person shares “the thing I enjoyed most today”, parents lay hands on the children and bless them, and then the candle is blown out. If your family has to work on Sundays, choose another day. The point is that one day a week the whole family stops together.

sun: In your family, who finds it hardest to stop during the week? What keeps them (or you) from stopping?
Did your family try resting this week? What did the children enjoy most? What was hardest for you to put down?
How could you help another busy family rediscover rest? For example, invite them on an outing, or share your family’s Sabbath routine.

lessons.title: On the Seventh Day God Rested
lessons.theme: Rest is a rhythm God designed for the home

v: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
You shall labor six days, and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.

lessons.still: Put down whatever is in your hands and let your body lean back in the chair. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you rested from your work, so I may pause too.” Stay quietly in that permission for a while, doing nothing.
teach: Genesis 2 says that when God had finished his work of creation, “he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done”, and “God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy”. The almighty God doesn’t get tired. His rest was not from weariness but for delighting, enjoying and declaring that “it is all good”. In God’s design, rest is not the time left over after the work is finished. It is a blessed day, set apart in the weekly rhythm.

The Ten Commandments say, “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” The most striking part comes next: “you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock”, none of you “shall do any work”. Rest is not a private devotion but a command for the whole household, including children, workers and animals. Christians today usually respond with Sunday worship and one day of rest a week. The point is not rules but remembering: God is the Creator and we are his creatures.

The Wu family in Kaohsiung runs a breakfast shop that was open seven days a week, and their children had helped in the shop since they were small. Later Mr. Wu decided to close one day a week, so that the family could go to church, eat lunch together and take a nap. He said, “In the first month I was afraid of earning less. Later I found we lost much less money than we feared, and gained far more laughter than we imagined.” Rest is a rhythm God has written into the family. It is a gift, not a punishment.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let God be God, and let people be people. Parents who never stop working often hear a voice in their hearts: “If I stop, this family will collapse.” That is wanting to take God’s place. Rest is admitting we are creatures and handing the world back to the Creator. This is humility: laying down power and returning to our place.
q: Who is God? — Almighty God also rested, and blessed the Sabbath day. What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — Does my family truly stop for one day in a week? Or are we rushing for seven days?
How should I respond? — Which day, or which stretch of time, can our family choose this week to stop together?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished!” and completed the work of redemption. Then his body lay in the tomb on the Sabbath, and on the first day of the week, early in the morning, he rose. He finished his work and entered rest, and he opened a new beginning for us. In him, our rest is not escape but living in what he has already finished.
lessons.pray: Lord who made heaven and earth, thank you for resting on the seventh day and blessing the Sabbath. I admit that I often treat rest as a waste and busyness as worth, and I let my children be swept along into never stopping. Teach our whole family to remember your rest, to set apart one day in the weekly rhythm for you, and, like you, to enjoy everything you have given. Amen.
acts: Look at next week’s calendar with your spouse and choose one day (or at least half a day) as the family’s time of rest
List three things you will “not do” on that day, for example no overtime, no tutoring, no big housework clean-up
Tell your child tonight, “God rests too, so our family will learn to rest together.”
lessons.noon: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” — Lord, in the middle of busyness, I remember that you are the Creator and I am your creature.

fam.key: God rests, so we rest together.

lamb.do: Choose a stretch of time, turn off the TV and phones, and lie with your child on a mat or bed. Look at the ceiling together, listen to music, breathe slowly, and hurry over nothing.
lamb.say: We rest together, and God loves to rest too.

sprout.story: In six days God made so many things: the sun, the moon, the sea, little fish, little birds, lions, and people too. On the seventh day God said, “Good, today let’s rest!” God sat down and looked at all he had made, and smiled and said, “How beautiful!” God wasn’t tired. He just wanted to enjoy it. So God gave us a day to rest, so that our family can slowly enjoy everything together.
sprout.ask: On a rest day, what would you most like to do with Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Play “Six Works and One Rest”: clap six times saying “work”, and on the seventh, put both hands on your chest and say “rest!” Repeat a few times, and at the end lie down together.

soldier.story: God created the world in six days and rested on the seventh, and he blessed that day. Later, when God gave Israel the Ten Commandments, one was: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” And not only grown-ups had to rest, but children, servants and animals too! A phone needs charging after long use, a field needs to lie fallow after long planting, and people are the same: if we run without stopping, we break down. God gave us the Sabbath because he loves us and knows we need to stop.
ask: Do you think our family has a time in the week when we really rest?
If there were one day when no one had to work or do homework, how would you spend it?
soldier.do: Draw a plan for “Our Family’s Sabbath”: write three things you want to do and three things you don’t want to do that day, and give it to Mom and Dad to consider.

youth.talk: Honestly, our family doesn’t seem to have a day of true rest. You have tutoring and homework at weekends, and I am often answering work messages. I read that in the Ten Commandments even children, servants and livestock had to rest, and I wonder whether we are living more wearily than the animals. I’d like us to try having one day a week when our family really stops. I need your opinion.
ask: What do you think would happen if for one day a week we touched no homework and no tutoring? What do you worry about?
What does “real rest” look like to you?
youth.do: Discuss with your child and choose a “rest time” he also agrees to, such as Sunday afternoon, when neither of you talks about homework or work. Try it for two weeks.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making such a beautiful world, and for giving us a day to rest. Please help our family to stop together, rest well and enjoy you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: You Were a Servant in Egypt
lessons.theme: Am I leading my child into rest, or sending him back to Egypt?

v: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you.
You shall labor six days, and do all your work;

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, in which you shall not do any work—neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you.

You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out of there by a mighty hand and by an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.

lessons.still: Think back over your child’s schedule this week, from morning to night, box by box. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and gently ask, “Lord, on this timetable, is there any place for my child’s heart to rest?”
teach: When Deuteronomy repeats the Ten Commandments, it gives another reason for the Sabbath: “You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out of there by a mighty hand and by an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.” Slaves have no right to rest. Only free people can stop. The Sabbath is the sign of freedom for God’s people. Each time we stop, we declare: we no longer belong to Pharaoh; we belong to God.

In Egypt, Pharaoh said of the Israelites, “You shall require from them the number of the bricks which they made before. You shall not diminish anything of it.” No straw, and the same number of bricks. Pharaoh’s system looked only at output, not at people. Today many Chinese families, without noticing, live in such a system: higher grades, more talents, earlier tutoring. A child’s worth seems to equal his “brick count”.

Mrs. Chen in Singapore had arranged six tutoring classes for her daughter. One day her daughter said, “Mom, I feel like a machine.” She froze, and saw she had been like Pharaoh, always demanding bricks from her child. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: what kind of parent am I? One who leads my child out of Egypt into rest, or one who, without realizing it, sends my child back to Egypt? This is not to say we shouldn’t nurture our children, but to ask: are these arrangements born of love and calling, or of anxiety and comparison?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset, from the worldly to the godly. The worldly mindset measures people by output, but the godly one sees people through love and identity. Focus on Jesus, not on how many points another family’s child scored or which famous school he got into. People matter more than tasks: don’t lose your child’s heart for the sake of grades.
q: Who is God? — He led his people out of slavery with a mighty hand, and used the Sabbath to remind them they were free. What does he want to lead your family out of?
Who am I? — On my child’s schedule, am I more like Moses leading him out of Egypt, or Pharaoh constantly demanding bricks?
How should I respond? — Which item in my child’s schedule did I add because of anxiety or comparison?
lessons.jesus: Jesus healed people on the Sabbath, and the religious leaders accused him of breaking the rules. He asked, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good or to do harm? To save a life or to kill?” Jesus brought the Sabbath back to God’s intention: to release people, heal people and restore people. He came to lead us out of every kind of bondage into real freedom.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for leading me out of sin and bondage and making me free. I admit that I often treat my children the way Pharaoh did, demanding more bricks through grades, talents and comparison. Shine your light on me, so that I see my child’s weariness, and give me courage to lift unnecessary burdens from him and lead him into your rest. Amen.
acts: Write down your child’s week and mark it in different colors: necessary, enjoyed, and added because of my anxiety
Today ask your child, “Which day of the week is the most tiring? Which activity takes the most strength out of you?”
Pray about one item in your child’s schedule, and ask God for wisdom whether to reduce it
lessons.noon: “You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt” — Lord, remind me today that my child and I are free people you have brought out.

fam.key: God has made us free, so we can rest.

lamb.do: Plan one fewer outing today and leave a stretch of empty time. Let your child crawl and play freely at home, with parents beside him, not rushing to teach him anything.
lamb.say: Slowly now, no hurry, God is with us.

sprout.story: Long ago the Israelites were slaves in Egypt. The wicked king Pharaoh made them make lots and lots of bricks every day, with no day off, and if they didn’t finish they were beaten. God felt so sorry for them and sent Moses to lead them out of Egypt. From then on, God said, “You are free now, and every seven days you shall rest one day!” The Israelites were so happy, because only free people can rest.
sprout.ask: Have you ever felt very tired and wanted to rest?
sprout.do: Play “Pharaoh and Moses”. One person is Pharaoh and shouts “Make bricks, quick!” and everyone pretends to carry bricks. Another is Moses and shouts “God says rest!” and everyone lies down to rest.

soldier.story: When the Israelites were slaves in Egypt, Pharaoh made them make bricks every day. Later he would not even give them straw, yet not one brick fewer was allowed. Slaves had no day of rest, because in Pharaoh’s eyes they were only tools for making bricks. After God led them out of Egypt, he gave them the Sabbath to remind them, “You are no longer slaves. You are my people!” Sometimes the homework, tutoring and competitions at school pile up so much that it is hard to breathe, as if we were back in Egypt. But God says your worth is not in how many bricks you make.
ask: Which day of the week is the most tiring for you? Why?
Do you think your worth comes from good grades, or from God loving you?
soldier.do: Write down all your activities for the week, circle the one you like most and the one that tires you most, and talk about them with Mom and Dad.

youth.talk: I want to ask you a question that may feel a bit awkward: do you ever feel that in our eyes you are just a report card? Recently I read about Pharaoh not giving straw yet demanding the same number of bricks, and it made me uneasy, because I seem to have been demanding “bricks” from you too: higher marks, better performance. I want to hear how you really feel. I won’t be angry.
ask: Which part of your current schedule makes you feel most like a machine?
If you could take one thing away, what would it be? Why?
youth.do: Parents and child go through his weekly schedule together and honestly discuss what each item means. Parents admit the parts they added out of anxiety, and together decide whether to adjust.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for leading us out of Egypt and making us free. We are not brick-making machines. We are your beloved children. Please let us rest well. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: The Sabbath Was Made for Man
lessons.theme: I believe: rest is trust, and stopping does not mean losing out

v: He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”
For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” You refused,
