lessons.still: Take a deep breath and say slowly, “You will be saved in returning and rest.” Breathe in again and say, “Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” Repeat three times, and let these two sentences be your breathing now.
teach: The Pharisees turned the Sabbath into a heap of rules, and even blamed the disciples for plucking ears of grain when they were hungry. Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” Rest is not another achievement to reach, nor a rule that makes us feel guilty, but a gift God gives people. The Lord is Jesus, not rules, and not our anxiety.

Isaiah says, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” Then comes: “You refused.” Israel refused to rest because they wanted to rely on Egypt’s horses and their own strategies. Many parents refuse to stop for the same reason: fear. Fear that the children will fall behind, that income will fall, that others will get ahead. Rest takes faith. It asks: do you really believe God will provide?

In the wilderness God told the people to gather two days’ manna on the sixth day, so they need not go out on the seventh. God proved by real provision: when you stop, I still feed you. Xiulan, a grandmother in Taipei who raises her two grandsons alone, says, “I used to think taking them to church on Sundays and letting them nap was a waste. Later I found that rested children finish Monday’s homework faster.” Today, write your “I believe”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the human viewpoint to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal. The human viewpoint says: stop and you fall behind. God’s viewpoint says: you will be saved in returning and rest, and your strength will be in quietness and in confidence. Conviction is turning God’s viewpoint into your own declaration, and letting Jesus be Lord of the Sabbath and Lord of our family’s timetable.
q: Who is God? — Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, and he made it for people. Do you believe he did it out of love?
Who am I? — What is the biggest fear behind my refusal to stop?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe stopping …; I believe God will …
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” He is not adding one more rule to our burden but inviting us to hand the heavy load to him, and to share with him one light yoke.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are Lord of the Sabbath. I believe you made rest for our sake, not to bind us. I admit that I refuse to stop because I am afraid and because I want to rely on myself. Today I declare: I believe that I will be saved in returning and rest, and my strength is in quietness and in confidence; I believe you will provide for our family’s needs. Help our whole family to enter your rest without fear. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations, such as: “I believe stopping will not make my child lose out, but will strengthen him.” “I believe God will provide for our family’s needs.”
Write down the one thing you are most afraid of losing if you stop, pray about it, and hand it to God
Tell your child, “Our family rests, not because we are lazy, but because we trust God.”
lessons.noon: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” — Lord, right now I return to your rest and find strength in you.

fam.key: We rest because we trust God.

lamb.do: While your child naps, put down your phone too. Sit quietly beside him for a while, or nap together, so your body and heart rest together.
lamb.say: Sleep in peace, God will take care of us.

sprout.story: When the Israelites were in the wilderness, every morning God sent good manna from heaven. God said, “On the sixth day gather two days’ worth, and on the seventh you needn’t gather any. Rest well.” Some people didn’t believe it and still went out to gather on the seventh day, and found nothing at all! Those who trusted God stayed home and rested, because they knew God had already prepared it.
sprout.ask: Do you think God will take care of our family? How does he take care of us?
sprout.do: Prepare two snacks, eat one today and keep one for tomorrow, and say, “God provides, so we can rest without worry!”

soldier.story: One Sabbath the disciples were hungry and picked some heads of grain to eat. The Pharisees said, “It is not allowed to work on the Sabbath. You broke the rule!” Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” This means God gave the Sabbath to help people, not to put pressure on them. In the wilderness God also used manna to tell Israel that on the seventh day they need not go out to gather, because God had already prepared it. To rest is to trust that God will take care of us.
ask: What difference do you think there is between resting and being lazy?
Have you ever been too afraid of running out of time to dare to rest?
soldier.do: Write an “I believe card”: “I believe God will take care of me, so I can rest.” Keep it on your desk, and read it this week when exams or homework pile up.

youth.talk: I have noticed that I don’t dare stop because I am afraid: afraid your grades will drop, afraid our family will lose out to others, afraid the work won’t get done. I read Isaiah saying, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” Then it says, “You refused.” I think “You refused” describes me. I want to learn to trust God. What about you? Do you ever feel that you can’t stop?
ask: In your school or among your friends, how is “rest” seen?
Have you ever rested and then done better afterward?
youth.do: Parents and child each write an “I believe” sentence, swap and read them, and pray for each other. When pressure comes this week, remind one another.

fam.pray: Jesus, thank you that you are Lord of the Sabbath. We trust you to take care of our family, so we can rest in peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Call the Sabbath a Delight
lessons.theme: Start today: designing our family’s Sabbath

v: “If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight, and the holy of the LORD honorable, and honor it, not doing your own ways, nor finding your own pleasure, nor speaking your own words,

then you will delight yourself in the LORD, and I will make you to ride on the high places of the earth, and I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father;” for the LORD’s mouth has spoken it.

lessons.still: Picture your family’s happiest day: where is it? What are you doing? Who is laughing? Bring this picture to the Lord and ask him, “Lord, could our family’s Sabbath be like this?”
teach: Isaiah says, “If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath … and call the Sabbath a delight, and the holy of the LORD honorable … then you will delight yourself in the LORD.” The Sabbath is not a boring day but “a delight”. Turning away your foot means stepping off the track of ordinary days. Not doing your own ways or finding your own pleasure means turning the focus from yourself to God and your family. The purpose of the Sabbath is to delight in the LORD.

The Lin family in Kuala Lumpur has four children and arranges its Sabbath with four words: stop, worship, play and connect. Stop: the night before, finish homework and housework, and begin with an opening ritual of lighting a candle and giving a blessing. Worship: go to church on Sunday and chat afterward about what you heard. Play: go outdoors, play board games and nap together. Connect: visit elders, invite friends for a meal, or phone relatives far away. In the evening, an ending ritual: each person says one thing they enjoyed most today.

You can also set a few “nots”: no homework or office work, no tutoring, no over-full schedule, and little screen time. If a parent works shifts or Sunday, choose another day, or start with half a day. A Sabbath doesn’t need to be perfect. It only needs to begin. What children will remember when they grow up is not which place they came in an exam on a certain day, but the smiles of parents who put everything down once a week to be with them.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice turns conviction into daily living. Don’t wait until you are not busy to rest, because that day will never come. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the Sabbath first brings the parents’ lives back before God, then repairs family relationships, and only then comes the week’s work. This is building what belongs to God at home.
q: Who is God? — He promises that if we call the Sabbath a delight, we will “delight yourself in the LORD”. Have you imagined God happily spending a day with your family?
Who am I? — Among stop, worship, play and connect, which is hardest for me?
How should I respond? — This week, plan a family Sabbath (or half a day), and write down the opening ritual, the content and the ending ritual.
lessons.jesus: When the disciples were so busy they had no time even to eat, Jesus said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” He took the initiative to invite his weary disciples to rest, and the invitation was to go “with me”. True rest is not only a vacation but being with Jesus.
lessons.pray: Lord, you invite us to call the Sabbath a delight. I admit our family often makes rest days busier than ordinary days, or stays anxious on them. Today I will begin to design our family’s Sabbath. Help us to stop, worship you, play together and connect with one another, so that on this day our children delight in you. Amen.
acts: Write a plan for “Our Family’s Sabbath” together: opening ritual, stop, worship, play, connect, ending ritual
Choose a specific opening ritual, such as lighting a candle the night before, praying together and parents blessing the children
List three things you will “not do” on the Sabbath, stick them on the fridge, and keep them yourselves as parents first
lessons.noon: “call the Sabbath a delight, and the holy of the LORD honorable” — Lord, teach our family to delight in you.

fam.key: Sabbath: stop, worship, play, connect.

lamb.do: On the family Sabbath, take your child outdoors to feel the sun, touch the grass and leaves, while Mom and Dad put down their phones and explore with him.
lamb.say: Today is a happy day. We play together and thank God together.

sprout.story: On rest days, Squirrel’s family does four things. Stop: Daddy Squirrel stops carrying acorns. Worship: everyone sings together to thank God. Play: they play hide-and-seek in the tree and roll about on the grass. Connect: they visit Grandma Squirrel, who lives under the big tree. In the evening Little Squirrel says, “I like rest days best, because everyone is together!”
sprout.ask: If our family’s rest day could have one fun thing, what would you like it to be?
sprout.do: Write “stop, worship, play, connect” on four sheets of paper, and let the child draw one thing he wants to do on each. Stick them on the wall as our family’s Sabbath plan.

soldier.story: The prophet Isaiah said the Sabbath should be “a delight”, not boring. One family arranges its Sabbath with four words: stop, worship, play and connect. The night before they finish homework and housework and light a candle to begin. The next day they go to church to worship God. In the afternoon they go hiking and play board games. In the evening they phone Grandpa and Grandma, who live in another city. Before bed each person shares one thing that made them happiest today. The children say it is the day of the week they look forward to most, better than a vacation.
ask: Which of “stop, worship, play, connect” does our family’s Sabbath most need to add?
What activity would you like to plan for the “play” part of the Sabbath?
soldier.do: Be in charge of designing the “play” for this week’s Sabbath: think of a game or activity everyone can join, and prepare it.

youth.talk: We would like to try having a real Sabbath in our home, not just another day with a to-do list. Here is my idea: the night before, put away homework and work; the next day go to church, share a good meal, and in the afternoon do something the whole family likes. I know you may have your own plans or want to go out with friends, so I’d like to design it with you rather than decide on my own.
ask: What should a “delightful” Sabbath include, and what should it not include?
Which part would you like to take charge of arranging?
youth.do: Ask your child to lead in designing the afternoon activity of one family Sabbath. Parents join in and put their phones down the whole time.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us a happy Sabbath. Please help us rest together, worship together, play together and love others together. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Give Diligence to Enter That Rest
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: let rest become a family habit

v: There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.
Let’s therefore give diligence to enter into that rest, lest anyone fall after the same example of disobedience.
“Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.”

lessons.still: Look back on this week. Was there a moment when you truly stopped? How did it feel? And was there a moment when you wanted to stop but couldn’t? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, without blame, simply seeing.
teach: Hebrews says, “There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his. Let’s therefore give diligence to enter into that rest.” That sounds like a contradiction: rest needs diligence? Yes, because in a world that cannot stop, stopping takes intention, faith and perseverance.

The psalm says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” The deepest meaning of rest is not sleeping well or having a vacation, but coming to know again, as we stop, that God is God. Mrs. Zhou in Auckland is a nurse who often works shifts and cannot always rest on Sundays. She and her children agreed that every Tuesday evening is “our family’s rest time”: cook a simple meal, read a passage together, play a game. She says, “The day is different, but the heart is the same.”

This week we learned that rest is God’s design, that we shouldn’t send our children back to Egypt, that rest is trust, and that we can design a Sabbath with stop, worship, play and connect. Today, review honestly: did our family truly rest this week? What was hardest to put down: parents’ phones, children’s homework, or anxiety in the heart? What shall we adjust next week? Perhaps fix the opening ritual, remove one tutoring class, or begin with half a day. Rest is a lifelong practice, and today is only the beginning.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition: the Sabbath is a weekly review and renewal. A proud parent thinks they do not need rest. A humble parent admits that they are limited. Focus on Jesus, not on your own schedule. Stop in him, and you will see the next step clearly.
q: Who is God? — He says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” This week, in rest, what new thing did you come to know about God?
Who am I? — How much of our family’s rest did we manage this week? What was the biggest obstacle?
How should I respond? — What shall we keep of next week’s family Sabbath, and what shall we adjust?
lessons.jesus: Joshua led Israel into Canaan, but did not lead them into true rest. Hebrews tells us that true rest is found in Jesus. He is our high priest who sympathizes with our weakness. When we fail again and again, he doesn’t look on in disappointment but invites us once more to enter his rest.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us this week. Sometimes we stopped, and sometimes we were still pulled along by busyness. Forgive my unbelief, and help me to give diligence to enter your rest. In each stopping, let our family come to know more that you are God and experience your presence more. Amen.
acts: Talk for ten minutes with your spouse: did our family rest this week? What did we enjoy most? What was the biggest obstacle? How will we adjust next week?
Ask your child, “When we were resting this week, did Dad and Mom become more like Jesus? What did you like best?” Just listen, without defending yourself
Write down one adjustment for next week’s Sabbath, and put that day in the whole family’s calendar
lessons.noon: “Be still, and know that I am God.” — Lord, right now I stop, and I know that you are God.

fam.key: When we stop, we know God is God.

lamb.do: Think back over this week and choose the moment your child was most relaxed and happiest (for example, a walk, a bath, lying down to music). Repeat that moment on the Sabbath each week.
lamb.say: We stop, and God is so very near.

sprout.story: Little Tortoise and Little Rabbit had a race. Little Rabbit ran and ran until he collapsed from tiredness. Little Tortoise walked slowly, stopping every little while to take a drink, look at the flowers and thank God. In the end Little Tortoise reached the finish line happily. Little Rabbit said, “So running without stopping isn’t always faster.” God says that when we stop and rest, we come to know that God is taking care of us.
sprout.ask: This week when our family rested, what did you like doing best?
sprout.do: Play the “Stop for a Moment” game: everyone walks around the house, and when someone shouts “Stop!” everyone halts and says, “God is God!”

soldier.story: Hebrews says we should “give diligence” to enter into rest. Does rest need effort? Yes! Because our world rarely stops: phones keep ringing, homework keeps coming, competitions keep happening. To stop takes determination. One nurse mom has to work shifts and can’t rest every Sunday, so she and her children agreed that Tuesday evening is their family’s rest time, when they cook together, read the Bible and play games. The day is different, but the heart of stopping to be with God is the same.
ask: Which part of our family Sabbath this week do you think was best? Which was hardest?
What would you like to add next week to make the Sabbath better?
soldier.do: A five-minute family meeting: each person names “the thing I enjoyed most about this week’s rest” and “one thing to improve about next week’s rest”, with parents going first.

youth.talk: This week we tried to rest, and honestly I didn’t do very well myself. I said I wouldn’t look at work messages, but I peeked a few times. I want to admit that first. Hebrews says to give diligence to enter that rest, and I found that stopping really takes effort and needs us to help each other. I’d like to hear what you thought of this week’s rest, and whether anything felt forced.
ask: This week’s rest time, did it feel like real rest, or like another family activity?
What would need to change to make the Sabbath a day you look forward to as well?
youth.do: Parents first admit one failure in resting, then ask the child to suggest one change, and the whole family tries it next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us rest together this week. Please help us remember every week to stop and know that you are God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

25.memT: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

mem.t: ‘Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.

sat.d: Go together to a river or park and gather some smooth stones (or cut stone shapes from cardboard). Back home, look back over these five weeks: the little rituals of morning and evening, the table, the bedtime blessing, the Sabbath, family worship. Let each person choose one thing “God has done in our family” and write or draw it on a stone with colored pens. In the evening, hold a family worship time: sing a song the children choose, read Joshua 4:6–7, let everyone hold their stone and say one thank-you, and finally place the stones in a glass jar and set it in the living room as our family’s memorial.

sun: Of this unit’s practices (morning and evening rhythms, the table, the bedtime blessing, the Sabbath, family worship), which one is most likely to last in your home? Why?
In your family worship, what draws your children in most? What bores them most?
Which family could you invite to join one of your family worship times, or with whom could you share how your family worships?

lessons.title: Magnify the LORD with Me
lessons.theme: Worship is something the whole family does together

v: I will bless the LORD at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.
My soul shall boast in the LORD. The humble shall hear of it and be glad.
Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.
One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.

lessons.still: Quietly say one short word of praise to the Lord: “Lord, you are good.” Say it again, more slowly. Let praise rise in your own heart first, and only then bring it into the midst of your family.
teach: Psalm 34 was written by David while he was on the run. He had just escaped the king of Gath by pretending to be mad. His situation was humiliating, yet he said, “I will bless the LORD at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.” Then he invited the people around him: “Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.” Worship begins in one person’s heart, but it does not stay there. It becomes the shared voice of a group. And a family is the smallest group of all.

Psalm 145 says, “One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.” Worship is handed down from one generation to the next. Children do not learn to worship only in Sunday school. They learn it at home, watching how their parents praise God, how they keep giving thanks in hard times, how they cheer at what God has done. A parent’s praise is the first soundtrack of a child’s faith. Children may not remember every lesson we taught, but they will remember Dad humming along to a song in the car, or Mom giving thanks to God beside a hospital bed.

Family worship can be very simple. Remember it in four words: sing, read, share, pray. Sing a song, read a short passage, share one thing God has done or one thing you are thankful for, and close in prayer. The mornings, evenings, mealtimes and bedtimes are already little altars; a weekly family worship of fifteen to twenty minutes is like the main course of the week. The Cai family in Hsinchu worships every Friday evening, and their children call it “Family Friday.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. The center of family worship is not the parents’ teaching, nor the children’s performance, but lifting up God’s name together. When the whole family turns its eyes toward Jesus at once, friction between us shrinks, because we are all looking at the same person.
q: Who is God? — He is worthy to be blessed “at all times,” even while David was running for his life. For which of his works will you praise him today?
Who am I? — In my home, is worship one parent’s job, the church’s job, or something the whole family does together?
How should I respond? — Which evening this week could our family set aside for a “sing, read, share, pray” time of worship?
lessons.jesus: At the end of the Last Supper, the Scripture says, “When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” On the heaviest night of his life, Jesus led his disciples in singing praise and then walked toward the cross. He is the one who leads our worship, and the one our whole family lifts up together.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are worthy to be blessed at all times. I confess that I often leave worship at church, and at home there is only busyness and discipline. Let your praise always be in my mouth, and let our whole family exalt your name together. Help our generation to tell the next generation of your works. Amen.
acts: Choose a fixed evening each week with your spouse for family worship, and write it in your calendar
When you are alone today, praise God with a song or a sentence, so that you become a worshiper first
At dinner, ask your children: “If our family sang one song together, which would you choose?”
lessons.noon: “Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.” — Lord, right now I lift you high in my heart. Please help my family lift you high together.

fam.key: We praise God together as a family.

lamb.do: Hold your baby and sway gently as you sing a simple song of praise, holding his little hands to clap along.
lamb.say: Let’s sing to God together. God is so happy.

sprout.story: When David was a little boy, he was a shepherd. While he looked after the lambs, he played his harp and sang to God. Later David faced many dangers. Bad men chased him and he hid in a cave, but he still sang, “I will praise God always! Come, everyone, let’s praise God together!” His friends in the cave heard him and began to sing too. Praising God is a happy thing we can all do together.
sprout.ask: What is your favorite song to sing to God?
sprout.do: Sing your child’s favorite song together, adding actions: clap, stamp, spin around. When the song ends, shout together: “God is so great!”

soldier.story: When David was running away, enemies caught him, and he escaped only by pretending to be mad in front of the king. Many people would have done nothing but complain. But David wrote a psalm that says, “I will bless the LORD at all times,” and he invited the people around him: “Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.” We don’t praise because everything is going well; we praise because God is always good. When a soccer team scores, the whole team cheers together. Family worship is the whole family cheering for God together.
ask: What do you think “lifting up God’s name together” means?
Is it easy or hard to praise God when you are sad? Why?
soldier.do: This week, be the “song captain”: choose a song and lead everyone in singing it at family worship. You can add an instrument or actions.

youth.talk: It seems we have always left worship to the church, and at home we hardly ever sing or read the Bible together. Maybe it feels awkward, or maybe we adults just aren’t used to it. I read that even while David was on the run, he invited the people around him to “exalt his name together.” I’d like to try one evening a week when we worship as a family. It wouldn’t be long, and I’d really like your help in designing it.
ask: What would make family worship most awkward or boring for you?
If you were planning a family worship time, what would you do?
youth.do: Invite your child to take charge of one part of the first family worship, such as choosing a song, playing the music or sharing a short thought, and as parents give your full support.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, you are so great, and you love us so much! We praise you together as a family, and we lift up your name together. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: You Have Perfected Praise
lessons.theme: Do I welcome my children’s voices, or tell them to be quiet?

v: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children who were crying in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the son of David!” they were indignant,
and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Did you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies, you have perfected praise’?”

lessons.still: Imagine your child singing and dancing in front of you, praising God in a gloriously messy way. What is your very first reaction? A smile, or a wish to tell him to be quiet? Ask the Holy Spirit to sit with you and show you that reaction.
teach: After Jesus cleansed the temple, the blind and the lame came to him, and he healed them. Children were shouting in the temple, “Hosanna to the son of David!” But the chief priests and scribes were “indignant.” They thought the children were too noisy, out of order, not reverent enough. Jesus answered, “Did you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies, you have perfected praise’?” What sounded like noise to the religious leaders was perfected praise to Jesus.

Many family worship times turn dull because parents unknowingly become the chief priests: sit properly, be quiet, listen to the end, memorize it all. Family worship becomes one more lesson, with Mom and Dad talking, the children listening, and whoever fidgets being corrected. The Guo family in Penang has five children, and the mother says, “Every family worship used to end with someone crying and someone being scolded. Then I noticed that the noisiest moments were often when the children were most engaged.”

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: what kind of parent am I? Am I a chief priest who wants the children quiet and tidy, or like Jesus, who welcomes children praising in their own way? A child’s praise may be off-key, may bounce around, may come with very strange questions, but it is his real worship. This is not to say family worship needs no order, only that children’s voices need a place in it. A good conductor does not silence every instrument; he lets each one sound at the right moment.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A self-ruled parent thinks worship has to be done my way; a self-emptied parent is willing to let God be praised through the children’s way. Pride grabs control; humility makes room. Let people be people and God be God. Let children be children, and let them draw near to God in a child’s way.
q: Who is God? — Jesus delights in the praise that comes from the mouths of children and nursing babies. What does this show you about how he sees your children?
Who am I? — In family worship, or at church, am I more like the indignant chief priests or like Jesus, who welcomed the children?
How should I respond? — How can I adjust our family worship so that the children’s voices have more room?
lessons.jesus: In the temple, Jesus healed the blind and the lame while welcoming the children’s praise. He did not scold the children for disturbing the solemn atmosphere; instead he spoke up for them. He shows us that worship in the kingdom can have children’s voices, shouts of joy, and imperfection.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for delighting in children’s praise. I confess that I am often like the chief priests, finding my children too noisy or not reverent enough, and turning family worship into my own pulpit. Forgive me. Teach me to welcome my children as they draw near to you in their own way, and help me to become like a child again and praise you simply. Amen.
acts: Think back to your last family worship or Bible reading and count: how much time did the parents speak, and how much did the children?
Today, let your child choose a song and sing it his own way, while the adults follow his actions
Tell your child: “God loves to hear you praise him, and Mom/Dad loves it too.”
lessons.noon: “Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies, you have perfected praise.” — Lord, help me to hear my children’s praise, and help me to praise you like a child.

fam.key: God loves children’s praise best.

lamb.do: Give your baby a bell, a little drum, or a spoon to tap on a bowl. Play a song and let him tap and shake as he likes, while you laugh and clap along.
lamb.say: You’re praising God! He hears you, and he loves it!

sprout.story: When Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a little donkey, lots of children ran around the temple shouting, “Hosanna! Hosanna!” Some grown-ups said angrily, “These children are too noisy!” But Jesus smiled and said, “When children praise God, it is the most beautiful praise of all!” When the children heard that, they shouted even louder.
sprout.ask: How would you like to praise Jesus? Sing, dance, or shout out loud?
sprout.do: Play a “Hosanna parade” as a family: use cushions or towels as palm branches, march around the house and shout together, “Hosanna! Jesus is King!”

soldier.story: When Jesus came into the temple, the children there shouted, “Hosanna to the son of David!” The chief priests and scribes were angry. They thought the children were too noisy and not reverent enough. But Jesus said that God receives perfect praise from the mouths of children. In Jesus’ eyes, your praise matters, and you don’t have to wait until you are grown up for it to count. It is like when Mom and Dad receive a card you drew. Even if the drawing is wobbly, they keep it carefully, because you made it with your heart.
ask: In family worship, do you feel your voice is valued?
If you could change one thing to make family worship more fun, what would it be?
soldier.do: Design a “new way to praise”: make up actions, tap out a rhythm, or draw a picture of praise, and lead the whole family in it at the next family worship.

youth.talk: I’ve noticed that our family Bible readings in the past were mostly me talking and you listening, and if you stopped paying attention I got upset. I read how Jesus welcomed the children’s shouts in the temple while it was the religious leaders who were angry, and I realized that sometimes I am like those leaders. I want our worship to be not my pulpit but a place where we draw near to God together.
ask: Which part of our past family Bible readings or prayers made you least want to join in?
How would you like to praise God? Through music, writing, drawing, or something else?
youth.do: As parents, apologize to your child for turning family worship into preaching in the past, and invite him to share a song or piece of music he truly loves, then listen and talk about it together.

fam.pray: Jesus, thank you for loving to hear children’s praise. Each one of us, big or small, will praise you with our own voice. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: In Spirit and Truth
lessons.theme: I believe: God is looking for our family to worship him

v: But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and imagine the Father searching for those who will worship him, and his gaze resting on your living room. Say to him, “Father, we are here, and we want to worship you.”
teach: The Samaritan woman asked Jesus whether people should worship on this mountain or in Jerusalem. Jesus said, “The hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.” Worship is no longer tied to one place or one form; what matters is spirit and truth. These words make every home a place of worship: the living room, the dining table, the bedside, even the car.

Spirit means a heart moved by the Holy Spirit, not merely outward ritual. Truth means being our real selves, not putting on a spiritual performance. What family worship fears most is not imperfection but unreality. A father can say, “This week I feel discouraged, but I still want to praise God.” A mother can say, “I lost my temper with you today, and I want to confess it to God first.” Real parents raise real children.

The He family in Toronto is bilingual: the parents speak Chinese and the children are used to English. They once argued over which language to worship in. In the end they decided to sing the English songs the children like, read the Bible in both languages side by side, and let everyone pray in the language they are most at ease with. Father He said, “God understands every language. What he wants is our hearts.” Today, write down your own “I believe”: I believe God is looking for our family. I believe what he wants is spirit and truth, not a perfect format.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, not your head, relying on yourself. Head-centered family worship cares whether the order is right, whether there is enough time, whether the children behave. Heart-centered worship cares whether we meet God. Conviction means letting go of perfectionism and believing that the Father is searching for us and welcomes our imperfect family.
q: Who is God? — Scripture says, “the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.” He goes looking for worshipers. Do you believe he is looking for your family too?
Who am I? — In family worship, do I care more about a perfect form or about spirit and truth?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: about our family’s worship, I believe…
lessons.jesus: Jesus took the initiative to go to Samaria and wait at a well for a woman people looked down on. He did not wait for her to become good before accepting her. He accepted her first, let her see her real self, and then led her to know true worship. He walks into our homes in the same way, meeting us before we are ready.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I believe you are looking for those who will worship you, and for our family too. I confess that I have often thought family worship had to be perfect and very spiritual to count, so I never began, or did it reluctantly. Today I declare that what you want is spirit and truth. Let our family worship you honestly before you. Amen.
acts: Write down three “I believe” statements, for example: “I believe God is looking for our family.” “I believe God wants our hearts, not a perfect order of service.”
At the next family worship, let the parents first share honestly one weakness or struggle from this week, and then praise God together
Ask your child: “In which language and in what way do you feel most at ease talking to God?”
lessons.noon: “The true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.” — Lord, right now I come to you with a true heart.

fam.key: God loves it when we worship him from the heart.

lamb.do: Close your eyes in front of your baby and pray in very simple, honest words, such as “Lord, I’m so tired today, but I love you.” Let your child see his parents talking to God for real.
lamb.say: We talk to God from our hearts, and he hears us.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu sang the wrong words during family worship. She felt shy and hid behind the sofa. Daddy crouched down and said, “Xiaoyu, God doesn’t mind whether you sing well. He cares whether you mean it.” Xiaoyu asked, “What does ‘mean it’ mean?” Daddy said, “It means you really love God in your heart and want to talk to him.” Xiaoyu thought for a moment, then came out from behind the sofa and said, “Then I really love God!” And she happily started singing again.
sprout.ask: What do you think it means to praise God from your heart?
sprout.do: Let everyone say, in their own words, one sentence about why they love God. It doesn’t have to be long, only true.

soldier.story: A Samaritan woman met Jesus at a well. She asked, “On which mountain should we worship God?” Jesus said that what matters is not where we worship, but worshiping in spirit and truth, because the Father is looking for people who worship him that way. Spirit means really wanting to be close to God in your heart, and truth means not pretending. Good friends don’t need to act in front of each other. We can tell God the truth: when we are happy, sad or angry, we can tell him everything.
ask: Are there times when you feel you have to “pretend” while worshiping God?
If you could worship God anywhere, where would you most like to be?
soldier.do: This week choose a “new place to worship”: the balcony, the car, a park bench, or your own room. Sing a song and say a prayer together there as a family.

youth.talk: I know that worship at church or at home can sometimes feel like we have to “look very spiritual.” Honestly, I often drift off during worship too and just go through the motions. Jesus said the Father is looking for those who worship in spirit and truth. That gives us great freedom: we can be real and don’t need to pretend. I want our family’s worship to be real, including real doubts and questions.
ask: What do you think “worshiping honestly” means? If you have doubts about faith, can you say them at home?
When do you feel you are closest to God in the most real way?
youth.do: Have a one-to-one chat between parent and child: each shares one real struggle or question about faith, with no rush to give answers, and finish with a short prayer together.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for looking for us. We don’t have to pretend. We want to love you and praise you from our hearts. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Psalms, Hymns, and Spiritual Songs
lessons.theme: Start today: a family worship that isn’t boring

v: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.
Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

lessons.still: Imagine your family gathered in the living room this evening, someone with an instrument, someone hugging a cushion. Invite the Lord to sit down in that picture, and say to him, “Lord, tonight’s worship is prepared for you.”
teach: Paul says, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.” Notice the words “one another.” Family worship is not parents speaking in one direction; the whole family teaches and encourages each other. “All wisdom” reminds us that methods can be varied and creative, as long as the center is the word of Christ.

A twenty-minute family worship can go like this. One, sing (five minutes): children take turns choosing songs, with instruments or actions if you like. Two, read (five minutes): read a short Bible story, and let the children act it out or draw it, or ask just one question: “What does this passage show us about God?” Three, share (five minutes): each person shares one thing they are thankful for this week, or one way God helped. Four, pray (five minutes): use a “prayer wheel.” Draw sections on a paper plate and write family, friends, school, church, missionaries, our country; wherever the pointer lands, pray for that. Finally, the parents lay hands on the children and bless them.

Give every age a role: little ones shake a bell and choose songs; primary-school children read and spin the wheel; teenagers lead the singing and host the sharing; grandparents share their testimonies. The Teng family in Singapore has three generations under one roof. Grandma tells the story of how she came to faith, and the grandson plays the music. Mrs. Teng says, “Before, I was carrying worship alone. Now we all do it together.” The key to avoiding boredom is to let everyone take part and add a little variety each time.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Family worship is where the whole family’s life is renewed together, and where relationships are joined. The spirit of 920 takes root here: every family member is my “2,” teaching and admonishing one another in worship and bearing the fruit of the Spirit.
q: Who is God? — He delights when we sing to him “with grace in your heart.” When did you last sing to him with a grace-filled heart?
Who am I? — In our family worship, who does most of the talking? Does everyone have a role?
How should I respond? — Tonight or this week, hold a “sing, read, share, pray” family worship and give every family member a role.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was twelve, he sat in the temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions. When his parents found him, he said, “Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” The boy Jesus was eager for his Father’s things and learned through conversation and questions. This reminds us that when children ask questions and take part in worship, it is part of their spiritual growth.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for letting your word dwell in our hearts richly. Today I want to begin a worship time that the whole family takes part in, not just me talking, but all of us teaching one another and singing to you together. Give me wisdom and creativity so that each child finds his place, and let our worship be full of joy and grace. Amen.
acts: Make a “prayer wheel”: divide a paper plate into six sections labeled family, friends, school, church, missionaries, our country, and add a pointer that can spin
Plan this week’s family worship and give each family member a role: choosing songs, reading, hosting the sharing, spinning the wheel, giving the blessing
When worship ends, ask each child: “Which part did you like best today?”
lessons.noon: “Teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.” — Lord, tonight fill the worship of our family.

fam.key: Sing, read, share, pray, all together.

lamb.do: Include your baby in the singing time of family worship. Give him a bell or a little drum to tap, and during prayer let him sit on your lap while you hold his hand.
lamb.say: We worship God together as a family, and you are part of us.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu’s family has a “family worship party” every Friday evening. Her big brother plays the ukulele, her little sister shakes the maracas, Daddy reads a Bible story, and Mommy leads the sharing. The most fun is the “prayer wheel.” Xiaoyu spins it, the pointer stops on “Grandma,” and everyone prays for Grandma. Xiaoyu says, “I love our family worship party best!”
sprout.ask: If our family had a worship party, what would you like to do?
sprout.do: Make a “prayer wheel” together: draw sections on a paper plate and let your child draw the faces of family members. Spin it, and pray for whoever the pointer lands on.

soldier.story: Paul wrote to the church in Colossae and said to teach and admonish one another with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. He said “one another,” so everyone can teach others and be taught by others. A family worship time is like a band: someone drums, someone plays the piano, someone sings. Everyone has a different part, and together it sounds good. If only one person is on stage and everyone else is in the audience, that isn’t a band; it’s a performance.
ask: In our family worship band, what part would you like to play?
What is the most fun way to read a Bible story? Acting it out, drawing it, or asking questions?
soldier.do: Be in charge of the “read” part of this week’s family worship: choose a Bible story and lead the family in reading it by acting or drawing.

youth.talk: I’d like to ask you for a favor. We are going to have a family worship time, and I don’t want it to feel like a class. You know today’s music better than I do, and you know better what won’t feel awkward. Paul says to “teach one another,” which means it isn’t only adults teaching children; you can teach us too. I really want to hear your ideas.
ask: What do you think a good family worship should include? What should it leave out?
Which part would you like to take on? Choosing songs, hosting the sharing, or leading prayer?
youth.do: Ask your child to lead one part of this week’s family worship, for example choosing two songs and sharing why he likes them, while the parents act as students and take part wholeheartedly.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting our whole family worship you together. Help each of us to love singing praise to you, reading your word, and praying for others. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Tell the Next Generation
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: looking back at our family rhythms and family altar

v: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.
For he established a covenant in Jacob, and appointed a teaching in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children;
that the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children,
that they might set their hope in God, and not forget God’s deeds, but keep his commandments,

lessons.still: Look back over these five weeks: morning and evening, the table, the bedtime blessing, the Sabbath, family worship. Like flipping through a photo album, look at each picture slowly and ask the Holy Spirit to point out what God has done in your home.
teach: Psalm 78 says, “We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.” The purpose is “that they might set their hope in God, and not forget God’s deeds.” The ultimate aim of the family altar is not to build a perfect set of family rituals, but to help our children remember God: who he is and what he has done, so that one day they too will “arise and tell their children.”

Over these five weeks, we have found our family’s rhythm again: in the morning we declare his love, in the evening his faithfulness; the table becomes an altar; we bless the children at bedtime; one day a week the whole family rests; and we worship together. Perhaps your family managed one or two of these, perhaps you have only just begun. The Huang family in Kota Kinabalu says that in these five weeks they steadily kept just one thing, the bedtime blessing. But now, when Dad is away on a business trip, the children phone and say, “Dad, you haven’t blessed me yet!” One small thing kept up beats five big things done once.

Today, please review honestly, and adjust deliberately. Which rhythm suits our family best? Keep it, and let it become your usual way of life. Which is hardest? Make it smaller, or move it to another time. Who has not yet been invited in? A spouse, a teenager, or grandparents who live far away? Write down the one or two family rhythms you will hold on to for the next three months. Remember, faith is told from one generation to the next.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last of the eight steps for changing a mindset is multiplication. The family altar is not only for our own family’s blessing; it is to be passed to the next generation and then to influence other families. This is the “3” in 235: becoming spiritual parents to our children. Share your family’s rhythms so that one family influences another.
q: Who is God? — He has “wondrous deeds” worth telling from generation to generation. What has he done in your home these five weeks?
Who am I? — Of these five weeks of family rhythms, which one has our family truly kept? Which has been hardest?
How should I respond? — Which one or two rhythms will our family keep for the next three months? With which family will we share them?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed, “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word.” His eyes looked ahead to generation after generation of believers, and he saw us. He prays for our home, and for our children’s children too.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us through these five weeks and building new rhythms in our home. Some we have kept, and some we are still learning. Help us to keep going, not for the sake of form, but so that our children will remember you and set their hope in you. Make our family a home that tells of your deeds, from one generation to the next. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for fifteen minutes: which family rhythm has borne the most fruit in these five weeks? Which one or two will you keep for the next three months?
Ask your children: “In these weeks, have Mom and Dad become more like Jesus? Which of our new family habits do you like best?” Only listen; don’t defend yourself
Write down one “testimony of our family” and tell it to your children at the next family worship
lessons.noon: “We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.” — Lord, today I want to remember your works and tell my children about them.

fam.key: We tell the next generation what God has done.

lamb.do: Open the photos from your baby’s birth until now, point to a picture, and tell one way God has kept and helped him. Finally hold him close and say thank you to God.
lamb.say: God has looked after you since the day you were born, and we will always remember.

sprout.story: When the Israelites crossed the Jordan River, God made the water stop and everyone walked across on dry ground. Joshua told twelve men to each take a stone and pile them up by the river. He said, “Later, when your children ask, ‘What do these stones mean?’ you will tell them, ‘God helped us here!’” The stones stayed there, and the story kept being told.
sprout.ask: Do you remember something wonderful God has done in our family?
sprout.do: Find a small stone and draw a smiley face on it. Tell one way God has helped our family, and put the stone where everyone can see it at home.

soldier.story: Psalm 78 says we must not hide the wonderful things God has done; we must tell them to our children, and when they grow up they must tell their own children. It is like a relay race, with every generation passing the baton of faith to the next. In these five weeks our family tried many new habits: morning and evening prayer, table talk, bedtime blessings, the Sabbath, family worship. Some went well, and some we are still learning. The most important thing is not to do it perfectly, but to keep passing on what God has done.
ask: Of the new habits in these five weeks, which do you like best? Which do you think needs changing?
If you have your own family one day, which of our family habits would you like to keep?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person picks one family habit to keep and one thing to adjust, and then the whole family votes on the one or two rhythms to keep for the next three months.

youth.talk: We have tried many things in these five weeks, and to be honest, some felt a bit forced to me, and some I didn’t keep up myself. I want to admit that first. The psalm says to tell God’s deeds to the next generation, and I began to wonder what you will remember about our family. I hope what you remember is not that we were busy or strict, but what God truly did in our home.
ask: Of the family rhythms in these five weeks, which helped you most? Which could we drop?
What do you think is the most real thing God has done in our family?
youth.do: Ask your child to decide together with you the one or two family rhythms to keep for the next three months. Parents share one “testimony of what God did in our family,” and ask the child to write it down or record it as a family keepsake.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for everything you have done in our home these weeks. We want to remember your works and tell others. Help us to keep loving you and following you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

26.memT: ‘Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.
